docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Open-source, self-hosted SWE agents for GitLab & GitHub

Turn issues into merge requests, answer review comments, and fix failing CI — with every agent running in a sandbox you control, the network egress you define, and the LLM provider you choose.

DAIV (pronounced "dive", from dev + AI) integrates directly with GitLab and GitHub through webhooks — no new tools to adopt, no context-switching. Beyond your Git workflow, DAIV plugs into your editor over MCP and ships with an optional self-hosted dashboard to chat with the agent, start and watch runs, schedule jobs, and review what changed. You host it, you pick the model, and every task executes in an isolated sandbox whose network access you define.

docs.title: Three ways to put DAIV to work
In your git platform
docs.text:
• Issue addressing — DAIV reads a labelled issue, proposes a plan, and — once you approve — opens a merge/pull request with the implementation.
  • Pull request assistant — answers reviewer comments, applies requested changes, and repairs failing CI/CD pipelines, all inside the merge/pull request thread.
  • Slash commands and skills — invoke /plan, /code-review, /help, and your own custom skills straight from issues and merge requests.

docs.title: From your editor and pipelines
docs.text:
• MCP endpoint — connect Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex CLI over the Model Context Protocol and delegate tasks without leaving your editor.
  • Jobs API — trigger agents programmatically from CI, scripts, or other tools, then poll for the result.

docs.title: From the dashboard
docs.text:
• Sessions — a unified workspace and history: chat with the agent live, start background runs, and see every execution — webhook, API, MCP, scheduled, or manual — in one list, with retries.
  • Scheduled jobs — run agents on any cron schedule: dependency audits, code-quality scans, stale-branch cleanup, and more.
  • Orchestration — let the agent fan work out as tailored jobs, across your other repositories or as new sessions on the same one, then report the combined result.
  • Sandbox environments — define a reusable runtime once: base image, CPU/memory, network egress policy, and encrypted secrets, scoped to the repositories you choose.
  • Per-run model & effort — pick the LLM and thinking effort for each run.
  • Notifications — know the moment work finishes, in the app, by email, in Rocket.Chat or on Telegram.
  • Merge metrics — track code velocity with commit-level DAIV-vs-human attribution.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
1. You create an issue: "Add rate limiting to the API endpoints"
  2. DAIV posts a plan: Analyzes the codebase and proposes implementation steps
  3. You approve: Comment @daiv proceed
  4. DAIV implements: Creates a merge request with the code changes
  5. Reviewer asks for changes: "@daiv use Redis instead of in-memory storage"
  6. DAIV updates the code: Modifies the implementation and pushes

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
DAIV is powered by Deep Agents, a general-purpose deep-agent framework built on LangGraph with sub-agent spawning, a middleware stack, and a virtual filesystem. On top of it, DAIV adds:

  • Subagents — specialized agents for fast codebase exploration and complex multi-step tasks.
  • Sandbox — secure command execution for tests, builds, linters, and package management inside an isolated Docker container.
  • MCP tools — external integrations over the Model Context Protocol, such as Sentry for error tracking.
  • Monitoring — trace every agent execution with LangSmith to analyze performance and spot issues.
  • Scalable Workers — background workers scale horizontally by adding replicas, with a dedicated scheduler for recurring jobs.
  • LLM providers — run on OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google, or on your own OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, llama.cpp, LiteLLM) — your keys, your choice.

For the tools the agent works with and when each is on, see Agent tools.

docs.title: Agent skills
docs.text:
Skills are modular capabilities that extend DAIV's agent with specialized knowledge and workflows. Each skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file with instructions the agent follows when the skill is triggered.

DAIV ships with built-in skills. You can also write your own, for one repository or for all of them.

docs.title: How skills work
docs.text:
Skills use a progressive disclosure pattern:

  1. At startup, DAIV reads the name and description from each skill's YAML frontmatter (about 100 tokens per skill).
  2. When triggered, DAIV reads the full SKILL.md content and follows its instructions.
  3. As needed, the agent reads the supporting files bundled with the skill (scripts, templates, configs).

This keeps context usage minimal until a skill is needed.

docs.title: Directory structure
docs.text:
Skills can live in any of these directories at the repository root:

  • .agents/skills/
  • .claude/skills/
  • .cursor/skills/

DAIV scans all three. When more than one holds a skill with the same name, .agents/skills/ wins over .claude/skills/, which wins over .cursor/skills/.

Text Only
my-repository/
├── .agents/
│   └── skills/
│       └── my-custom-skill/
│           ├── SKILL.md           # Required
│           └── scripts/
│               └── helper.py      # Optional supporting files
└── src/

DAIV does not copy built-in skills into your repository, and writes nothing to .agents/skills/. It loads them from its own global skills location (/workspace/skills inside the agent), a separate source next to the per-repository directories.

docs.title: Override priority
docs.text:
DAIV resolves a skill name in this order, highest priority first:

  1. Per-repository skills, committed in the repository's .agents/skills/, .claude/skills/ or .cursor/skills/.
  2. Custom global skills, mounted from the host or uploaded in the dashboard.
  3. Built-in skills, shipped with DAIV.

A custom global skill overrides the built-in skill of the same name, and a per-repository skill overrides both. To override a built-in skill in one repository, commit a skill with the same name to that repository.

The agent's system prompt lists the global source as Global Skills, and marks the last source, .agents/skills, (higher priority).

docs.title: Skill security
docs.text:
Use skills from trusted sources only

Skills give the agent instructions and access to scripts. Use only skills you wrote or got from a source you trust.

Before you commit or upload a skill:

  • Audit every file in it.
  • Review its scripts carefully, because the agent can run any executable code in a skill.
  • Check its external references, because a skill that fetches data from external URLs adds risk.

docs.title: Create a skill
docs.text:
To add a skill to one repository, create a directory for it and commit it. You need write access to the repository.

  1. In .agents/skills/ at the repository root, create a directory named after the skill, with lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only (for example changelog).
  2. In that directory, create SKILL.md.
  3. Add the YAML frontmatter with a name that matches the directory name and a description.
  4. Below the frontmatter, write the instructions the agent follows.
  5. Optional: add supporting files next to SKILL.md, such as scripts or templates.
  6. Commit the directory to the repository.

DAIV loads the skill in runs on a branch that contains it. To have the agent walk you through these steps instead, run @daiv /skill-creator (see /skill-creator).

docs.title: SKILL.md format
docs.text:
Every skill requires a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter:

Markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: Brief description of what this skill does and when the agent should use it
---

# My Skill

## Instructions

1. First, do this
2. Then, do that
3. Finally, verify the result

Required fields:

Field Constraints Description name Max 64 chars, lowercase alphanumeric and hyphens, must match the directory name Unique identifier for the skill. This is what users type after /. description Max 1024 chars What the skill does and when to use it. The agent matches user requests against this text, so include trigger phrases.

Optional fields:

Field Description license License name or reference to a bundled license file compatibility Environment requirements (max 500 chars) metadata Arbitrary key-value pairs for additional properties allowed-tools Space-delimited list of tool names the skill recommends using

docs.title: Write a good description
docs.text:
The description field is how the agent decides whether to use your skill. Include specific trigger phrases:

YAML
# Good: includes trigger phrases the agent can match
description: >
  Diagnose and fix CI/CD pipeline failures. Use when the user mentions
  "pipeline is failing", "CI broken", "fix the build", or "debug the tests".

# Bad: too vague for the agent to match
description: Helps with CI/CD issues.

docs.title: Write specific instructions
docs.text:
Tell the agent exactly what steps to follow:

Markdown
## Instructions

1. Fetch the merge request diff using the platform tools
2. For each changed file, check for:
   - Missing error handling
   - Unvalidated inputs
   - Hardcoded credentials
3. Report findings grouped by severity (High / Medium / Low)

docs.title: Bundle supporting files
docs.text:
Skills can include helper scripts, templates and reference documents. Reference them by paths relative to the skill directory:

Text Only
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   └── validate.py
└── templates/
    └── report.md
Markdown
## Resources
- Run `scripts/validate.py` to check prerequisites
- Use `templates/report.md` as the output format

docs.title: Example: changelog skill
docs.text:
Markdown
---
name: changelog
description: >
  Update the CHANGELOG.md file when changes are made. Use when the user
  asks to "update the changelog", "add a changelog entry", or after
  completing a feature implementation.
---

# Changelog Maintenance

## Instructions

1. Read `CHANGELOG.md` from the repository root
2. Determine the change type: Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed
3. Add an entry under the `## Unreleased` section
4. Follow the existing format and style in the file
5. Keep entries concise: one line per change

## Format

Use [Common Changelog](https://common-changelog.org/) format:

```markdown
## Unreleased

### Added
- New feature description
```

docs.title: Set branch and commit conventions
docs.text:
DAIV generates the branch names and commit messages for its changes. To make it follow your conventions, describe them in the repository's context file: AGENTS.md, or the file that context_file_name names in .daiv.yml. .daiv.yml has no option for the conventions themselves.

  1. Open the context file in the repository root.
  2. Add a section for each convention you want DAIV to follow.
  3. Commit the file.

For example:

Markdown
## Branch naming
Use: pr/<issue-id>-<kebab-summary>

## Commit messages
Use: (<ISSUE-ID>) <type>: <summary>
Where <type> is one of: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, test

The angle-bracket parts belong to the convention: DAIV fills in the issue ID, type and summary for each change.

Without a convention, DAIV names branches <type>/<short-kebab-summary> and writes commit subjects in the Conventional Commits style, <type>: <short summary>, with a type of feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor or test.

docs.title: Custom global skills
docs.text:
A custom global skill is available in all repositories, unlike a per-repository skill. It has the same format as a built-in skill, a directory containing a SKILL.md file, and DAIV loads it from a directory on the host. You put skills there in one of two ways:

  • Mount a directory of skills into the containers.
  • Upload a ZIP archive in the dashboard, as an admin.

Both use the same directory, DAIV_AGENT_CUSTOM_SKILLS_PATH, once it is mounted into the app container and into every container that runs the agent, so you can use both. A mounted skill appears in runs but not on the Skills page, which lists only uploaded skills.

DAIV materializes the skills at each agent invocation, so a new skill or a new file takes effect on the next task without a container restart. DAIV does not pick up an edit to a file it has already loaded, so replace the skill by upload, or recreate the containers that run the agent after editing a mounted file. A plain restart is not enough, because the cache lives in the container's /tmp. With Docker Compose, run docker compose up -d --force-recreate worker worker-interactive. With Docker Swarm, run docker service update --force <stack>_worker and docker service update --force <stack>_worker-interactive, replacing <stack> with your stack name.

docs.title: Mount a directory of global skills
docs.text:
1. On the host, create a directory with your skills, one subdirectory per skill:

    Text Only
    custom-skills/
├── my-workflow/
│   ├── SKILL.md
│   └── scripts/
│       └── helper.py
└── team-review/
    └── SKILL.md

  2. In your docker-compose.yml or stack.yml, mount the directory at /home/daiv/data/skills into app, which receives dashboard uploads and needs it read-write, and into worker and worker-interactive, which run the agent and can mount it read-only:

    YAML
    app:
  volumes:
    - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills
worker:
  volumes:
    - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills:ro
worker-interactive:
  volumes:
    - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills:ro

  3. Recreate the three containers.

A service-level volumes: replaces the list it inherits, so keep each service's existing media-volume line (see Deployment). To mount the directory elsewhere, set DAIV_AGENT_CUSTOM_SKILLS_PATH (see Environment variables).

docs.title: Upload a global skill
docs.text:
An upload replaces a skill of the same name

If a custom skill with the same name exists, uploading replaces it for every repository. DAIV moves the old version to .trash/ under DAIV_AGENT_CUSTOM_SKILLS_PATH and removes it on the next upload or delete after 24 hours.

You need an admin account and a ZIP archive that meets the ZIP requirements.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → Skills.
  2. Select Upload skill.
  3. Under Skill zip, choose the ZIP archive.
  4. Select Upload.
  5. If DAIV shows Replace existing skill, choose the ZIP archive again and select Replace.

The skill appears under Custom skills. DAIV records which admin uploaded it.

docs.title: ZIP requirements
docs.text:
DAIV validates the archive before it stores it:

Constraint Limit Top-level directory Exactly one, named after the skill (a valid slug: lowercase alphanumeric and hyphens, max 63 chars) SKILL.md Required at <skill-name>/SKILL.md, with name (matching the directory) and description in its frontmatter Compressed size 5 MiB max Unpacked size 25 MiB max File count 200 max Path depth 8 levels max Per-file size 1 MiB max Allowed file types .md, .py, .json, .yaml, .yml, .txt, .sh, .toml, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .svg, .gif

DAIV rejects symlinks, absolute paths, .. path traversal and hidden path segments. It drops __pycache__, .pyc, .git and .gitignore entries silently.

docs.title: Manage global skills in the dashboard
docs.text:
The Skills page needs an admin account. Custom skills lists the skills uploaded in the dashboard, and Built-in skills lists the ones DAIV ships. Each card shows the skill's invocation count and, when its entry names one, its model. A custom skill whose name matches a built-in skill shadows it, and its card carries an Overrides built-in warning icon. A skill that you only mounted loads in runs but has no card or page, so it cannot be downloaded or deleted here.

Select a skill to open its page, which has four tabs:

  • SKILL.md: the skill's instructions.
  • Files: the files in the skill.
  • Models: the model the skill runs on (see Run a skill on another model).
  • Usage: the invocations over the last 30 days, and the latest runs that invoked the skill, each linking to its run in its session.

To download a custom skill's original ZIP archive, select Download zip on its card menu or its page.

docs.title: Delete a custom skill
docs.text:
Deleting removes the skill from every repository

DAIV moves the skill to a recycle bin for 24 hours before it removes it permanently. Download the ZIP archive first if you may need it. A custom skill that shadowed a built-in skill stops doing so: the built-in skill applies again.

You cannot delete a built-in skill.

  1. On the Skills page, find the skill under Custom skills.
  2. Open its card menu and select Delete.
  3. Select Delete skill.

docs.title: Run a skill on another model
docs.text:
Once the agent invokes a skill, its model calls run on the skill's model until your next message. The model comes from the skill's models.skills entry in the repository's .daiv.yml, else its entry on the Models tab or in DAIV_AGENT_SKILL_MODELS, else the skill file's metadata.model, else the run's model. Skill and subagent models gives the order and the entry format.

The Models tab changes a skill's model for every repository, built-in skills included, without copying or editing the skill file. On /code-review it also sets the model of each detector the skill ships (see Subagent model precedence). A skill that exists only in repositories, or that you only mounted, has no page: give it a model with DAIV_AGENT_SKILL_MODELS, or with a models.skills entry in each repository's .daiv.yml.

A built-in or global skill file can name its own model in metadata.model, as a model spec (provider-slug:model, as in subagents):

YAML
---
name: changelog
description: Update CHANGELOG.md for the current changes.
metadata:
  model: openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
---

DAIV ignores a repository skill's metadata.model, because the file comes from the branch the run works on, which the author of a merge request controls.

The run's thinking level carries over. The run's model serves any model call whose conversation no longer fits the skill model's context window. Once the skill model fails a call, the run's model serves that call and every later one in the run, before the run's fallback models. Switching models starts a fresh prompt cache on each side, so a cheaper skill model pays off only for skills that do substantial work.

When a configured entry names a provider that is unknown, disabled or missing its API key, the skill runs on its metadata.model, else the run's model, and DAIV logs the failure at ERROR. A metadata.model that DAIV can't use keeps the run's model, logged the same way.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools extend DAIV's agent with access to external services. You manage MCP servers from the dashboard on two pages:

  • MCP Servers, in the sidebar's Settings menu as MCP servers, shows your personal servers and a read-only list of the global servers that load in every run.
  • Global MCP Servers, in the sidebar's Settings menu under Admin as Global MCP servers, is where admins manage the built-in and custom global servers.

The DAIV app opens the connections itself at runtime, so no sidecar containers are required. DAIV skips a server that does not return its tools within the load timeout (see Environment variables).

docs.title: Server settings
docs.text:
Each server is a row with these settings:

Setting Description Name Unique slug of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, up to 80 characters. You cannot change it after you create the server. new and test are reserved. Description Optional text. Status Active loads the server in every run (for a personal server, every run that acts as its owner). On-demand loads it only in runs that opt in, for example with mcp_overrides in the jobs API. Disabled never loads it. Transport HTTP (streamable) or SSE. URL The MCP endpoint, an http or https URL of up to 200 characters. Headers HTTP headers sent to the server. Each header is a literal value, encrypted at rest, or an env_ref, the name of an environment variable that DAIV resolves at runtime. Tool filter Which of the server's tools the agent sees (see Tool filtering).

There is no scope field on the form: the page you create the server from decides it.

The Tool filter section is hidden until it has something to act on. On a new server it appears after a successful Test connection. On an existing server it appears once DAIV has synced the server's tools, or when a filter is active. The Refresh tools button next to the heading syncs the tools again, and the heading shows when the last sync ran and how many tools it found.

docs.title: Tool filtering
docs.text:
Set Tool filter mode to one of:

  • None: the agent sees all the server's tools.
  • Allow only listed tools: the agent sees only the listed tools.
  • Block listed tools: the agent sees all tools except the listed ones.

A filter other than None needs at least one tool name. An allow-list fails closed: a tool that disappears upstream stops being exposed.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
MCP connections bypass the sandbox egress proxy

MCP connections originate from the DAIV app and worker containers, so the sandbox egress proxy does not apply to them. Restrict outbound access at your network layer if you need to.

  • DAIV encrypts header values at rest and never renders them back into the form. An env_ref header keeps the value out of the database entirely.
  • Prefer allow-lists that exclude tools that change data, as the seeded Sentry filter does.

docs.title: Built-in servers
docs.text:
DAIV seeds two built-in servers that point at the official remote MCP endpoints. You can edit a built-in server's URL, headers and tool filter, but you cannot rename or delete it, only disable it.

Server URL Status Tool filter sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp?disable-skills=seer,docs,project-management Disabled, because the endpoint requires authentication Allow only listed tools, with read-only tools only context7 https://mcp.context7.com/mcp Active, and works without credentials at low rate limits Allow only listed tools: resolve-library-id and query-docs

docs.title: Enable the Sentry server
docs.text:
You need an admin account and a Sentry User Auth Token with the read scopes org:read, project:read, team:read and event:read.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → Global MCP servers.
  2. Under Built-in, select Edit on the sentry server.
  3. Under Headers, select Add header.
  4. Enter Authorization as the header name.
  5. Enter Sentry-Bearer <your token> as the value, and leave the mode as literal.
  6. Select Test connection. DAIV reports how many tools it discovered.
  7. Optional: under Tool filter, adjust which tools the agent sees.
  8. Under Status, select Active.
  9. Select Save.

Replace <your token> with your Sentry token. Sentry-Bearer, not Bearer, is Sentry's scheme for passing an API token directly to its hosted MCP. To keep the token out of the database, set the header's mode to env_ref and enter the name of an environment variable that holds the whole Sentry-Bearer <your token> string.

docs.title: Raise the context7 rate limits
docs.text:
You need an admin account and an API key from context7.com/dashboard.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → Global MCP servers.
  2. Under Built-in, select Edit on the context7 server.
  3. Under Headers, select Add header.
  4. Enter CONTEXT7_API_KEY as the header name.
  5. Enter your API key as the value.
  6. Select Save.

docs.title: Add a server
docs.text:
You can add any server that DAIV reaches over HTTP or SSE. A server that only speaks stdio needs a bridge first. Any member can add a personal server. Only admins can add a global one.

  1. In the sidebar's Settings menu, open the page for the server's scope: MCP servers for a personal server, or, as an admin, Global MCP servers under Admin for a global one.
  2. Select New server.
  3. Enter a Name.
  4. Choose a Transport.
  5. Enter the URL.
  6. Optional: select Add header and enter each header's name, mode and value.
  7. Select Test connection. DAIV reports how many tools it discovered.
  8. Optional: under Tool filter, choose a Tool filter mode and select the tools.
  9. Set Status.
  10. Select Save.

Test connection fails after 5 seconds. A personal server's headers are always literal (see Personal servers).

docs.title: Stdio-only servers
docs.text: DAIV connects over HTTP and SSE only. To use a stdio-based MCP server, wrap it with a stdio-to-HTTP bridge in its own container, then add the bridge's URL as a server. Run one bridge container per MCP server, so a failure in one does not affect another.

docs.title: Connect an on-premise Sentry
docs.text: Sentry's hosted MCP serves only sentry.io. The official @sentry/mcp-server package is stdio-only, so for a self-hosted Sentry you expose it over HTTP yourself and point the sentry server's URL at it. You have two options.

docs.title: Bridge the stdio package
docs.text:
Any stdio-to-HTTP bridge works. This example uses supergateway.

Run the bridge in stateful mode

Pass --stateful. In stateless mode every tool call starts a fresh child process chain, which can exhaust the system's thread limit under concurrent load. Pass --sessionTimeout in milliseconds (300000 works well) to clean up idle sessions.

  1. Add the bridge to your Compose file:

    YAML
    mcp-sentry:
  image: supercorp/supergateway:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  command:
    - --stdio
    - "npx @sentry/mcp-server@latest --host=sentry.example.com"
    - --outputTransport
    - streamableHttp
    - --healthEndpoint
    - "/healthz"
    - --stateful
    - --sessionTimeout
    - "300000"
  environment:
    SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN}
  healthcheck:
    test: ["CMD", "wget", "--spider", "-q", "http://localhost:8000/healthz"]
    interval: 30s
    timeout: 5s
    retries: 3
    start_period: 30s

  2. Set SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN in the environment that the Compose file reads.

  3. Start the container.
  4. In the sidebar, select Settings → Global MCP servers.
  5. Under Built-in, select Edit on the sentry server.
  6. Set URL to http://mcp-sentry:8000/mcp.
  7. Under Headers, remove the Authorization header, because the bridge authenticates with its own SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN.
  8. Select Test connection.
  9. Under Status, select Active.
  10. Select Save.

Replace sentry.example.com with your Sentry host. For a Sentry that serves plain HTTP, add --insecure-http to the npx command.

docs.title: Deploy Sentry's worker
docs.text: The sentry-mcp repository ships the open-source Cloudflare worker behind mcp.sentry.dev. Deploying your own instance gives you an HTTP endpoint without a bridge. Set the sentry server's URL to your worker, and keep the Authorization: Sentry-Bearer <token> header on it.

docs.title: Personal servers
docs.text:
Every member, admins included, can add personal MCP servers from the MCP Servers page. New server there always creates a server that you own. Personal servers use the same transports, tool filters and Test connection as global custom servers, with these differences.

Where they load. A personal server loads only in runs where DAIV knows whom the run acts as. Those are chat sessions, dashboard-started runs, jobs submitted through the API or MCP interface, and runs that a GitLab or GitHub event starts for a person who signed in to DAIV with that platform account (an issue label or mention, or a mention on a merge request a DAIV session owns). A session's CI fixes act as its owner, and a resumed delegation as the user who delegated. A mention on a merge request no session owns, or by someone who never signed in with that account, has no acting user, and DAIV loads global servers only.

Header values are always literal. A personal server's headers cannot be an env_ref, so a member cannot probe the DAIV host's environment through their own configuration.

Name collisions. A personal server cannot take a global server's name when you create it. If an admin later adds a global server with the same name, the global server wins while it is Active or On-demand: DAIV skips the personal server in every run, and the MCP Servers page flags it with a Shadowed badge.

Admin oversight. On the MCP Servers page, admins have an owner dropdown, set to You by default, to list any member's personal servers. Admins can disable, delete or refresh those servers. They cannot edit them or see their header values.

docs.title: Resolve a name collision
docs.text:
You cannot rename a server, so you delete the shadowed personal server and create it again under another name.

Deleting a server deletes its headers

DAIV removes the server and its stored headers permanently, and the form never shows header values. Keep the values somewhere else before you delete. A new server starts with no headers.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → MCP servers.
  2. Find the server marked Shadowed, and note its settings. Have its header values from your own records, because the form never shows them.
  3. Select Delete on it.
  4. On the confirmation page, select Delete.
  5. Select New server.
  6. Enter a Name that no global server uses, then re-enter the other settings and headers (see Add a server).
  7. Select Save.

docs.title: Repository configuration
docs.text: A .daiv.yml file in the root of a repository's default branch changes how DAIV behaves in that repository: who can trigger it, which features run, and which models it uses. A repository without the file uses the defaults on this page and the site-wide settings.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
YAML
# Repository settings
default_branch: main
context_file_name: "AGENTS.md"
suggest_context_file: true
session_link: true

# Access control
allowed_usernames:
  - alice
  - bob

# Files whose diff content the commit and merge request writer does not see
omit_content_patterns:
  - "*.min.js"
  - "*.svg"
  - "*.lock"

# Feature toggles
issue_addressing:
  enabled: true

pull_request_assistant:
  enabled: true

slash_commands:
  enabled: true

pipeline_watch:
  enabled: true
  max_attempts: 3

orchestration:
  enabled: false

memory:
  enabled: true

# Model overrides
models:
  agent:
    model: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
    fallback_model: "openrouter:openai/gpt-6.1-sol"
    thinking_level: "medium"
  diff_to_metadata:
    model: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
    fallback_model: "openrouter:openai/gpt-6.1-sol"
  skills:
    code-review: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
  subagents:
    cr-security: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5"

docs.title: How DAIV reads the file
docs.text: DAIV always reads .daiv.yml from the platform's default branch, whatever the default_branch option says. It caches the file for 1 hour per repository, and a push to the default branch clears the cache, so a change you merge takes effect after that push. If the file is missing, DAIV uses the defaults. If DAIV cannot parse the file or one of its values, it logs an error and uses the defaults for the whole file. Model entries under models.skills and models.subagents are the exception: DAIV checks them when a run uses them, so a typo there never drops the rest of the file.

docs.title: Repository settings
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description default_branch str \| null Repository default Base branch for merge requests. context_file_name str \| null "AGENTS.md" Name of the AGENTS.md guidance file. Set to null to disable. suggest_context_file bool true Suggest creating the context file when DAIV opens a merge request and the file is missing. See AGENTS.md suggestion. session_link bool true Link back to the DAIV sessions that produced the changes, from the description of merge requests DAIV opens and from a DAIV-Session trailer on every commit. See Linking back to sessions.

The context file tells DAIV about your repository's structure, conventions and constraints. Generate one with the /init skill; see Slash commands and skills. For branch names and commit messages, see Set branch and commit conventions.

suggest_context_file and session_link also have site-wide switches in Site configuration. DAIV applies them only when both the repository and the site allow them, so true here cannot turn on a feature the site turned off.

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
Access control restricts which users can interact with DAIV on this repository. It matters most on public repositories, where you want to stop arbitrary users from triggering DAIV.

Option Type Default Description allowed_usernames list[str] [] Usernames allowed to interact with DAIV. When empty, all users are allowed. YAML
allowed_usernames:
  - alice
  - bob
  - charlie

When the list is empty or omitted, all users can interact with DAIV. When it lists users, only they can trigger DAIV through issues, comments and merge request reviews. Username matching is case-insensitive.

Warning

The allowlist decides who can trigger DAIV, not who it reads. On a merge request a DAIV session owns, a comment that doesn't mention DAIV is remembered from anyone and shown to that session's next run as context (see Pull request assistant). On a public repository, treat those comments as untrusted input.

docs.title: Omitted diff content
docs.text:
omit_content_patterns lists files whose changes stay in the diff, but whose content DAIV replaces with a placeholder before the diff reaches the model that writes commit messages and merge request descriptions. It keeps large generated files out of that model's input.

Option Type Default Description omit_content_patterns list[str] ["*package-lock.json", "*pnpm-lock.yaml", "*.lock", "*.svg"] Path patterns whose diff content is left out of generated commit messages and merge request descriptions.

Patterns follow fnmatch syntax and match against the file's path in the repository.

docs.title: Feature toggles
docs.text:
All features are on by default. To turn one off, set its enabled option to false:

YAML
issue_addressing:
  enabled: false

pull_request_assistant:
  enabled: false

slash_commands:
  enabled: false
Section Option Default Description issue_addressing enabled true Issue addressing pull_request_assistant enabled true Pull request assistant slash_commands enabled true Slash commands and skills pipeline_watch enabled true Pipeline watch: set it to false to stop DAIV watching CI on the merge requests it publishes. pipeline_watch max_attempts site-wide Pipeline watch: the maximum number of fix attempts before DAIV hands the merge request back. DAIV caps it at the site-wide limit. orchestration enabled true Orchestration: let the agent delegate sub-jobs to other repositories, or to new sessions on this one. memory enabled true Repository memory: capture observations from finished runs, consolidate them, and add them to the system prompt of later runs. Set it to false to opt this repository out.

pipeline_watch.enabled and memory.enabled apply only while the matching site-wide setting is on too: Pipeline Watch and Memory in Site configuration. The other toggles apply to the repository alone.

docs.title: Model overrides
docs.text:
A repository can use different models from the site's, for example smaller models on simple projects and larger ones on complex projects. A model is written as a model spec such as openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5; see LLM providers.

The model for a run comes from the first source in this list that sets one, highest priority first:

  1. A model picked for the run, in the agent picker or as agent_model through the API and MCP.
  2. The daiv-max issue label, described in Issue addressing. Max mode uses the site's max thinking level, not thinking_level.
  3. The models section of .daiv.yml.
  4. Site settings: environment variables or the Site Configuration page.

DAIV tries the model from the highest source that sets one first. The models.agent model and fallback follow it, or the site's models where the file sets none.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
The main DAIV agent handles issue addressing, pull request assistance and all interactive tasks.

Option Type Default Description models.agent.model str site setting Primary model. models.agent.fallback_model str site setting Fallback if the primary model fails. models.agent.thinking_level "minimal" \| "low" \| "medium" \| "high" \| "xhigh" \| null site setting Thinking depth. Set to null to disable.

A model picked for a single run is tried first, with the model and fallback above after it, and a thinking level picked for a run beats thinking_level.

docs.title: Diff to metadata
docs.text:
The diff to metadata agent generates pull request titles, descriptions and commit messages from diffs.

Option Type Default Description models.diff_to_metadata.model str site setting Primary model. models.diff_to_metadata.fallback_model str site setting Fallback if the primary model fails.

docs.title: Skill and subagent models
docs.text:
Run a skill or a subagent on a chosen model in this repository, by name. An entry overrides the site's entry for the same name only; every other site entry still applies. Site entries are set in the dashboard: a skill's on the Models tab of its page, which also holds the code-review detectors', and the general-purpose and explore subagents' under Configuration → Agent.

Option Type Default Description models.skills.<name> str \| null site entry Model for the skill's model calls, from its invocation until your next message. models.subagents.<name> str \| null site entry Model for every call the subagent makes. YAML
models:
  skills:
    code-review: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
    plan: null   # unset: the site entry, if any, applies
  subagents:
    cr-security: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5"
    my-repo-subagent: "openrouter:z-ai/glm-5.2"

Replace <name> with the name of a skill or subagent. For a given name, the model resolves in this order, first match wins:

  1. this repository's entry;
  2. the site's entry (a skill page's Models tab, or Configuration → Agent → Subagent models);
  3. the model the subagent file, or a built-in or global skill file, declares (a repository skill's metadata.model is ignored);
  4. the run's model.

A model picked for the run, daiv-max, or an exact model passed to the jobs API does not override these entries. Configured models run with the run's thinking level.

DAIV checks the values when a run uses them, not when the file loads, so a typo never drops the rest of .daiv.yml. An entry that can't be used falls back to the model the file declares, else the run's model, not to the site entry, and DAIV logs the failure as an error. Names that match no skill or subagent are ignored. See Agent skills and Subagents.

docs.title: Issue addressing
docs.text: Issue addressing turns an issue into code. DAIV reads a labelled issue, posts an implementation plan, waits for your approval, and opens a merge request (GitLab) or pull request (GitHub) with the changes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. You create or update an issue and add a bot label.
  2. DAIV reads the issue title, description, and any attached images.
  3. DAIV posts a plan as a comment on the issue.
  4. You review the plan and approve it, or comment with the changes you want, and DAIV revises the plan.
  5. DAIV implements the plan and opens a merge or pull request.
graph TD
    A["Create issue with daiv label"] --> B["DAIV analyzes issue"]
    B --> C["Plan posted as comment"]
    C --> D{"Approve?"}
    D -- "@daiv proceed" --> E["DAIV implements changes"]
    D -- "Comment with changes" --> B
    E --> F["Merge/Pull request created"]

docs.title: Issue labels
docs.text:
Add one of these bot labels to an issue to hand it to DAIV:

Label Behavior daiv Generates a plan and waits for approval before implementing daiv-auto Generates a plan and executes it immediately without waiting for approval daiv-max Uses a more capable model with deeper reasoning; see Max mode

Labels are case-insensitive (DAIV, Daiv, and daiv all work). You can combine labels: daiv-auto with daiv-max runs the plan at once, on the more capable model.

When the merge request DAIV opened for an issue merges, DAIV archives the issue's session. A label or mention on the issue then starts nothing until someone unarchives the session, and DAIV replies with a link to it.

docs.title: Approve a plan
docs.text:
With the daiv label, DAIV waits for your approval after it posts a plan and makes no code changes before it. To approve the plan:

  1. Open the issue and read the plan DAIV posted.

  2. Add a comment that mentions DAIV, for example:

    Text Only
    @daiv proceed

The exact wording is not a keyword. DAIV reacts to any comment that mentions it (@daiv); it reads your comment together with the plan it posted and acts on your intent. A comment like @daiv looks good, go ahead works the same as @daiv proceed.

Your comment can also carry feedback or extra instructions. DAIV either applies them while it implements the plan or revises the plan from them. If you disagree with the plan, comment with the changes you want and DAIV updates the plan.

docs.title: Answer a question from DAIV
docs.text: When the issue or your feedback is ambiguous in a way that changes the work, or the choice is yours to make, DAIV can post a question instead of guessing. The question mentions you and ends with "reply mentioning @daiv with your answer." To answer, leave a new comment that mentions DAIV. On GitLab, DAIV posts its question inside the discussion thread of the comment that triggered it, so replying in that same thread keeps the conversation together; on GitHub the question is always a top-level comment.

docs.title: Max mode
docs.text: The daiv-max label switches DAIV to the site's max model with its max thinking level, which suits complex issues that need deeper analysis. An administrator sets both, with the DAIV_AGENT_MAX_MODEL_NAME and DAIV_AGENT_MAX_THINKING_LEVEL variables or in Site configuration; the environment variables reference lists their defaults.

docs.title: Run DAIV again
docs.text: To run a second plan on an issue DAIV already addressed, add a new comment that mentions @daiv and says what you want. DAIV updates the existing merge or pull request instead of creating a new one. Adding the label again does not start a run: DAIV ignores a label on an issue it already reacted to.

docs.title: When a run fails
docs.text: If an unexpected error stops DAIV while it implements a plan, DAIV opens a draft merge or pull request to keep the changes it already made.

docs.title: AGENTS.md suggestion
docs.text:
When DAIV creates a merge request for a repository that doesn't have an AGENTS.md file (or whatever context_file_name is configured to), DAIV adds a comment suggesting you create one. The comment includes a one-click link that opens an issue with the daiv-auto label already set. When you submit that issue, DAIV runs the /init skill at once, with no approval step, and opens a merge or pull request with the generated AGENTS.md.

To stop the suggestion on one repository, set suggest_context_file: false in its .daiv.yml. To stop it on every repository, set DAIV_SUGGEST_CONTEXT_FILE_ENABLED to false. Repository configuration and the environment variables reference describe both.

docs.title: Turn off issue addressing
docs.text:
Issue addressing is on by default. To turn it off for a repository, add this to its .daiv.yml:

YAML
issue_addressing:
  enabled: false

Repository configuration lists every feature toggle and who can trigger DAIV.

docs.text:
• Repository configuration — restrict who can trigger DAIV and turn features on or off
  • Slash commands and skills — steer an issue with /plan and custom skills
  • Pull request assistant — what happens once the merge request is open
  • Sandbox — where the implementation is built and tested

docs.title: Jobs API
docs.text:
The jobs API runs DAIV agents outside the git webhook flow. You send a prompt and a list of repositories, DAIV returns a job ID for each run, and you poll that ID for the result.

Use it to run agents from a CI pipeline, chain agent tasks, trigger runs from Slack bots, scripts or other tools, or start a one-off run with curl. To run a prompt on a recurring schedule without any external trigger, use scheduled jobs.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • A DAIV account with an API key, created as described in Create an API key.
  • Write access to every repository you name in repos.
  • For multi-repository sessions (shared_session), a daiv-sandbox release with path-scoped egress rules and repository seeding. Deploy the sandbox release first: with an older sandbox the run fails before any command runs, with an error that says so. Single-repository runs are unaffected.

docs.title: Create an API key
docs.text:
An API key belongs to one user and authenticates the jobs API and every other API surface, including the MCP endpoint, chat completions and the sessions API. Create it from the dashboard, or from the command line for headless provisioning.

Warning

DAIV shows the full key once, when you create it, and cannot show it again. Copy it before you leave the page; if you lose it, revoke the key and create another.

To create a key in the dashboard:

  1. Open the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar and select API keys (/accounts/api-keys/).
  2. In Create a new key, enter a name, for example CI/CD.
  3. Select Create key.
  4. Select Copy next to Your new API key.

To create a key from the command line, run django-admin in the DAIV app container:

Bash
docker compose exec app django-admin create_api_key <username> --name "my-key"

Replace <username> with the username of the key's owner. The command prints the key once, in the form prefix.secret. For the --expires-at option and its time-zone rule, see create_api_key.

Warning

Revoking a key cannot be undone. The key stops authenticating immediately on every API surface, so any script or client that uses it fails until you give it another key.

To stop a key from working, select Revoke next to it on the API keys page.

Admins see every user's keys; other users see their own.

docs.title: Authenticate a request
docs.text:
Pass the key as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of every request:

Bash
curl -X POST https://daiv.example.com/api/jobs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <api-key>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '...'

Replace <api-key> with your key. A missing or invalid key returns 401.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text: DAIV limits job submissions per authenticated user and returns 429 Too Many Requests when you exceed the limit. The same budget applies to the MCP endpoint and to chat completions. An admin sets the rate in Configuration under the Jobs group, or with DAIV_JOBS_THROTTLE_RATE; the default and the accepted formats are in Environment variables.

docs.title: Submit a job
docs.text:
Send a POST request to /api/jobs with a prompt and the repositories to run it on. For example:

Bash
curl -s -X POST https://daiv.example.com/api/jobs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DAIV_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "repos": [{"repo_id": "mygroup/myproject"}],
    "prompt": "List all Python files and summarize the project structure"
  }'

DAIV answers 202 Accepted:

JSON
{
  "batch_id": "5b9e8a3c-9b7e-4c0d-a1f5-7e2c8d4b1a90",
  "jobs": [
    {
      "job_id": "1adfbf7a-917e-4f2e-8f54-17a27c006ec5",
      "repo_id": "mygroup/myproject",
      "ref": null,
      "thread_id": "9c1e8a3c-9b7e-4c0d-a1f5-7e2c8d4b1a90",
      "status": "READY"
    }
  ],
  "failed": []
}

Each entry in jobs is an independent run, so poll each job_id separately. Its status is READY when the run can start, or QUEUED when the session named by thread_id is busy; see Job lifecycle. DAIV reports a repository it rejects before enqueuing, such as an unknown repo_id, in failed as {repo_id, ref, error}, and still runs the rest of the batch.

For every field of the request, see Request fields.

docs.title: Poll job status
docs.text:
Send a GET request to /api/jobs/{job_id}. DAIV answers 200 OK:

JSON
{
  "job_id": "1adfbf7a-917e-4f2e-8f54-17a27c006ec5",
  "status": "SUCCESSFUL",
  "thread_id": "9c1e8a3c-9b7e-4c0d-a1f5-7e2c8d4b1a90",
  "result": "Here are the Python files...",
  "merge_request_url": null,
  "artifacts": [
    {
      "id": "3f1c2b6e-0d7a-4f0e-9c4b-2a8d6e1f5b70",
      "title": "Dependency audit",
      "filename": "dependency-audit.html",
      "content_type": "text/html",
      "kind": "html",
      "size": 48213,
      "url": "https://daiv.example.com/dashboard/sessions/9c1e8a3c-9b7e-4c0d-a1f5-7e2c8d4b1a90/artifacts/3f1c2b6e-0d7a-4f0e-9c4b-2a8d6e1f5b70/",
      "download_url": "https://daiv.example.com/dashboard/sessions/9c1e8a3c-9b7e-4c0d-a1f5-7e2c8d4b1a90/artifacts/3f1c2b6e-0d7a-4f0e-9c4b-2a8d6e1f5b70/raw/?download=1"
    }
  ],
  "error": null,
  "created_at": "2026-03-27T18:22:39.012Z",
  "started_at": "2026-03-27T18:22:39.401Z",
  "finished_at": "2026-03-27T18:22:52.402Z"
}

merge_request_url holds the merge request DAIV opened when the agent committed and pushed code changes, and is null otherwise, for example on a read-only triage run. In a multi-repository session it is the main repository's merge request, else the first one opened. thread_id identifies the thread the job ran on; pass it back as thread_id on a new submission to continue the conversation.

artifacts lists the files the agent published with its publish_artifact tool, such as reports, datasets and charts; see Artifacts. Each entry has the viewer page (url), a direct download (download_url), and a kind (markdown, html, image, text or other) that says how the viewer renders it. Opening either URL needs a signed-in DAIV user who can see the run. An artifact that a later job on the same thread revises keeps its ID and URLs, and appears under the job that first published it and under every job that revised it, with its current file (Revise an artifact). The list is empty for a run that published nothing, and fills as the run progresses, so you can read it while the job is RUNNING. If DAIV cannot list the artifacts, artifacts is empty and artifacts_error says why; the rest of the status is unaffected.

result holds the agent's last response in full, not the rest of the run's messages. DAIV deletes a finished job's stored task result after 14 days, and from then on result holds the stored summary of the response, cut at 2,000 characters; the job's token usage and cost are kept. The MCP get_job_status tool behaves the same.

For the meaning of each status, see Job status values.

docs.title: Answer a question
docs.text:
When a job comes back WAITING_INPUT, the agent stopped to ask you a question instead of guessing. To answer it:

  1. Read question for the questions asked, and result for their rendered text.

  2. Send a new POST /api/jobs request with the same thread_id and your answer as prompt:

    Bash
    curl -s -X POST https://daiv.example.com/api/jobs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DAIV_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "repos": [{"repo_id": "mygroup/myproject"}],
    "prompt": "Use PostgreSQL.",
    "thread_id": "9c1e8a3c-9b7e-4c0d-a1f5-7e2c8d4b1a90"
  }'

  3. Poll the new job_id. DAIV starts a new run that continues the agent's work from where it stopped.

The thread_id rules in Request fields apply to the answer too: repos has exactly one entry, or for a multi-repository session the main repository alone or the session's full list, and the thread's most recent run must be yours.

You do not have to poll for the question. When a job ends in WAITING_INPUT, DAIV sends you a notification listing the questions, unless you muted it. For a multi-repository batch, the run counts in the batch rollup, and appears in the email and Rocket.Chat versions, once every repository's run has settled.

docs.title: Request fields
docs.text:
These are the fields of the POST /api/jobs body.

Field Type Required Description repos array of objects yes 1–20 repositories to run against. Each item is { "repo_id": "group/project", "ref": "branch", "prompt": "..." }. ref is optional, must be a branch that exists on the remote, and defaults to the repository's default branch. prompt is optional, must not be blank, and replaces the batch prompt for that repository only. A new merge or pull request targets ref, and DAIV assigns it to the API key's owner when their DAIV account is OAuth-linked to the git platform. prompt string yes The prompt to send to the agent. It runs as an independent job against each repository in repos, except one that gives its own prompt, and it titles the batch. agent_model string no The model for this batch. DAIV rejects an invalid model and thinking-level combination with 400. agent_thinking_level string no The agent's reasoning effort: minimal, low, medium, high or xhigh. DAIV rejects an invalid combination with 400. muted boolean no Mute notifications for every job in this batch. Default false. environment string no The sandbox environment, by name or ID, for every job in the batch. DAIV rejects an environment it cannot resolve with 400. shared_session boolean no Run all repositories in repos in one session instead of one job each. At most 5 entries. See Multi-repository sessions. thread_id string (UUID) no Continue an existing thread. repos must hold exactly one entry (a multi-repository session also accepts its full list), the thread's most recent run must be yours, and the session must not be an archived session; otherwise DAIV returns 400. If the session is busy, the job joins the session's next run for its branch in QUEUED state, which starts once the current run ends; see Job lifecycle. references array of objects no Up to 20 external work-item references, such as Jira, Sentry or RT tickets and git platform issues, that DAIV links into the merge or pull request it creates. Each item is { "key": "PROJ-123", "url": "https://…", "provider": "jira", "relation": "relates" }, and only key is required. The per-field rules are in References; DAIV rejects an invalid reference with 422 and stores nothing. mcp_overrides object no MCP servers to switch on or off for every job in the batch, relative to the default set: {"grafana": true} adds an on-demand server, {"sentry": false} drops an active one. Names are those of the global servers and your own personal ones. DAIV rejects an unknown name with 400, and a value other than true or false with 422. On a continued thread (thread_id) the overrides apply on top of the thread's own, so a server you do not name keeps its setting. DAIV returns a continuation that would change them while another run on the thread is unfinished in failed, since that run would pick them up too.

DAIV validates the body strictly and rejects unknown fields with 422, use_max and notify_on included. Use muted to silence notifications, and agent_model and agent_thinking_level to choose the model.

docs.title: Job status values
docs.text: Status Meaning QUEUED The job is the session's next run, waiting for its current run to finish. Only occurs for thread continuations (thread_id supplied). READY The job is waiting for a worker. RUNNING The agent is executing. SUCCESSFUL The run completed, and result holds the agent's last response. WAITING_INPUT The agent stopped to ask you a question. This is a final state, not a step towards SUCCESSFUL. question holds the questions asked, and result their rendered text. FAILED The agent hit an error, and error holds a message.

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
For GET /api/jobs/{job_id}:

Code When 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 404 The job ID is not found or is not a valid ID.

For POST /api/jobs:

Code When 400 The request is invalid: a bad agent_model or agent_thinking_level; no agent_model given and no system default model configured (a model set only in .daiv.yml does not count); an unresolvable environment; an unknown MCP server in mcp_overrides; an invalid shared_session list (more than 5 entries, a repository listed twice, or a per-repository prompt); or an invalid thread_id continuation (an unknown or unowned thread, an archived session, more than one repository for a single-repository session, a ref on a multi-repository session, or anything but the main repository alone or the full list in order). 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 404 A repository in repos is not found, or you lack write access to it. The response does not say which one. 422 The body is malformed or has unknown fields, for example use_max or notify_on, or a references entry is invalid. 429 You exceeded the rate limit.

docs.title: Multi-repository sessions
docs.text:
By default, several entries in repos fan out into independent jobs, one session per repository. To let the agent work across repositories in one conversation, for example a backend change and the client that consumes it, set shared_session: true:

JSON
{
  "repos": [
    {"repo_id": "mygroup/backend"},
    {"repo_id": "mygroup/client", "ref": "develop"}
  ],
  "shared_session": true,
  "prompt": "Add a `locale` field to the profile endpoint and use it in the client."
}
  • You can also start such a session from the dashboard chat, which takes the same list: see Start a chat over several repositories.
  • repos takes up to 5 entries, the first being the main one, each repository at most once, and no per-repository prompt: the session runs the one prompt.
  • The response holds one job and one thread_id. The job's repo_id is the first entry, the main repository.
  • You need write access to every repository. If one is missing or unknown, the call fails with the usual opaque 404.
  • The main repository's .daiv.yml, model, sandbox environment, skills, subagents and memory drive the session. DAIV checks it out at /workspace/repo and the others at /workspace/repos/<repository path>. The agent is told about them and reads their AGENTS.md.
  • The agent reads the main repository's memory, but a multi-repository run adds no observations to it, since its transcript holds the other repositories' code.

docs.title: Merge requests
docs.text:
At the end of each turn, every repository that changed gets its own commit, branch and merge request. Unchanged repositories get nothing, and one repository failing to publish does not stop the others. Each merge request's description lists the session's other merge requests as platform references (group/project!12, owner/repo#12), which the platform links and titles only for readers who can see that repository. External references, such as a support ticket, go into every merge request, but only the main repository's closes them; the others relate to them. GitLab or GitHub issue references go only into the main repository's.

The job status adds two lists:

Field Meaning merge_requests [{"repo_id": "...", "url": "..."}], one per opened or updated merge request. publish_errors [{"repo_id": "...", "error": "..."}], one per repository that could not be published.

merge_request_url stays: the main repository's merge request, else the first one opened.

docs.title: Continuing a multi-repository session
docs.text: Pass the session's thread_id. shared_session is optional and ignored, because the session decides whether a continuation is shared: a single-repository session continues as one even with shared_session: true. Send the main repository alone, or the identical list in the same order, and no ref. Anything else returns 400. Each repository continues on its stored working branch. If that branch is gone because its merge request was merged, the repository falls back to its default branch and opens a new merge request the next time it changes.

docs.title: Visibility and CI
docs.text:
A multi-repository session, with its runs, transcript, artifacts and merge request links, is visible only to its owner, admins, and users who can read every repository in it.

The session owns every merge request it opens, the main repository's and each other repository's, so their CI watch results and @daiv comments reach the session's inbox. The session's next run handles a CI failure or a mention on any of them, on the main repository's branch with every repository checked out, and DAIV answers a mention on the merge request it was made on. Each merge request has its own CI fix attempts. In the dashboard, a multi-repository session continued in chat keeps all its repositories and its main repository cannot be switched, and the session page lists every repository and merge request.

docs.title: Job lifecycle
docs.text:
A job moves through these statuses:

  1. POST /api/jobs creates the job as READY, or as QUEUED when you supply a thread_id and the session is busy.
  2. A QUEUED job becomes READY when the session's current run finishes.
  3. A worker picks up a READY job and it becomes RUNNING.
  4. A RUNNING job ends as SUCCESSFUL when the agent completes, WAITING_INPUT when the agent asks a question, or FAILED when the agent errors.
  5. A WAITING_INPUT job does not change. Your answer is a new job: POST /api/jobs with the same thread_id and your answer as prompt. It starts at READY, or at QUEUED when the session is busy.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> READY: POST /api/jobs
    [*] --> QUEUED: POST /api/jobs (thread continuation, session busy)
    QUEUED --> READY: The session's current run finishes
    READY --> RUNNING: Worker picks up job
    RUNNING --> SUCCESSFUL: Agent completes
    RUNNING --> WAITING_INPUT: Agent asks a question
    RUNNING --> FAILED: Agent errors
    SUCCESSFUL --> [*]
    WAITING_INPUT --> [*]: Answer with a new job on the same thread_id
    FAILED --> [*]

A job starts in QUEUED only when you supply a thread_id and the session is busy. The job then joins the session's next run for its branch (ref, or the session's branch when you leave it out), which starts at READY once the current run ends. Everything waiting for the session on that branch goes into the same run: another job, a chat message, a CI failure DAIV is fixing. So two jobs sent while the session is busy can return the same job_id; poll it once and read one result for both. A job on a different branch gets a next run of its own. Every other submission starts at READY.

SUCCESSFUL, WAITING_INPUT and FAILED are final for that job. WAITING_INPUT does not progress to SUCCESSFUL on its own; it waits for a new job on the same thread (see Answer a question).

docs.title: Poll from a shell script
docs.text:
Replace <api-key> with your DAIV API key before you run the script.

Bash
#!/bin/bash
DAIV_URL="https://daiv.example.com"
API_KEY="<api-key>"

# Submit (single-repo batch)
JOB_ID=$(curl -s -X POST "$DAIV_URL/api/jobs" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"repos":[{"repo_id":"mygroup/myproject"}],"prompt":"List all TODO comments"}' \
  | jq -r '.jobs[0].job_id')

echo "Job submitted: $JOB_ID"

# Poll until done
while true; do
  RESPONSE=$(curl -s "$DAIV_URL/api/jobs/$JOB_ID" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY")
  STATUS=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r '.status')

  case "$STATUS" in
    SUCCESSFUL) echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r '.result'; break ;;
    FAILED)     echo "Job failed"; exit 1 ;;
    *)          sleep 10 ;;
  esac
done

docs.title: Chain two jobs in a scheduled GitLab pipeline
docs.text:
This job in a scheduled GitLab CI pipeline triages support tickets, then creates issues from the report:

YAML
# .gitlab-ci.yml
triage-and-create-issues:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
  script:
    # Step 1: Triage tickets
    - |
      JOB_ID=$(curl -s -X POST "$DAIV_URL/api/jobs" \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $DAIV_API_KEY" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{
          "repos": [{"repo_id": "mygroup/myproject"}],
          "prompt": "Triage the RT queue and identify code-related tickets. Return a summary with ticket IDs, descriptions, and priorities."
        }' | jq -r '.jobs[0].job_id')

    # Step 2: Poll until done
    - |
      while true; do
        STATUS=$(curl -s "$DAIV_URL/api/jobs/$JOB_ID" \
          -H "Authorization: Bearer $DAIV_API_KEY" | jq -r '.status')
        [ "$STATUS" = "SUCCESSFUL" ] && break
        [ "$STATUS" = "FAILED" ] && exit 1
        sleep 30
      done
      TRIAGE=$(curl -s "$DAIV_URL/api/jobs/$JOB_ID" \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $DAIV_API_KEY" | jq -r '.result')

    # Step 3: Chain — create issues from the triage report
    - |
      curl -s -X POST "$DAIV_URL/api/jobs" \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $DAIV_API_KEY" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d "$(jq -n --arg prompt "Based on this triage report, create GitLab issues for each actionable item: $TRIAGE" \
          '{repos: [{repo_id: "mygroup/myproject"}], prompt: $prompt}')"

Store DAIV_URL and DAIV_API_KEY as CI/CD variables in your GitLab project settings, and turn on Mask variable and Protect variable for the API key.
