docs.title: MCP endpoint
docs.text:
DAIV runs a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server endpoint at /mcp/, so an AI coding assistant can delegate tasks to the DAIV agent from your editor or terminal.

The DAIV agent reads and modifies code, runs commands in a sandbox, creates commits and branches, opens merge or pull requests, and debugs CI/CD pipelines. Through the endpoint, your local assistant offloads these tasks to DAIV and gets the results back.

docs.title: Connect your editor
docs.text:
You need:

  • A DAIV account.
  • An MCP client that supports the Streamable HTTP transport. Claude Code, Cursor and Codex CLI do.
  • The address of your DAIV instance. The examples use https://daiv.example.com; replace it with yours.

On first use, an interactive client opens a browser window where you sign in with your DAIV account. The client stores the OAuth 2.0 token and refreshes it. To authenticate without a browser, for a CI job or script, see API key authentication.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Run:

Bash
claude mcp add daiv --transport http https://daiv.example.com/mcp/

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
Add DAIV to .cursor/mcp.json for one project, or to ~/.cursor/mcp.json for all projects:

JSON
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "daiv": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://daiv.example.com/mcp/"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
Add DAIV to .codex/config.toml for one project, or to ~/.codex/config.toml for all projects:

TOML
[mcp_servers.daiv]
url = "https://daiv.example.com/mcp/"

Any other MCP client that supports the Streamable HTTP transport connects to the same /mcp/ URL.

docs.title: API key authentication
docs.text:
A client that cannot complete the browser sign-in sends an API key instead. Create the key as described in Create an API key, then pass it in an Authorization: Bearer header. Any MCP client that lets you set request headers can do this.

An API key belongs to your user, not to one surface. A key that authenticates against the MCP endpoint has the same access on the jobs API and the chat API, and revoking it cuts off all of them at once.

In Claude Code, run:

Bash
claude mcp add daiv --transport http https://daiv.example.com/mcp/ \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <prefix.secret>"

In Cursor's mcp.json, set the header:

JSON
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "daiv": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://daiv.example.com/mcp/",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <prefix.secret>" }
    }
  }
}

Replace <prefix.secret> with your API key.

docs.title: Available tools
docs.text:
Tool Description submit_job Submit a prompt to the DAIV agent as a batch of jobs, one independent job per repository. Returns a batch_id and a jobs list. See submit_job parameters. get_job_status Get the status and result of a submitted job, plus the artifacts it published or revised (reports and other files, with viewer and download URLs; see Artifacts). A WAITING_INPUT status means the agent stopped to ask a question: question holds it and result its rendered text, and you answer with submit_job using the same thread_id. With wait=True it blocks until the job completes; a WAITING_INPUT result also ends the wait, since it is final. list_repositories Discover the repositories DAIV can access, optionally filtered by search (partial name match) or topics. DAIV serves them from its local repository catalog, a periodically synced mirror, not a live platform call. Ordered by slug, so a search that matches more repositories than limit is fully reachable by paging. list_environments List the sandbox environments you can see: your own USER environments plus all GLOBAL ones, ordered by scope then name, with no environment-variable values at all. Use a returned name or id as the environment argument of submit_job. get_environment Look up one sandbox environment by name or UUID. Returns the full details with secret environment-variable values masked, or nothing if the environment is not in your visible scopes. list_jobs List your recent agent runs, newest first, optionally filtered by repo_id and status. Returns a lean summary per run plus next_cursor; use get_job_status for one run's full result text. schedule_job Create a recurring or one-off scheduled run that you own. See schedule_job parameters. list_scheduled_jobs List your scheduled jobs, newest first, optionally filtered by enabled_only or repo_id.

The four listing tools (list_jobs, list_scheduled_jobs, list_environments and list_repositories) share one pagination contract. Pass an optional limit (default 20, at most 50) and cursor, and read back { "<items>": [...], "next_cursor": <token or null> }. To page, call again with cursor set to the previous next_cursor until it is null. A cursor encodes only a sort position, so reuse it with the same filters.

docs.title: submit_job parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Required Description repos yes 1–20 entries of {repo_id, ref, prompt}. ref is the branch the agent starts from; it is optional, defaults to the repository's default branch, and must be a branch that exists on the remote (a commit SHA fails the clone). prompt is optional, must not be blank, and replaces the batch prompt for that repository only. A merge or pull request the job opens targets that branch, and DAIV assigns it to the token's owner when their DAIV account is OAuth-linked to the git platform. prompt yes The instruction. It runs as an independent job against each repository, except one that gives its own prompt. wait no Block until every job in the batch completes, for up to 10 minutes in total, and return each job's status with its artifacts. Default false. agent_model no Override the model, as provider_slug:model_name, for example openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5. The provider slug must match an enabled provider. Without it, DAIV uses the repository's models.agent model, else the system default. agent_thinking_level no Reasoning effort: minimal, low, medium, high or xhigh. Without it, DAIV uses the repository's models.agent thinking level, else the system default. muted no Mute this run's notifications. Default false. DAIV rejects notify_on with an unknown-argument error. environment no The sandbox environment to run every job in, by name or UUID; find names with list_environments. Without it, DAIV resolves a runtime for each repository. shared_session no Run up to 5 repos in one session instead of one job each. The first repository is the main one. The response holds one job, and get_job_status and list_jobs add merge_requests and publish_errors. See Multi-repository sessions; the dashboard chat starts them too, from its Workspace card. thread_id no Continue an existing thread, by the UUID from an earlier submit_job or get_job_status response. repos must hold exactly one repository (a multi-repository session also accepts its full list, in order), whose latest activity is yours. An archived session cannot be continued. This is also how you answer a WAITING_INPUT job: submit the answer as prompt with the same thread_id. If the session is busy, the job joins its next run for the job's branch and comes back QUEUED; jobs that join the same next run share its job_id (see Job lifecycle). references no Up to 20 external work-item references to link into the merge or pull request DAIV creates. See References. mcp_overrides no MCP servers to switch on or off for every job in the batch, relative to the default set: {"grafana": true} adds an on-demand server, {"sentry": false} drops an active one. Names are those of the global servers and your own personal ones; DAIV returns an unknown name, or a value other than true or false, as an error. On a continued thread (thread_id) the overrides apply on top of the thread's own, so a server you do not name keeps its setting. DAIV returns a continuation that would change them while another run on the thread is unfinished in failed, since that run would pick them up too.

The response holds a batch_id, a jobs list with one entry per submitted job (each with its job_id, repo_id, ref, thread_id and status), and a failed list for repositories DAIV could not enqueue. The tool shares the jobs API rate limit. For the full response schema, see the jobs API.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Each entry of references is an object with these fields:

Field Required Description key yes The issue or ticket identifier, 1–64 characters, matching [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._/#-]*, for example PROJ-123, 42 or DAIV-1V. When relation is closes, the key must be a bare identifier, with no / and no #: DAIV emits it next to a closing keyword, where namespace/project#7 would be a valid cross-project reference and would close an issue in someone else's project. url no An http or https URL for the work item, up to 500 characters, used as the link target. DAIV renders it into a markdown link destination in the merge or pull request description, so percent-encode anything outside the RFC 3986 URL character set, parentheses included. A space, a newline or a ) would end the link and let the rest of the value become body text the git platform parses. provider no The ticketing system: gitlab-issue, github-issue, sentry, jira, or any other lowercase alphanumeric-and-hyphen string up to 32 characters. Default generic. relation no relates (default) only links. closes opts into auto-close on merge where the provider supports it.

How each provider renders:

  • gitlab-issue and github-issue write the platform's own closing or relating line in the description. GitLab and GitHub close an issue when a merged description contains a closing keyword that references it.
  • sentry with relation: "closes" writes a Fixes <short-id> line in the description and as a commit trailer. Sentry resolves an issue whose short ID appears in a Fixes commit line that reaches the tracked branch, which also needs the Sentry and repository integration set up on Sentry's side: DAIV only writes the syntax.
  • jira adds a Refs: <key> commit trailer for dev-panel linking, a link and never a workflow transition. Its description entry is a plain reference link.
  • Any other provider is accepted and renders as a plain reference link.

DAIV writes the merge or pull request description only when it first creates the request. On a continued thread (thread_id set), DAIV merges newly supplied references into the session's set when the run that takes the job starts, deduplicated by (provider, key) with the first-seen entry winning, and a session keeps at most 50 references across all turns. References from a later turn reach that turn's commit trailers, but do not rewrite the description of an existing request.

docs.title: schedule_job parameters
docs.text:
schedule_job takes name, prompt, a repos list of 1–20 {repo_id, ref} entries, and a frequency with its companion field. It refuses any other key in a repos entry, a per-repository prompt included. The optional agent_model, agent_thinking_level, environment, mcp_overrides and muted work as on submit_job.

frequency Companion field daily, weekdays, weekly time, as HH:MM in 24-hour form. weekly runs on Mondays. custom cron_expression, a five-field cron expression. once run_at, an ISO 8601 date and time in the future. DAIV tolerates about 60 seconds in the past. A value without an offset is read in the server's time zone. hourly None.

New schedules are always enabled. The response includes the schedule id and the computed next_run_at. To edit, disable or delete a schedule, use the dashboard.

docs.title: Usage examples
docs.text:
Once connected, ask your assistant in plain language:

  • "Ask DAIV to refactor the authentication module in mygroup/myproject to use JWT tokens."
  • "Submit a job to mygroup/myproject on the develop branch: fix the broken CI pipeline."
  • "Check the status of my last DAIV job."

Tip

Be specific: include file paths, function names, error messages or branch names. The more context you give, the better the result.

docs.title: Repository memory
docs.text: Repository memory is what DAIV remembers about a repository from its past runs: how the project builds and tests, facts about the code, mistakes to avoid and what reviewers ask for. Later runs on the same repository start with that knowledge, so you do not repeat it in each prompt. Memory is per repository, and DAIV never shows what it learned on one repository to a run on another.

docs.title: How memory forms
docs.text:
Memory forms in three steps, none of which needs you to act.

  1. Extraction. When a run finishes, DAIV reads the session's transcript and asks the extraction model for candidate observations. It stores each one as pending, under one of five categories:

    Category What it captures Build & test How the project builds, tests and lints Codebase fact Durable facts about the code and its layout Pitfall Mistakes and traps a run should avoid repeating Reviewer preference What the repository's reviewers ask for Workflow Conventions for working on the repository

  2. Consolidation, which DAIV also calls dreaming. An hourly sweep finds the repositories that are due, and the consolidation model folds their pending observations into the repository's entries. Environment variables lists the settings that choose the extraction and consolidation models. For each observation it adds a fact, corrects or merges existing entries, confirms a duplicate, or discards noise. DAIV rewrites only the entries an operation names.

  3. Injection. DAIV renders the surviving entries into one document, grouped by category in a fixed order with one line per entry. No model is involved in rendering, so the same entries always give the same document. A later run on the repository gets the document appended to its system prompt, under the header # Learned repository memory (auto-generated from past runs; may be stale — verify before relying on it). A multi-repository session gets the main repository's memory only.

docs.title: What a run contributes
docs.text:
DAIV extracts observations from every finished run, failed ones included. It extracts nothing from:

  • A run started from the dashboard chat.
  • A run in a multi-repository session, whose transcript holds the other repositories' code.
  • A run whose session's working state expired before DAIV read it. Environment variables gives how long that state lives.
  • A run that failed or was cancelled before it started.
  • A run in a session where the agent has not replied yet.

docs.title: When a repository is consolidated
docs.text:
A repository is due when either of these holds:

  • It has at least a set number of pending observations.
  • Its oldest pending observation is older than a set number of days, so a quiet repository still forms memory.

In both cases DAIV consolidates only if the last attempt was longer ago than the minimum interval. A failed attempt counts, so a repository whose rounds keep failing is retried at the same pace as a healthy one. DAIV applies at most 50 operations from a round. Observations named only by the rest stay pending for the next round.

Environment variables gives the thresholds and their defaults.

docs.title: Read a repository's memory
docs.text:
Memory, in the sidebar's Settings menu under Agent setup, lists the repositories you can read that have memory activity. Each row shows whether the repository has a document (Document or No document), when it was last consolidated, how many observations are pending and how many exist in total. Search by repository name, or filter by All, Document, No document or Pending.

Select a repository to open its page:

  • The header shows when the repository was last consolidated and the document's size in lines and bytes. Before the first consolidation it reads Never consolidated.
  • Consolidated document shows the text DAIV adds to later runs.
  • Observations lists every observation with its status (Pending, Consolidated or Discarded) and its category. Filter by either, and select View source run to open the run it came from.

docs.title: Who can read a repository's memory
docs.text: You can read a repository's memory when you have read access to the repository on your Git platform, and admins can read every repository's. A repository you cannot read does not appear in the list, and its page returns a 404. A pending observation can quote the repository's code, which is why read access is the rule. Accounts and roles explains how DAIV learns your access.

docs.title: Consolidate a repository now
docs.text:
An admin can run a round without waiting for the hourly sweep. The round ignores the thresholds and the minimum interval. You need memory on site-wide, because the Consolidate now button is absent while it is off.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → Memory.
  2. Select the repository.
  3. Select Consolidate now.

DAIV queues the round and shows Consolidation queued for <repository> (<n> pending observation(s)).. It queues nothing in two cases and says why:

  • There are no pending observations: Nothing to consolidate for <repository> — no pending observations.
  • The repository has a stored document but no entries: <repository> has a memory document but no entries, so consolidating would discard it. An administrator must run `backfill_memory_entries --repo-id <repository>` on the server first.

If the repository's .daiv.yml sets memory.enabled to false, the button still shows and DAIV still reports the round as queued, but the round skips the repository.

From a shell, consolidate_memory consolidates one repository in the foreground, and refuses to run while fewer than 10 observations are pending unless you pass --force. backfill_memory_entries rebuilds a repository's entries after an upgrade or a repair.

docs.title: Turn memory off
docs.text:
Memory has two switches, and a repository's memory works only while both are on:

  • The site-wide switch, in the Memory group of the site configuration. Site configuration lists the group, and Environment variables lists the DAIV_MEMORY_* variables that set the same values.
  • A repository's memory.enabled in .daiv.yml. Repository configuration describes it. A repository can opt out, but it cannot switch memory on where the site has it off.

While memory is off, DAIV extracts and consolidates nothing, and later runs get no document. The document and observations stay, and the dashboard shows them.

docs.title: Size limit
docs.text:
The document has a limit in lines and in bytes, 200 lines and 10240 bytes by default, so memory stays a short briefing and not an archive. Environment variables gives the settings that change them.

While the document fits, DAIV evicts nothing. When a round pushes it over a limit, DAIV evicts the least recently confirmed entry of the category with the most text, and repeats until the document fits. A small category is never drained to make room for a large one. DAIV never evicts the last remaining entry, even if it alone exceeds the limit. An evicted entry no longer appears in the document, and the dashboard does not show it.

docs.title: Merge metrics
docs.text: DAIV records every merge request (GitLab) or pull request (GitHub) merged into a default branch. For each merge it counts the lines changed and attributes them to DAIV or to people, commit by commit. The dashboard's Insights page shows the totals as code velocity.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Platform as GitLab / GitHub
    participant DAIV as DAIV
    participant Dashboard as Insights page

    Platform->>DAIV: merge event
    DAIV->>DAIV: skip unless the target is the default branch
    DAIV->>Platform: fetch diff statistics and the commit list
    DAIV->>DAIV: attribute each commit by author email
    Dashboard->>DAIV: read the totals for the chosen period

The steps below give the same flow in text.

  1. DAIV receives a merge event. GitLab sends a merge_request webhook with action: merge; GitHub sends a pull_request webhook with action: closed and merged: true.
  2. DAIV checks the target branch. It records only merges into the repository's default branch, and ignores merges into feature or release branches.
  3. DAIV fetches the data. A background task fetches the merge's diff statistics and its commit list from the platform API.
  4. DAIV attributes the lines. It compares each commit's author email with DAIV's bot commit email, and splits the lines added and removed into DAIV's and people's.
  5. DAIV shows the totals. The Code velocity section of the Insights page uses the same period filter as the agent activity counters: Today, 7 days, 30 days, 90 days or All time, with 7 days as the default.

If a platform call fails, DAIV still records the merge. When only the diff statistics fail, DAIV takes the lines changed from the sum over the commits; a figure whose own fetch failed stays at zero.

docs.title: Code velocity metrics
docs.text:
Everyone sees the Code velocity section, counted over the repositories they can read (administrators: every repository). It stays hidden when the period has no merges. The period filter at the top of the page applies to every figure.

Figure on the page What it counts merges Merge and pull requests merged into default branches involved DAIV The share of merges with at least one DAIV-authored commit, with both counts of commits by DAIV The share of commits authored by DAIV, with both counts lines changed Lines added and removed across all merges Merges over time Merges per day (per week for 30 and 90 days, per month for all time), split into those that involved DAIV and those by people only. Hidden for Today

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
DAIV identifies its own commits by matching the commit author email against its bot email:

  • GitLab: the bot user's commit_email, else its public_email, else its email, else <username>@users.noreply.gitlab.com
  • GitHub: <user_id>+<app_slug>[bot]@users.noreply.github.com

docs.title: Mixed authorship
docs.text: A merge request can hold commits from both DAIV and people. When a person opens one and then asks DAIV for follow-up changes with @daiv, DAIV splits the lines by each commit's author.

docs.title: Commit limits
docs.text: On GitLab, DAIV attributes the first 100 commits of a merge request. On GitHub, the platform lists at most 250 commits per pull request.

docs.title: Squash merges
docs.text: A squash merge collapses the commits into one on the target branch, but the platform API keeps the original commit list. DAIV attributes lines from that list, so squash merges are attributed like any other.

docs.title: Turn on merge metrics
docs.text:
Merge metrics need no configuration: DAIV records merges as soon as it receives merge events.

  • GitLab: DAIV registers merge_requests_events on each repository's webhook when it creates it. To add the event to webhooks registered earlier, run docker compose exec app django-admin setup_webhooks --update; see setup_webhooks.
  • GitHub: DAIV registers nothing. Subscribe your GitHub App to Pull request; Platform setup lists every event the App needs.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Sessions — the run history behind the DAIV-authored commits these metrics attribute
  • Issue addressing — the workflow that produces most DAIV-authored merges

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
DAIV tells you when your work needs attention. When a run finishes with something to look at, such as an issue found, a situation that needs review or an outright failure, DAIV writes an in-app notification and delivers it to external channels: email, Rocket.Chat and Telegram. Clean runs stay silent and appear only in their session, under Sessions.

Notifications are per user. Each recipient gets their own copy, delivered through that user's own channels.

docs.title: What produces a notification
docs.text:
DAIV classifies every finished run and notifies only when the outcome warrants it. The classifications that notify are found-issues, needs-attention, needs-input and failed. A run classified all-clear is silent: it appears in its session, under Sessions, and produces no notification. The exception is a run that a CI failure woke: it always notifies its owner, all-clear included (see pipeline watch).

A run is needs-input when the agent stopped to ask you a question instead of guessing. The notification's subject says the run is waiting for your answer, and its body lists the questions; open the session to answer them. A run that an issue or merge or pull request webhook started is the exception: DAIV posts its question as a comment on the issue or request, which mentions whoever triggered the run, so DAIV sends no separate notification for it.

Runs that webhooks start, such as issue addressing and the pull request assistant, report back in the issue or request thread. Like runs you start from the dashboard, the jobs API or the MCP endpoint, they also notify their initiator when the outcome notifies. To silence a run you start through the API or MCP, pass the muted flag.

These events cover runs and schedules:

Event When it fires Recipients Job finished (job.finished) A single agent run finishes with an outcome that notifies. The user who started the run. Job batch finished (job_batch.finished) Every run in a multi-run batch has finished. DAIV sends one rollup, not one message per run. The batch owner and, for a scheduled batch, its subscribers. Schedule finished (schedule.finished) A run of a scheduled job finishes with an outcome that notifies. The schedule's owner and subscribers. Schedule can't run (schedule_dispatch.failed) A scheduled job fails to start a run. DAIV sends it once per failing streak, even when the schedule is muted. The schedule's owner.

A batch is a group of runs that share a batch ID, for example a scheduled job that fans out across several repositories. For a multi-run batch, DAIV suppresses the per-run notifications and sends one Job batch finished rollup once the last run has finished. The rollup says how many runs notified and how many were all-clear. A run waiting for an answer counts as notifying, and the rollup lists it right after the failures.

Other notifications, such as the one DAIV sends when pipeline watch runs out of attempts, are described with their features.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
DAIV reaches you through channels. In-app notifications are always on. Email, Rocket.Chat and Telegram are external channels, and your administrator decides which of the last two appear.

Channel What you get What it needs In-app Notifications in the sidebar shows your unread count and opens your full history at /dashboard/notifications/. Nothing. Email A message to your account email address. Nothing. DAIV keeps a verified email channel in sync with your account address, so there is nothing to connect. Rocket Chat A direct message from the DAIV bot. An administrator has enabled Rocket.Chat, and you have connected your @username. Telegram A direct message from the DAIV bot. An administrator has enabled Telegram, and you have connected your chat.

A message about a run includes the run's summary. For a run waiting for an answer, that is the list of questions.

docs.title: The in-app list
docs.text:
DAIV writes an in-app entry for each run whose outcome notifies, and none for an all-clear run.

  • /dashboard/notifications/ lists your full history. Filter it with All, Unread and Read, or select Mark all as read. Opening a notification marks it read. The Settings link opens your notification channels.
  • The unread badge next to Notifications and the session lists in the sidebar update live over a server-sent events stream (GET /api/nav/events), so a new notification or a run starting or finishing appears without a reload. The stream needs Redis. Without it, they show their values from when the page loaded.

docs.title: Connect a channel
docs.text:
Email and in-app need no setup. Rocket.Chat and Telegram need an administrator to enable them first, and you then connect your own account on the channels page.

You need:

  • For Rocket.Chat, an administrator who has enabled it in Settings → Configuration → Rocket Chat, with the instance URL, bot user ID and auth token. See Site configuration.
  • For Telegram, an administrator who has enabled it in Settings → Configuration → Telegram, as described in Set up Telegram. Telegram delivery to chats that are already linked needs only outbound internet access, but connecting a new chat needs DAIV reachable from the internet over HTTPS. On an instance without public ingress, you cannot link new chats.
  • Until the channel is enabled, its row does not appear on your channels page.

To open the channels page, select Notification channels in the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar (/accounts/channels/).

docs.title: Connect Rocket.Chat
docs.text:
1. On the Notification channels page, find the Rocket Chat row.
  2. Enter your Rocket.Chat @username. DAIV strips a leading @.
  3. Select Connect.

DAIV checks the username against the Rocket.Chat instance. On success, the row shows a Verified badge and your handle. If the user is unknown or the instance is unreachable, DAIV shows an error and saves nothing: it stores no unverified binding.

To stop Rocket.Chat delivery, select Disconnect in the same row.

docs.title: Connect Telegram
docs.text:
A Telegram bot cannot start a conversation with you, so connecting is a handshake: you message the bot first, through a single-use link that DAIV gives you.

Warning

The link links whichever Telegram chat opens it first to your DAIV account. Do not forward it or share it.

  1. On the Notification channels page, find the Telegram row.
  2. Select Connect. DAIV hands you off to Telegram.
  3. In Telegram, open the chat with the DAIV bot. Telegram sends /start for you.
  4. Read the bot's reply, which confirms the connection, and check that the row on your channels page shows Verified and your Telegram handle.

You have nothing else to confirm, because messaging the bot is the verification.

The link works for 10 minutes and stops working as soon as any chat is linked to your account. If it expires, the bot tells you, and you start again from the channels page. If the row shows Not ready — ask an administrator to finish the Telegram setup. instead of Connect, ask your administrator to finish the setup.

A few rules apply to the link:

  • DAIV keeps at most one Telegram chat per account and one account per chat. Connecting from a different Telegram account replaces the previous link, and /start from a chat that is linked elsewhere moves it to you.
  • The bot links only one-to-one chats. If you add it to a group and send /start there, it replies Message me directly — DAIV notifications are per-account and cannot go to a group. and links nothing.

To stop Telegram delivery, do any one of these: select Disconnect on your channels page, send /stop to the bot, or block the bot in Telegram. Each unlinks the chat, and the row goes back to Not configured; select Connect to link again.

If DAIV could not be told that you blocked the bot, for example because its webhook was unreachable or Telegram refused the chat for another reason, the link stays on the row marked Unverified and delivers nothing. Select Connect to redo the handshake. If that does not clear it, select Disconnect, then Connect.

docs.title: Muting
docs.text:
Notifications fire on outcomes that notify, and you have no per-outcome setting. The only control is muting:

  • Scheduled runs. A schedule's Mute notifications setting, off by default, silences every notification for that schedule's runs: no in-app entry and no external delivery. It does not silence Schedule can't run, which reports that the schedule did not run at all. Muting applies to the owner and every subscriber alike.
  • Other runs. Runs you start from the dashboard, the jobs API or the MCP endpoint notify you on an outcome that notifies. Pass the muted flag in the API or MCP call to silence a run.

A muted run produces no in-app entry at all: muting is full silence. DAIV has no setting for turning email off while keeping in-app notifications.

docs.title: How delivery works
docs.text:
When a run finishes with an outcome that notifies, DAIV records the notification, then one delivery for each external channel, and sends each delivery from a background worker:

  • A channel with no usable connection, such as Rocket.Chat or Telegram before you connect, or a channel DAIV does not know, is recorded as skipped rather than attempted.
  • DAIV retries a transient failure, up to three attempts in all, waiting 1 minute before the second and 5 minutes before the third. A permanent failure, such as a refused recipient or a disabled channel, is marked failed and not retried. When the provider names its own wait, as Telegram's flood control does, DAIV delays the next attempt to at least that long, up to one hour.
  • Blocking the DAIV bot in Telegram normally unlinks your chat at once. When that message does not reach DAIV, DAIV notices the refusal on the next delivery instead. It keeps the link and marks it Unverified, because that condition never recovers by itself and retrying would only use up attempts. Later notifications are skipped, until you redo the handshake.
  • The in-app entry does not depend on external delivery. DAIV writes it even when every external channel is skipped or fails.

docs.text:
• Scheduled jobs: recurring runs with a mute setting and a subscriber list.
  • Jobs API: submit runs programmatically, with a muted flag.
  • Sessions: every notification links to its session or batch in the sessions list.
  • MCP endpoint: submit jobs from MCP clients, with a muted flag.

docs.title: Orchestration
docs.text:
Orchestration lets the agent hand work to new, independent jobs — on your other repositories or on its own — and pick up again once they have all finished, to report the combined outcome or carry on.

Use it to:

  • Coordinate multi-repository changes — bump a shared library in every service that depends on it.
  • Route tickets — read an issue queue and dispatch each ticket to the repository that owns it.
  • Fix findings one by one — triage Sentry, then open one fix per finding, each in its own merge request.
  • Split off a side fix — while working on a task, hand an unrelated problem you agreed to fix to a job of its own.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When orchestration is on, the agent gets a delegate_jobs tool. It takes a one-line goal and up to 10 targets, each a repository (another one, or the agent's own), an optional branch and a prompt written for that target. DAIV starts one independent job per target (a leg), and the coordinator ends its turn.

Each leg is an ordinary agent job in a session of its own: a fresh clone, its own context and budget, and its repository's .daiv.yml, skills and sandbox environment. A leg always publishes to a new branch and merge request of its own, even when the branch it starts from already has an open merge request, so legs never push onto each other's work or onto yours.

When the last leg finishes, DAIV queues a new run on the coordinator's session — a Delegation Resume run — whose prompt lists every leg's outcome, branch, merge request and reply. If the coordinator is still busy — its turn has not ended, or a chat turn or another run started on its session meanwhile — the resumed run waits for that run to finish, then starts from the branch that run left the session on. The coordinator picks up from there: it checks the results, reports them where the request came from (a comment on the ticket, for example), merges a leg's branch into its own, or delegates another batch. The resumed run can stop to ask a question like any other job, unless the coordinator's session was started by a schedule or a CI watch, where nobody is around to answer.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Coord as Coordinator session
    participant A as Leg A
    participant B as Leg B

    Coord->>A: delegate_jobs(goal, targets)
    Coord->>B: (same call)
    Note over Coord: ends its turn
    A-->>Coord: finished
    B-->>Coord: finished
    Note over Coord: resumed with every leg's outcome

The flow in text: the coordinator calls delegate_jobs and ends its turn, each leg runs on its own, and DAIV resumes the coordinator once every leg has finished, with every leg's outcome.

Nothing polls while the legs run: the coordinator holds no worker and spends no tokens until it is resumed.

When a leg comes back incomplete or wrong, the coordinator does not have to start over: a target that names the leg's session id (thread_id) is a leg follow-up. It continues that leg in its own session, with its earlier conversation, on its branch and merge request, so the fix lands where the leg's work already is. A leg follow-up joins the batch of the call that sent it, alongside any new legs, and the coordinator is resumed once all of them have finished.

docs.title: Turn off orchestration
docs.text:
Orchestration is on by default on every repository. To stop a repository's agent from splitting work off, add this to its .daiv.yml:

YAML
orchestration:
  enabled: false

A repository needs no configuration to receive delegated work: a leg is a normal job. Repository configuration lists every feature toggle.

docs.title: Where a leg's work lands
docs.text:
A target's ref is the branch the leg starts from and the branch its merge request targets:

  • Omit it for the repository's default branch: the leg's change stands on its own, in a merge request against the default branch.
  • Give the coordinator's current branch to build on its work, even when that is the default branch: such a leg starts once the coordinator's turn ends, from the branch that turn published to, so it sees everything the turn changed and its merge request targets that branch. When the coordinator is resumed it can merge the leg's branch into its own, or leave the leg's merge request for review.

docs.title: Following up a leg
docs.text:
Each leg in the resume names its session id. To fix or extend a leg's own work — its tests still fail, a reviewer asked for a change, its reply leaves a question open — the coordinator follows it up: it calls delegate_jobs with a target that has the leg's thread_id, its repo_id, no ref, and a prompt saying what to do next. For work that stands apart from every leg's, it delegates a new leg instead.

A leg follow-up:

  • Works where the leg's work is. It runs in the leg's session, with the leg's earlier conversation, and pushes to the leg's branch and merge request, even one a reviewer approved or set to merge when its pipeline passes: your platform's approval rules decide whether that push resets the approvals. A leg that published nothing opens a branch and merge request of its own, as a new leg would, never the branch it started from.
  • Waits its turn. When the leg's session is busy — fixing CI on its merge request, or answering a person's chat — the leg follow-up waits in its inbox, as Leg follow-up, until the session is free. It then runs alone, never in the same run as other waiting requests, and sees what happened meanwhile (a push to the branch, for example) as context.
  • Runs once. It is never retried: if its run fails, the batch reports it as failed and the coordinator decides whether to send another.
  • Stops when its merge request is gone or its session is archived. If the leg's merge request was merged or closed while the leg follow-up waited, it stops when it would start, without changing anything, and the coordinator reads not run: its merge request was merged (or closed) with the advice to delegate a new leg. If the leg's session is archived while it waits, it stops at once and the coordinator reads not run: its session was archived.

It runs as the user who triggered the coordinator's run, keeps the coordinator's mute and cannot ask questions, like a leg. That user's repository access is checked when it is sent, as for a new leg, and again when its run starts: one refused there is reported as failed.

docs.title: Following and cancelling the legs
docs.text:
Between resumes, the coordinator has two more tools:

  • check_delegated_jobs reports where its batches stand: each leg's status (queued, running, stopping, succeeded, failed, cancelled, or not run for a leg follow-up whose merge request was merged or closed, or whose session was archived), session, branch, merge request and reply. Given a batch_id it reports that batch, with replies up to 4,000 characters; without one, the session's five latest, with replies up to 1,000. The agent uses it when you ask how the work is going, never to wait for the legs: the resume comes on its own.
  • cancel_delegated_jobs cancels a batch's unfinished legs, or only the ones it names by thread_id, leg follow-ups included. A queued leg never starts, and cancelling a waiting leg follow-up leaves every other request waiting on the leg's session in place. A running leg shows as stopping until it stops, within about ten seconds, and may push to its branch or open a merge request before then. If it finishes first, it keeps its outcome. A cancelled leg's session shows it as stopped, and Notifications count it as failed.

The agent cancels when you ask it to, or when the work a leg does is no longer wanted. The coordinator is still resumed once the batch has finished, with the cancelled legs marked as such, unless every leg was cancelled: then no resume comes.

docs.title: Choose between task and delegate_jobs
docs.text: Use When Subagents (task) Focused or parallel work that fits in the current turn and the current workspace. Subagents share the run's working tree and report back within the turn. delegate_jobs on the same repository Work too big for one turn, or a separate change that deserves its own merge request. delegate_jobs on other repositories Work that belongs there.

docs.title: Write the prompts
docs.text:
A leg sees only its own prompt — not the coordinator's conversation, the ticket, or anything the coordinator looked up. Each target's prompt must therefore carry everything that leg needs, and should end with the no-change convention: "If there is nothing to change, reply saying so and make no changes."

A target can also carry references, linked into the leg's merge request like the Jobs API's; relation: closes resolves the issue on merge where the provider supports it.

JSON
{
  "goal": "Apply the CVE-2026-12345 patch",
  "targets": [
    { "repo_id": "mygroup/service-auth", "prompt": "Bump the auth library to 3.2.1 (CVE-2026-12345). If there is nothing to change, reply saying so and make no changes." },
    { "repo_id": "mygroup/service-api", "ref": "release/2.x", "prompt": "Update the auth dependency to 3.2.1 and fix any breaking import. If there is nothing to change, reply saying so and make no changes." }
  ]
}

The goal only titles the batch; it is never sent to a leg.

docs.title: Rules and limits
docs.text:
Rule Why At most 10 targets per call, leg follow-ups included Split larger fan-outs across calls. One level deep A leg gets no delegate_jobs tool, even on a repository with orchestration on, nor does a leg follow-up's run. One leg follow-up outstanding per leg A leg still working — on its first run, a leg follow-up, or waiting for the coordinator's turn — is refused a leg follow-up; the coordinator is resumed when it finishes and can follow it up then. A call that names one leg twice is refused as a whole. A leg follow-up names a leg of its own coordinator, its repository and no branch Otherwise that target is refused with what to do instead, and the call's other targets still start. An archived leg, one DAIV lost track of, and one whose merge request was merged or closed are refused too. A leg follow-up always wakes the leg Even at the leg's limit of runs in a row nobody asked for; its run still counts toward that limit, so CI fixes after it stay limited. Replies up to 4,000 characters The resume and the status of one batch show each leg's reply from its full final answer up to 4,000 characters, the overview of the latest batches up to 1,000; a cut reply says so and points to the leg's session. Every leg forks its own branch Any number of legs may start from the same branch, the coordinator's own included; each opens its own merge request. A leg given the coordinator's current branch waits for its turn to end So it starts from what the coordinator published, which is a new branch when the coordinator started on the default branch. A leg that omits ref starts at once. Legs run as the user who triggered the coordinator's run Targets that user cannot write to come back as failures; the rest still start. A run with no DAIV user behind it (e.g. a mention from an account not linked to DAIV) cannot delegate. The resumed run runs as the same user, and fails instead of starting if that user can no longer write to the coordinator's repository. Legs cannot ask questions Nobody is watching a leg, so it decides or reports instead of stopping for input. Legs and the resumed run keep the coordinator's mute A muted job or schedule stays quiet through its delegations. Only the coordinator's session can check or cancel its legs The tools see the batches their own session delegated, and no other session's. At most 3 runs in a row nobody asked for After three runs in a row on the coordinator's session that no person started, DAIV only remembers a finished batch instead of resuming it, until a person starts a run there, and tells the session's owner. Failing legs cannot loop the coordinator. The session inbox describes the limit.

If no target starts, the tool says so and no resume comes: the coordinator deals with the failures in the same turn. If the resumed run cannot be queued when the last leg finishes, or gives up waiting for the coordinator's session, DAIV retries it within a few minutes, and it starts any leg left waiting after the coordinator's turn ended.

The resumed run's summary never quotes DAIV's own error text, so the coordinator cannot post it on a public ticket: a leg that failed on DAIV's side links to its session instead.

docs.title: Ticket triage across repositories
docs.text:
A coordination repository can hold no production code at all and act as a routing hub:

  1. Attach your ticketing system as an MCP server (Jira, Linear, Request Tracker, …), so the coordinator can read tickets and comment on them.

  2. Write the routing rules in its AGENTS.md:

    Markdown
    # Routing rules

- Tickets tagged `backend` → mygroup/service-api
- Tickets tagged `frontend` → mygroup/service-web
- Unclassified tickets → skip, comment "needs triage label"

  3. Trigger it with a scheduled job that polls the queue, or from your ticketing system through the Jobs API:

    Text Only
    Fetch the open tickets not yet dispatched. Route each one with the rules in AGENTS.md and delegate one
target per ticket. When the legs finish, comment the merge request links on each ticket.

docs.title: One fix per Sentry finding
docs.text:
With orchestration on in the application's own repository and the Sentry MCP server enabled, a single prompt — run by hand or from a scheduled job — triages and fans out:

Text Only
Triage the unresolved Sentry issues of the last 24 hours. For each one worth fixing, delegate a fix on this
repository's default branch, with the issue's details in the prompt and the issue in `references` with
relation `closes`. When the fixes finish, summarise what was fixed and what was left alone, with links.

Each fix opens its own merge request against the default branch, linked to its Sentry issue.

docs.title: A side fix during a task
docs.text: While the agent works on a task in chat, it may come across an unrelated problem. It proposes the fix; once you agree, it delegates it, either on the default branch for a merge request of its own, or on the task's branch to merge it into the task. Either way the task's session carries on, and the agent tells you where the fix landed when the leg finishes.

docs.title: Seeing the batch
docs.text:
Every leg is its own session in the Sessions list, and the legs of one call share a batch. The coordinator's session page shows where each leg stands now, not where it stood when it was delegated:

  • Transcript — each delegate_jobs call is a Delegated jobs card: its goal, and one row per leg with its state, merge request and session.
  • Sidebar — the Delegated jobs section of the Info tab lists the legs batch by batch, newest first.

A leg is Queued, Starts after this turn, Running, Stopping, Finished, Failed, Cancelled, Lost (it started, but DAIV lost track of it), or Not run: merge request merged / closed / session archived (a leg follow-up that stopped before it ran). A leg that served several batches, through leg follow-ups, is listed under each batch and counted once in the Delegated jobs count, and the call card marks a leg follow-up's row as Leg follow-up. An open page updates within a few seconds of a leg starting or finishing. In both places, a leg whose session you cannot see shows only its repository, branch and state. A leg's own session page links back to the coordinator's (Delegated by) when you can see it.

The coordinator's session then shows the resumed run with the legs' summary. Notifications treat the legs as a batch, so you get one rollup when they need a look.

Why not call DAIV's own MCP endpoint?

submit_job starts the same kind of jobs, but a caller can only poll or block for the result. That suits an editor or a script; inside an agent run it would hold a worker while the legs wait for one, with no way to resume afterwards. delegate_jobs ends the coordinator's turn and resumes it when the work is done.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Repository configuration — the orchestration toggle
  • Jobs API and MCP endpoint — a batch can also give each repository its own prompt
  • Subagents — parallel work inside one turn

docs.title: Pipeline watch
docs.text: After DAIV publishes a merge request, it watches the merge request's CI and tells the session that published it what happened. A CI failure on a commit DAIV pushed wakes that session, up to a configurable number of times, to look at the failure and fix it; if the failure is not something a code change can fix, the run explains why instead of pushing. Everything else CI reports, a pass or a pipeline that needs a person, is remembered by the session and shown to the agent the next time it runs.

docs.title: Turn on CI events
docs.text: Pipeline watch reacts to CI events, and each platform delivers them differently. Without these events, DAIV hears of CI only through the reconciler's poll, which re-reads a watched merge request that nothing was heard of for 30 minutes, so a failure can wait 30 minutes or more. On GitHub, DAIV also cannot read CI at all until the App's Actions permission is Read-only.

docs.title: GitLab
docs.text:
DAIV registers pipeline_events on a repository's webhook when it creates the webhook. To add the event to webhooks DAIV registered earlier, run this on the host that runs DAIV:

Bash
docker compose exec app django-admin setup_webhooks --update

setup_webhooks describes the command.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
setup_webhooks does nothing on GitHub, because a GitHub App's event subscriptions are central, not per repository. Subscribing the App covers every repository it is installed on:

  1. Open your GitHub App's settings page and select Permissions & events.
  2. Under Repository permissions, set Actions to Read-only. This permission lets the App subscribe to Workflow run and read job logs.
  3. Under Subscribe to events, select Workflow run.
  4. Select Save changes.
  5. If Actions is a new permission for the App, ask each installation owner to accept it, from GitHub's email or the installation's Configure page. Pipeline watch stays off on an installation until its owner accepts.
  6. After the next workflow run, open Advanced → Recent Deliveries and check for a workflow_run delivery.

Platform setup lists every event the App needs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as DAIV Agent
    participant Session as Publishing session
    participant Watch as Pipeline Watch
    participant CI as GitLab / GitHub CI

    Agent->>Session: publish (records the pushed commit)
    CI-->>Watch: pipeline event (terminal state)
    Watch->>Watch: judge the head pipeline
    alt green
        Watch->>Session: CI passed (remembered)
    else needs a person (blocked / manual / canceled / skipped)
        Watch->>Session: CI stopped (remembered)
    else failure
        Watch->>Session: CI failed (wakes it, or remembered with a reason)
        Session->>Agent: run with the failed jobs and the pipeline link
        Agent->>CI: push a fix, or explain and push nothing
    end

The steps below give the same flow in text.

  1. The publishing session owns the merge request. When a run publishes, its session claims the merge request and records the commit DAIV pushed. A later publish from another session of the same person moves the merge request to that session; a publish from another person's session leaves it where it is and tells the owning session. Which runs claim a merge request lists the cases.
  2. Pipeline event. A webhook from GitLab (pipeline_events) or GitHub (workflow_run) delivers the terminal result. CI is also judged right after a publish, because the event can arrive before the claim exists. Only the merge request's head pipeline is judged; a pipeline an older push started is ignored.
  3. Judgment. See Conservative judgment below.

  4. Waking the session. A failure wakes the owning session only when all of these hold. The first one that does not is recorded as the reason the failure was only remembered, and the agent sees it the next time it runs.

    Condition Reason when it fails The watch is on for the repository and for this merge request Watch off The pipeline ran on the commit DAIV last pushed Not DAIV's commit No CI run looked at that commit yet Already examined Attempts are left Attempts spent DAIV has not started three runs in a row on the session without a person (see The session inbox) Too many runs in a row

  5. The CI run. DAIV runs it in the publishing session, on the merge request's branch, with a prompt naming the failed jobs and the pipeline URL. The agent reads the job logs through its gitlab / gh platform tool, then pushes a fix or explains why it pushed nothing. It can't ask a question: nobody is there to answer. If the session is busy, the failure waits and joins the session's next run.

  6. A run that pushes nothing explains, without giving up. No push means no new pipeline, so the session shows CI as failing with a link to that run's explanation, and you receive its summary as a run notification. Retrying the same pipeline by hand does not wake the session again: the commit was already examined. If the retry passes, the session shows CI passing.
  7. Attempts spent. When a failure on a new DAIV commit finds no attempts left, the merge request's owner is notified once for that commit. A run a person starts that publishes to the merge request gives the attempts back.
  8. Reconciler. A cron task runs every 10 minutes and re-reads the CI of each watched merge request nothing was heard of for 30 minutes, whatever it last reported, so a missed webhook (a manual retry's, say) is repaired. On GitLab it reads the branch's latest pipeline; on GitHub, the latest run of each workflow on the branch's head commit. A pipeline already judged in its status is skipped without reading its jobs. Nothing expires: the watch observes until the merge request is merged or closed. Each tick re-reads at most 200 branches, the longest-quiet first, and a branch it could not read is tried again on the next tick.

docs.title: Conservative judgment
docs.text:
DAIV errs toward remembering rather than spending an attempt on something it cannot fix. The decision table:

Rows are evaluated top to bottom; the first match wins.

Pipeline state Jobs Outcome still in progress (created, pending, running, preparing, …), or no pipeline found any Not judged — nothing posted; the next event or the reconciler looks again skipped zero jobs Not judged — a ci.skip push records this in place of a pipeline blocked, manual, canceled, skipped any Stopped — remembered, shown as needing a person any zero jobs Stopped — remembered, shown as needing a person failed at least one non-allow_failure failed job Failed — may wake the session failed no job reports failed at all (e.g. a config error) Failed — may wake the session failed every failed job is allow_failure Passed — effectively a pass success at least one job Passed

Why zero-job pipelines are stopped, not passed: a GitLab .gitlab-ci.yml that includes a cross-project template from a private repository resolves as the pushing identity. An ephemeral project-scoped token cannot read that private repository, so GitLab produces a pipeline with no jobs. Treating it as green would let a misconfigured pipeline pass silently; treating it as a failure would burn every attempt on a pipeline that was never going to run.

Why blocked/manual/skipped/canceled are stopped: these states reflect a human decision or an external gate. DAIV does not know whether to wait or act, so it remembers the result and lets you decide.

docs.title: CI status on the session page
docs.text: The sidebar's repository cards show CI for each open merge request the session owns. A card shows Waiting for CI while no result has arrived since DAIV last pushed or while a run is looking at a failure. It then shows Passing, Failing or Needs a person. A failing merge request links the last run that looked at a failure, whose summary says what it found.

docs.title: Turn the watch on or off for a merge request
docs.text:
The Fix CI failures switch turns the watch on or off for one merge request. With it off, DAIV still remembers CI results but never wakes the session. Turning it on gives the merge request its attempts back and judges the branch's latest pipelines again at once (on GitHub, every workflow's), so a failure reported while the watch was off, or while no attempts were left, wakes the session. A commit a run already looked at is not looked at again. You need to be able to run agents on the repository.

  1. Open the session that owns the merge request.
  2. In the repository card, open the ⋯ menu.
  3. Select Fix CI failures. A check mark shows the watch is on.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Every CI run produces the usual run notification, with the run's summary, so you hear what it found whether it pushed a fix or explained why it didn't. When attempts run out on a new DAIV commit, the merge request's owner gets one CI still failing notification for that commit, linking the owning session. A merge request whose owning session has no DAIV user behind it gets that outcome, and each CI run's summary, as a merge request comment instead.

docs.title: Limit or turn off pipeline watch
docs.text:
An administrator sets the site-wide switch and attempt cap under Configuration → Pipeline Watch, or with DAIV_PIPELINE_WATCH_ENABLED and DAIV_PIPELINE_WATCH_MAX_ATTEMPTS. With the switch off, no CI failure wakes a session, and sessions remember each failure with the reason Watch off. By default a merge request gets 3 fix attempts. Site configuration and the environment variables reference describe both settings.

A repository can only tighten the site-wide values. Set its options in .daiv.yml:

YAML
pipeline_watch:
  enabled: true
  max_attempts: 2

enabled: false stops CI failures on the repository from waking a session. max_attempts is capped at the site-wide value, and enabled: true does not turn the watch on where the site turned it off. Repository configuration lists both options.

docs.title: GitHub: allow_failure jobs
docs.text: The GitHub Actions API does not say which jobs are required, so DAIV treats every failed job as required. The verdict itself still comes from the workflow run's own conclusion, so a tolerated job's failure cannot by itself spend an attempt — a run that concludes success is green. What differs from GitLab is narrower: DAIV cannot exclude a tolerated job from the failure list it hands the agent, and it never reads a failed run as green on the grounds that every failure was tolerated.

docs.title: GitHub: one event per workflow, not per push
docs.text: A workflow_run event reports a single workflow, not the branch's whole CI. A repository with several workflows on one push delivers one event per workflow, each judged on its own — so the first workflow to finish green can show CI as passing while another is still running or about to fail. Repositories that split required checks across workflows should expect the status to flip as each workflow reports. A session that delegated the work is told its CI passed only once the latest run of every workflow on the commit has passed.

docs.title: GitLab: child pipelines
docs.text: A child pipeline (trigger: include:) runs on its parent's branch and commit, so DAIV ignores it and judges the parent pipeline, which is the merge request's result. For a child's failure to count, trigger it with strategy: depend, so the parent pipeline fails with it.

docs.title: GitLab: merge-request pipelines and the reconciler poll
docs.text: The reconciler's fallback poll lists pipelines by branch (ref=<source branch>). Detached merge-request pipelines are not on the branch ref — GitLab records them under refs/merge-requests/<iid>/head — so on projects that run only merge-request pipelines the poll finds nothing. This is harmless: a read that finds no pipeline posts nothing, so those repositories are driven entirely by the pipeline webhook.

docs.title: Which runs claim a merge request
docs.text:
How the merge request was published Session that owns it Issue addressing (daiv, daiv-auto or daiv-max label, or a mention on an issue) The issue's session Job runs — REST API, MCP submit_job, scheduled jobs The job's session Chat turn The chat session A CI run in the owning session Stays with that session, keeping the attempts spent Review addressing (DAIV answering comments on a merge request no session owns) None

Review addressing is excluded deliberately. It pushes to a merge request someone else may own, so babysitting that pipeline would put commits nobody asked for on their branch. Reviewers who want CI fixed can ask for it in a comment.

docs.title: What pipeline watch does not do
docs.text:
• Watches only merge requests DAIV published. There is no opt-in label to watch an existing merge request.
  • Does not distinguish flaky from real failures. Every failure on DAIV's commit may wake the session; the attempt cap bounds the cost, and a run that finds nothing to fix says so.
  • Does not react to CI on the default branch. The watch is scoped to the merge request's branch.

docs.title: Pull request assistant
docs.text:
The pull request assistant answers when you mention DAIV in a comment on a GitLab merge request or a GitHub pull request. DAIV applies review feedback, answers questions about the change, and fixes failing pipelines. The /code-review skill adds a full review: DAIV posts its findings as one review report.

On GitLab this works on merge requests, on GitHub on pull requests. This page says "pull request" for both.

docs.title: Ask DAIV on a merge request
docs.text:
To ask DAIV for something on a pull request:

  1. Open the pull request.

  2. Add a comment that mentions DAIV:

    Text Only
    @daiv <your request>

    Replace daiv with your DAIV bot's username if it differs, and <your request> with what you want.

DAIV reacts to your comment with an eyes emoji to confirm it received the request, then replies or pushes changes to the branch.

docs.title: Where to comment
docs.text:
You can mention DAIV in two places:

  • Inline on the diff — comment directly on specific lines of code. This reaches DAIV only on a merge request a DAIV session owns (see A merge request DAIV published)
  • General discussion — comment in the pull request conversation

DAIV sees the diff and the comment's position, so an inline comment tells it exactly what you mean.

docs.title: A merge request DAIV published
docs.text:
When a DAIV session published the merge or pull request, a mention goes to that session instead of starting a new one: the session that owns it (see The session inbox). It picks up where the session left off, and acts as you: as the DAIV account you signed in to with that GitLab/GitHub account, with its personal MCP servers, never as the session's owner. If you never signed in to DAIV with that account, the run gets no personal tools, even when a DAIV user shares your username. Its final message, or its question, is posted in the thread of your mention; when you mentioned DAIV in several threads before it answered, the full reply goes in the latest one, and each other thread gets a line linking to it.

A mention on a diff line reaches DAIV only on a merge request a session owns. On GitHub this also needs the App subscribed to Pull request review comment (see Platform setup). Comments that don't mention DAIV aren't answered, but the owning session remembers them, and its next run sees them. It remembers them from anyone but DAIV itself, even from people left out of allowed_usernames; only a mention needs its author on that list.

docs.title: Apply code changes
docs.text:
Ask DAIV to modify code based on your review feedback:

Text Only
@daiv use Redis instead of in-memory storage
Text Only
@daiv add error handling for the case when the API returns null
Text Only
@daiv move this logic to a separate helper function

docs.title: Answer questions
docs.text:
Ask DAIV about the code to help you make review decisions:

Text Only
@daiv why is this import inside the method instead of at the top?
Text Only
@daiv is this approach thread-safe?

docs.title: Fix failing pipelines
docs.text:
When CI/CD fails, ask DAIV to investigate and fix it:

Text Only
@daiv the pipeline is failing, can you fix it?

DAIV inspects the pipeline logs, identifies the root cause, and pushes a fix to the branch.

docs.title: Answer a question from DAIV
docs.text: When your request is ambiguous in a way that changes the work, or the choice is yours to make, DAIV can post a question instead of guessing. The question mentions you and ends with "reply mentioning @daiv with your answer." To answer, leave a new comment that mentions DAIV. On GitLab, DAIV posts its question inside the discussion thread of the comment that triggered it, so replying in that same thread keeps the conversation together; on GitHub the question is a top-level comment, unless you asked on a diff line of a merge request a session owns, where it is posted in that thread.

docs.title: Conversation continuity
docs.text: DAIV keeps its context across the mentions on one pull request. Each new mention builds on the earlier ones, so DAIV knows the history of changes and discussion. If DAIV drifts or gets stuck, comment @daiv /clear to reset the conversation; see Slash commands and skills.

docs.title: Review reports
docs.text:
DAIV posts each review as a single comment on the pull request — findings grouped by severity (Critical / Important / Suggestions), open questions for the author, and, when there are Critical or Important findings, a short list of recommended actions. On GitLab, reviews stack: a re-review posts a new report covering only the commits since the previous one (after a force-push, the next report covers the full change again and says so). If a review could not cover one of its dimensions — say the security detector failed — the report says so, and the next review re-covers that span rather than treating it as done. A review requested when nothing has changed since the last one answers with a one-line "already reviewed" note instead of a fresh report.

On GitHub the report carries no tracking marker: re-review scope comes from the conversation history on the pull request rather than from the reports themselves, so it is lost if that conversation is cleared — after which the next report covers the whole pull request again.

To ask about a finding or have DAIV apply a fix, reply on the pull request and mention DAIV.

docs.title: Custom review rules
docs.text:
Define team-specific review rules in .agents/review-rules.md at the repository root. Write them in plain language, one rule per bullet, with any path scope expressed in prose:

  • Every external API call in src/payments/** must set an explicit timeout.
  • Never log request or response bodies.
  • New Celery tasks must be idempotent.

The code review agent checks for rule sources at the start of every review and, when any exist, runs a dedicated cr-custom-rules detector against the diff; each violation it posts cites the rule it enforces.

.agents/review-rules.md is optional: rules already written in your repository's AGENTS.md and .agents/AGENTS.md are a secondary source, which the agent mines for concrete conventions it can check against the diff. When sources disagree, .agents/review-rules.md wins. The detector is skipped only when none of these files exist.

Every custom-rule finding passes the same confidence gate and skeptical aggregation as built-in findings, so a noisy AGENTS.md does not flood the review.

docs.title: Turn off the assistant
docs.text:
The pull request assistant is on by default. To turn it off for a repository, add this to its .daiv.yml:

YAML
pull_request_assistant:
  enabled: false

Repository configuration lists every feature toggle.
