docs.title: Sandbox environments
docs.text:
A sandbox environment is a named, reusable sandbox runtime: a base image, CPU and memory limits, an egress policy, encrypted environment variables, and the repositories it applies to. You define it once, and DAIV reuses it for every run, chat, scheduled job, and API or MCP call that lands in a matching repository.

An environment is how you give the agent a toolchain image, outbound network access to install dependencies, or a secret such as an API token or a private registry credential. When no environment matches a run (none selected, none bound to the repository, and no global default), the run has no sandbox and the agent gets no bash tool.

To manage environments, select Settings → Sandbox environments in the sidebar (/dashboard/sandbox-envs/). Settings is the cog beside your account at the bottom of the sidebar. Global environments lists the shared environments, and My environments lists yours.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
An environment has one of two scopes:

Scope Who sees it Who manages it User Only you You Global Everyone Administrators

Any signed-in user creates, changes and deletes their own User environments. Only administrators create, change and delete Global environments, and only they can make one the default. Other users see Global environments in the list and can select them for a run. In the form, the Scope choice offers only Personal to other users, and offers Shared with everyone (a Global environment) to administrators as well.

When DAIV picks an environment for a repository, a User environment that claims the repository wins over a Global one, so you can override an organization-wide setup for the repositories you care about.

docs.title: Global default
docs.text:
One Global environment can be the default. DAIV falls back to it when no other environment matches a repository, and it supplies the CPUs, memory and environment variables that other environments leave unset (see How an environment is resolved). A fresh install seeds a global environment named Default with a base image, set as the default. With no global default, a run that matches no environment has no sandbox.

To make an environment the global default, as an administrator:

Changing the default replaces sandboxes

The default's settings flow into the effective runtime of every session that inherits from it, so making another environment the default replaces those sessions' sandboxes on their next turn, and anything installed in them or left uncommitted is lost.

  1. In Global environments, find the environment.
  2. Select Make default. The environment gets a default tag, and the previous default loses it.

You cannot delete the global default: DAIV shows Set another global environment as default before deleting this one. Make another environment the default first.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
You need a base image for the environment, such as python:3.14. To let the agent install dependencies, you also need to know which hosts it must reach.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → Sandbox environments.
  2. Select New environment. The New sandbox environment drawer opens.
  3. Fill in the fields in the table below, starting with Name and Base image.
  4. Select Save. The drawer closes, and the environment appears in its list.
Field What to enter Name A label of up to 80 characters, unique within its scope. Required. Description Free text. Optional. Scope Personal for a User environment, or Shared with everyone for a Global one. Only administrators see the second choice. Base image The image the sandbox runs, for example python:3.14, node:22 or ubuntu:24.04. Required. Environment variables Name and value pairs for the sandbox, each plain or secret. See Environment variables. Repositories The repositories the environment claims, as owner/repo or group/subgroup/repo. See Repository bindings. Network Off (the default) or On. On shows the Network access section. See Network access and egress policy. Resources Expand it to set Memory and CPUs. Each is Use default or Custom. Memory A whole number of at least 1, with the unit MiB or GiB. CPUs A number of at least 0.25, in steps of 0.25.

Use default leaves Memory or CPUs unset, so the value comes from the global default environment. If that sets none either, DAIV asks for no limit. On the global default itself, the option reads Unconstrained. Network never comes from the global default: each environment sets its own.

docs.title: Change an environment
docs.text:
Changing an environment replaces the sandbox

A change to the base image, memory, CPUs, environment variables or egress policy replaces the sandbox of every existing session that uses the environment, on that session's next turn. The new sandbox starts from the repository, so anything installed in the old one, and anything a stopped turn left uncommitted, is lost.

To change an environment:

  1. In Sandbox environments, select Edit next to the environment.
  2. Change the fields, as in Create an environment.
  3. Select Save.

DAIV replaces a session's sandbox when the environment the turn resolves to differs from the one the sandbox started from. The comparison uses the environment merged over the global default, so switching the session to another environment, or changing the global default, replaces the sandbox too. DAIV updates a new git token on the running sandbox instead of replacing it.

docs.title: Delete an environment
docs.text:
Deleting cannot be undone

Deleting an environment destroys its stored environment variables and credentials. Sessions that recorded it fall back to the global default, which replaces their sandboxes on their next turn.

  1. In Sandbox environments, select Delete next to the environment.
  2. Select Delete to confirm Delete environment "<name>"?.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Each variable has a name and a value. A name is a shell identifier: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit. An environment has at most 100 variables, and the encrypted values together may not exceed 32 KiB.

  • Select + Add variable to add a row, or Paste .env to import lines such as KEY=value. DAIV skips comments and blank lines, and you choose whether to merge (names that already exist are kept) or to replace all current variables.
  • Set a row's toggle to Secret to hide its value. DAIV never shows a stored secret again: the dashboard shows the placeholder 🔒 keep existing, and API and MCP responses show ******. When you save, a secret keeps its stored value unless you type a new one.

DAIV encrypts the values with Fernet before it stores them and decrypts them when a run needs them, using DAIV_ENCRYPTION_KEY (see Environment variables). If the key changes and DAIV can no longer decrypt the stored values, the form refuses to save until you re-enter every secret value. Agent runs continue without the unreadable variables.

docs.title: Network access and egress policy
docs.text:
An environment with Network set to Off has no outbound network access. With Network set to On, the sandbox reaches only the hosts the Network access section allows, through the egress proxy of daiv-sandbox. The proxy can add a credential to a request, so a credential never enters the sandbox.

The egress proxy needs a CA certificate and key on the sandbox service (see Deployment files). Without them, a run that uses an environment with Network On stops instead of running with unrestricted network access.

DAIV runs git, including the push that publishes a run, from inside the sandbox. So DAIV always allows the run's git platform (GitLab or GitHub) and authenticates it with a short-lived token that the git platform mints at DAIV's request for the run, even when Network is Off. You never list it. Otherwise a Network Off environment stays isolated, and the git platform is opened only when the run holds a push token, so evaluation runs without one stay fully isolated.

docs.title: Allowed hosts
docs.text:
Allowed hosts lists one rule per host:

Control Meaning Host field A host name or a glob such as pypi.org or *.github.com. Select + Add host to add a rule. All methods or Read-only The HTTP methods the rule covers. Read-only covers GET, HEAD and OPTIONS. + credential An HTTP header name, such as Authorization, and a value. The proxy adds the header to every request to the host.

Unlisted hosts sets what happens to a request that matches no rule:

  • Deny blocks it.
  • Allow lets it through.

With Network On, the policy must permit something. DAIV rejects a policy that has no allowed host and sets Unlisted hosts to Deny, with Network is On but the egress policy permits nothing. Add at least one allowed host, set the default to allow, or switch Network to Off. To block all general outbound traffic, set Network to Off. DAIV then stores no egress policy.

The proxy always inspects the TLS traffic of every reachable host, which is what lets it add credentials and enforce the method rules. You cannot turn that off.

DAIV encrypts credential values with Fernet before it stores them, and never sends them back to the browser or in an API or MCP response. A saved credential shows the placeholder 🔒 keep existing, and saving keeps it unless you type a new value. An environment has at most 100 allowed-host rules and 100 credentials, and the encrypted credentials together may not exceed 32 KiB. A credential header name must be a valid HTTP header name, and its value cannot contain a line break.

If DAIV cannot decrypt an environment's egress credentials at run time, or its egress configuration is invalid, the run starts with no network access.

docs.title: Repository bindings
docs.text:
The Repositories field lists the repositories the environment claims. To add one, type owner/repo or group/subgroup/repo and select + Add. When a run targets a claimed repository and no environment is selected, DAIV picks this one (see How an environment is resolved).

A repository can be claimed by one environment per scope. For User environments, that means one of your own. DAIV rejects a binding that overlaps another environment of the same scope and names that environment. The same repository can still appear in one User environment and one Global environment, and the User one wins.

docs.title: How an environment is resolved
docs.text:
When a run is requested, DAIV picks its environment for each repository in this order, records the choice on the run, and a session keeps the environment of its first run:

  1. Selected environment. An environment chosen for the run overrides everything below. See Choose an environment for a run.
  2. User binding. Your User environment that claims the repository.
  3. Global binding. A Global environment that is not the default and that claims the repository.
  4. Global default. The Global environment marked as default.
  5. None. The run has no sandbox, and the agent gets no bash tool.
flowchart TD
    A[Run requested for a repo] --> B{Environment<br/>selected?}
    B -- Yes --> Z[Use it]
    B -- No --> C{User env binds<br/>this repo?}
    C -- Yes --> Z
    C -- No --> D{Global env binds<br/>this repo?}
    D -- Yes --> Z
    D -- No --> E{Global default<br/>exists?}
    E -- Yes --> Z
    E -- No --> F[No sandbox]

Runs that a webhook starts, such as issue addressing, skip step 2: DAIV does not match User environments for them, even when the author has a DAIV account. They start at step 3.

DAIV then merges the chosen environment over the global default to get the effective runtime. The chosen environment wins for the base image, memory and CPUs when it sets a value, and the global default fills the rest. The environment variables of both are combined, and the chosen environment's variables replace same-named ones of the default. The egress policy is the exception: it comes from the chosen environment alone, so an environment with Network Off never inherits the default's policy.

The run starts from the recorded choice, so changing a binding afterwards moves no existing run. A run that a session's inbox starts, such as a pipeline watch CI fix, uses the environment recorded on the session. For a run on behalf of someone else, such as a reply to another person's mention, DAIV never uses the session owner's User environment. It resolves one for that person instead: their own, a repository binding, or the global default. A session with no recorded environment, because its publishing run had none, it started before any environment existed, or its environment was deleted, runs on the global default.

docs.title: Choose an environment for a run
docs.text:
You do not have to bind an environment to a repository, because you can select one for a run. A selected environment always wins. Each surface has its own control, described on its page:

  • The run composer and the chat workspace, in Sessions: the environment pill in the run composer, and the Environment field in the chat workspace. Both stay on Auto until you choose.
  • A schedule, in Scheduled jobs: pin every run of the schedule to one environment.
  • The environment field of POST /api/jobs, in the Jobs API.
  • The environment argument of the submit_job tool, in the MCP endpoint, which also has the list_environments and get_environment tools to look environments up.

Auto means DAIV resolves the environment as above.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text: The sandbox is the isolated runtime where DAIV's agent runs shell commands: tests, linters, dependency installs, build scripts and git inspection. daiv-sandbox, a companion service, starts and manages it. The agent reaches it through the bash tool, and a command policy decides which commands it may run.

docs.title: What the agent can do
docs.text:
With a sandbox, the agent can:

  • Run tests and linters to validate changes.
  • Install and update dependencies (npm, pip, uv and others), which needs network access.
  • Inspect git state (git status, git diff, git log).
  • Execute build scripts and generators.
  • Run any command that the command policy allows.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The agent runs commands only when it has a sandbox, and installs only when the sandbox has network access:

  • A base image. A run has a sandbox only when its sandbox environment sets a base image. When no environment matches the run (none selected, none bound to the repository, and no global default), the run has no sandbox and the agent gets no bash tool. A fresh install seeds a global Default environment, so a fresh install starts with a sandbox. See How an environment is resolved.
  • Network access for installs. Installing or updating dependencies reaches package registries such as npm and PyPI. A sandbox has no outbound network access unless its environment has Network set to On and an egress policy that allows the registries, so these commands fail until you set both. See Network access and egress policy.

docs.title: Sandbox session lifetime
docs.text:
A sandbox session works on the repository's code and keeps its state between commands, so the agent can install a dependency in one step and use it in the next.

When a run ends, whether it finished, failed or stopped, DAIV stops the sandbox session. The next turn of the same session restarts it, so what the agent installed is still there. The turn starts from a fresh sandbox instead when the session's environment changed or the sandbox service no longer has the old one.

docs.title: Command timeouts
docs.text:
Each command times out after 5 minutes. The agent can give a command it expects to run longer, such as a full test suite or a build, a longer timeout, up to the sandbox timeout (DAIV_SANDBOX_TIMEOUT, see Environment variables). A sandbox timeout below 5 minutes lowers the default too. A timed-out command ends with exit code 124.

DAIV adds advice to the output of a timed-out command: run it again with a larger timeout when there is room, or narrow it down. With daiv-sandbox 0.5.0 a timed-out command can keep running in the sandbox, so DAIV also tells the agent to stop it before running it again.

docs.title: Command policy
docs.text: Not every command is safe for an AI agent to run. DAIV checks each command against a command policy before it reaches the sandbox. A command DAIV cannot parse is blocked, and the agent gets the reason.

docs.title: Built-in rules
docs.text:
DAIV always blocks the following commands. No setting overrides them.

Category Blocked commands Git history mutation git commit, git push, git reset, git rebase, git merge (except git merge --no-commit --no-ff <ref> with no flag that commits or fast-forwards, and git merge --abort), git pull, git cherry-pick, git revert, git am, git reflog delete, git filter-branch, git filter-repo Branch switching git checkout, git switch Git index manipulation git add, git stage, git hash-object, git update-index, git read-tree, git commit-tree Destructive operations git clean, git restore . Branch and tag deletion git branch -D and git branch --delete, git tag -d and git tag --delete Git configuration git config Platform CLI tools gitlab, gh, python -m gitlab

DAIV commits, pushes and manages branches through its own tools, so the sandbox is for everything else. DAIV pushes the branch the run started on, so the agent cannot switch branches and restores files with git restore <path> instead of git checkout.

The agent can still merge a branch in, for example to resolve a merge request's conflicts with its target branch. It runs git merge --no-commit --no-ff <ref> and resolves the conflicts, and DAIV commits the result as a merge commit at the end of the turn, listing the files that conflicted. If a conflicted file still contains conflict markers, DAIV commits and pushes nothing, and says so in its reply.

The policy checks every command in the invocation, including those in chains, pipelines, if and case statements, loops, subshells and functions. It looks past leading variable assignments, so HUSKY=0 git commit is blocked. It does not look inside command or process substitutions ($(…), backticks, <(…)), variable expansions (git $cmd), bash -c or eval strings, or wrappers such as env, and it compares words exactly as written, so /usr/bin/git push, \git push and git "push" pass. It is a guardrail that stops the agent's plain invocations, not a security boundary.

docs.title: Global rules
docs.text:
An operator can block more commands with DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_DISALLOW, a JSON array such as ["curl", "npm publish"]. See Environment variables for the variable. Each entry is a command name followed by the arguments that must appear after it, in that order but not necessarily next to each other, so npm publish also blocks npm run publish.

  • For git, the first argument must be the git subcommand itself: git revert blocks git -C repo revert but not git log --grep revert.
  • When a git option the policy does not know comes before the subcommand, the rule matches its arguments anywhere, so an unfamiliar option cannot hide a blocked subcommand.
  • Matching ignores case and the order of bundled short flags, so rm -rf also blocks rm -fr.

DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_ALLOW takes the same format and has no effect (see Precedence).

The policy is global: there is no per-repository or per-environment policy. DAIV ignores a sandbox.command_policy section left in .daiv.yml from v2.0.0 without a warning, so move its disallow entries to DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_DISALLOW.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
DAIV checks the rules in this order and stops at the first that applies:

  1. Built-in rules always win and cannot be overridden.
  2. Configured disallow rules from DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_DISALLOW cannot be overridden by an allow rule.
  3. Configured allow rules from DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_ALLOW allow only what step 4 already allows, so they change nothing.
  4. Default: every other command is allowed.

docs.title: Sandbox configuration
docs.text: A sandbox environment holds a sandbox's base image, CPUs, memory, network access and environment variables, not .daiv.yml. See Sandbox environments to create one and to see how DAIV picks the environment for a run.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs
docs.text:
Scheduled jobs run DAIV agents on a recurring basis, with no CI pipeline or cron script. You give a prompt, one or more repositories and a frequency, and DAIV starts the runs when they are due.

Use a schedule for recurring work such as a weekly dependency audit, a nightly code-quality scan, closing stale branches every Monday, a periodic summary of recent changes for a changelog draft, or a check for TODO comments or outdated documentation.

docs.title: Create a schedule
docs.text:
You need access to the repositories you want to run against. A schedule runs with its owner's repository permissions, so DAIV must be able to confirm that you have write access to each repository; see When a schedule can't run.

  1. In the sidebar, select Manage schedules, the list icon beside Scheduled.
  2. Select Create schedule.
  3. Enter a Name, for example Weekly dep audit.
  4. In the prompt box, describe what the agent does in each run.
  5. Select Add repository and choose one to 20 repositories. Each entry has its own branch; leave it on the default to start from the repository's default branch.
  6. Choose a Frequency, then fill the field it shows (see Frequency options).
  7. Optionally set the other fields in Schedule fields.
  8. Select Create schedule.

The schedule is active as soon as you save it. To pause it, see Manage schedules.

docs.title: Schedule fields
docs.text:
Field Description Name A short label for the schedule. Prompt box What the agent does. It has the same form as a jobs API prompt. Repositories One to 20 repositories, each with its own branch. A merge or pull request a run opens targets that branch, and DAIV assigns it to the schedule's owner when their DAIV account is OAuth-linked to the git platform. Each run fans out into one agent run per repository. Agent picker The model and thinking level the runs use. The picker starts on the instance's default model, and the schedule stores the model it shows. A run tries that model first, then the repository's models.agent model as a fallback. A schedule created over MCP without agent_model has no stored model and uses the repository's model, else the system default; see schedule_job parameters. Environment picker The named sandbox environment the runs use. It defaults to Auto, which resolves an environment for each repository. Frequency How often the schedule runs; see Frequency options. Time The time of day for Daily, Weekdays and Weekly schedules. Cron Expression The five-field cron expression for a Custom schedule. Date & time The moment a Once schedule fires. Intent What the schedule is for: Watch & find, Do & change or Report. The default is Watch & find. Mute notifications Silences all notifications for this schedule's runs, in-app and external. Off by default. The owner still gets the Schedule can't run notice. Subscribers Other DAIV users who get the finish notifications; see Subscribers. Enabled On the edit page only. When off, the schedule does not run until you turn it on again.

Schedule times are read in the instance's fixed time zone, and a schedule has no time zone of its own; see Time zone.

docs.title: Frequency options
docs.text:
Frequency Cron equivalent Notes Hourly 0 * * * * Runs at the top of every hour. Daily {mm} {HH} * * * Runs once a day at the time you set. Weekdays {mm} {HH} * * 1-5 Runs Monday through Friday at the time you set. Weekly {mm} {HH} * * 1 Runs every Monday at the time you set. Custom Your expression Any valid five-field cron expression: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. For example 0 */6 * * * runs every 6 hours, and 0 9 1-7 * 1 runs on the first Monday of the month. Once None Runs a single time at the Date & time you set.

A Once schedule runs one time, then retires: DAIV disables it, gives it no next run, and shows it as a read-only Fired card. You cannot re-enable a fired one-off schedule; use Duplicate to run it again (see Manage schedules).

docs.title: How scheduled runs start
docs.text:
Every minute, DAIV checks for enabled schedules that are due. For each one it:

  1. Starts one agent run per target repository, through the same task backend as the jobs API, and records the batch ID.
  2. Records the run time and adds one to the run count.
  3. Works out the next run time from the schedule's frequency. A Once schedule retires instead.

If a schedule fails to start, DAIV still moves its next run time forward, so it does not fire again every minute. If even that recovery fails, DAIV disables the schedule. Either way, DAIV records the failure on the schedule and tells the owner; see When a schedule can't run.

A schedule never starts twice when a check overruns the minute, and one schedule's failure does not stop the others. A schedule whose owner is inactive is skipped. After downtime, the times a schedule missed collapse into a single run, and DAIV then moves to the next time after now.

A scheduled run cannot ask you a question, because nobody is there to answer. The agent does not get the ask-the-user tool.

docs.title: Time zone
docs.text: DAIV reads schedule times in the Europe/Lisbon time zone, and a schedule has no time zone of its own. A daily schedule set to 09:00 fires at 09:00 Europe/Lisbon all year, across daylight saving changes. The zone is fixed in the settings; see Time zone.

docs.title: Manage schedules
docs.text:
On the Scheduled Jobs page, each schedule has an actions menu:

  • Pause or Resume the schedule, without opening the edit page.
  • Run now to start a batch immediately instead of waiting for the next scheduled time. You land on the resulting session, or on the Sessions list filtered to the batch when it spans several repositories.
  • Duplicate the schedule to create a new one pre-filled from it. It is the only way to run a fired one-off schedule again.
  • Delete the schedule; see Delete a schedule.

A fired one-off schedule offers only Duplicate and Delete. To change a schedule, including its Enabled setting, select its card to open the edit page.

Each schedule card shows its name, its status (Active, Failing, Paused or Fired), its frequency, its target repository (or "N repositories" when it has several), its next and last run times, its run count and its owner's avatar. Selecting the run count opens the Sessions list filtered to that schedule's sessions.

Non-admin users see only their own schedules. Admins see everyone's, and the owner avatar on each card shows whose it is.

docs.title: Delete a schedule
docs.text:
Warning

Deleting a schedule removes it permanently and cannot be undone. A run that is already running completes, but DAIV starts no new runs. The sessions the schedule produced remain, but its subscribers lose access to them.

  1. In the schedule's actions menu, select Delete, or select Delete schedule on its edit page.
  2. On the confirmation page, select Delete schedule.

docs.title: When a schedule can't run
docs.text:
A scheduled run can fail to start. Most often, DAIV could not confirm that the schedule's owner has write access to one of its repositories, because schedules run with their owner's repository permissions. It can also be an unexpected error, including every repository in the batch failing to start. When that happens:

  • The schedule card shows Failing with the reason, and the edit page explains how to fix it. A paused schedule reads Paused but keeps the reason.
  • The owner gets one Schedule can't run notification per failing streak, even when the schedule is muted. Subscribers get none, since they cannot fix the owner's access.
  • A recurring schedule keeps trying at each scheduled time. A one-off schedule retires; give it a new date and time and enable it to try again.

The failing state clears at the next scheduled run that starts, or when you change the schedule's repositories. Run now does not clear it.

docs.title: Subscribers
docs.text:
A schedule's owner can add other DAIV users as subscribers, who get the schedule's finish notifications. A subscriber:

  • Receives the same notifications as the owner on notify-worthy outcomes, unless the schedule is muted. Muting silences the owner and every subscriber alike, and there is no per-subscriber setting. The outcomes are found issues, needs attention, needs input and failed.
  • Gets read-only access to the sessions the schedule produces: the session detail, transcript and run timeline.
  • Does not see the schedule in their own list, and cannot edit, pause, run or delete it.

Only the owner or an admin can change a schedule's subscribers.

To add a subscriber:

  1. Open the schedule's form and find Subscribers.
  2. Select Add subscriber and search for a user by username, email or name.
  3. Select a result to add the user.
  4. Select Save changes.

To remove a subscriber, select the × on their chip in Subscribers, then select Save changes. A subscriber cannot unsubscribe themselves; ask the owner or an admin.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs and the jobs API
docs.text:
Scheduled jobs and the jobs API start the same kind of agent run. They differ in what starts it:

Jobs API Scheduled jobs Trigger An HTTP request The schedule, on its own Authentication API key Dashboard sign-in Management Programmatic Web UI Use A one-off or script-driven run A recurring run

To create schedules from a script, call the schedule_job tool of the MCP endpoint, or trigger runs from an external scheduler, such as a GitLab CI scheduled pipeline or system cron, through the jobs API.

docs.title: Schedule templates
docs.text: A schedule template is a reusable starting point for a schedule. It carries the same settings as a schedule (prompt, default repositories, frequency, time or cron expression, agent model and thinking level, intent and mute setting), plus an optional description that helps people choose. A template has no sandbox environment and no Date & time. When you start a schedule from a template, DAIV copies the template's values into the schedule form, and you can change any of them before you save. Editing or deleting a template never changes the schedules made from it.

docs.title: Start a schedule from a template
docs.text:
You need at least one template; an admin creates them. Then:

  1. Open the template gallery from the Schedules page, with From template or, on an empty list, Start from template. In the create form, use Browse templates.
  2. Search for a template. Each card shows its name, frequency, default repositories and description, and you can expand it for the full detail.
  3. Select Use on the template you want. If the create form has unsaved changes, DAIV asks Discard your current changes and apply this template? so you do not lose work.
  4. Adjust the pre-filled fields, then select Create schedule.

docs.title: Create a schedule template
docs.text:
Creating templates needs the admin role.

  1. In the sidebar, select Settings → Schedule templates.
  2. Select New template.
  3. Fill in the Name and an optional Description, then the same settings as a schedule. Repositories are optional: leave them empty to let people choose when they create the schedule.
  4. Select Create template.

docs.title: Delete a schedule template
docs.text:
Warning

Deleting a template removes it from the gallery and cannot be undone. Schedules made from it are unchanged.

Open the template and select Delete template, then confirm with Delete template.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
DAIV records every agent execution in a session: one persistent conversation with the agent, tied to a repository and ref. Every way you can trigger DAIV (webhooks, the jobs API, the MCP endpoint, scheduled jobs, or a chat you type yourself) produces a session, and every time the agent runs in that session adds a run to it.

Your own sessions are listed in the app sidebar. The search icon beside its Sessions heading opens the full list (/dashboard/sessions/), with every session you can see. A session's page holds its transcript, its run timeline, and its timing and usage.

docs.title: Who can see a session
docs.text: Admins see every session on every repository. Other users see their own sessions, sessions on repositories they can read on the Git platform, the sessions started by a GitLab or GitHub account they signed in to DAIV with (matched by the account's id, not its username), and the sessions of scheduled jobs they subscribe to. The same scoping applies to a session's page, its live updates and its retries.

docs.title: Sessions and runs
docs.text:
A session is the conversation. It has a repository, a ref, an origin (how it was first triggered), a title, and an optional link to an issue, a merge request, a schedule or a user.

A run is one agent execution inside a session. Retries, chat turns and API submissions that continue the session each add a run to the same session.

A run starts as Queued (waiting for the session's current run to end) or Pending, then becomes Running, and ends as Done, Needs input or Failed.

A run's record, with its token usage and cost, stays after DAIV deletes its full result: Poll job status describes what a finished run's result holds by then.

A chat is a session whose origin is Chat, and each message you send is a run. A webhook event on an issue or merge request creates a session tied to it, and the single agent invocation is its first run.

A session can also span several repositories. A jobs API or MCP request with shared_session opens one session over up to 5 repositories, the first being the main one. The agent edits them together, each changed repository gets its own merge request, and the session page lists every repository and merge request. Only admins and users who can read all of its repositories can see such a session.

docs.title: Session origins
docs.text:
Each session carries the origin that created it:

Origin Source Example Chat The dashboard chat You type a prompt and read the reply as it streams API Run Jobs API POST /api/jobs A CI pipeline or script submits a prompt MCP Run MCP endpoint submit_job tool Claude Code or Cursor delegates a task Scheduled Run Scheduled jobs dispatch A weekly dependency audit fires on Monday UI Run The dashboard's background run form You start a run from the dashboard Issue Webhook A GitLab or GitHub issue event An issue is labelled daiv MR/PR Webhook A GitLab or GitHub merge request event A reviewer mentions @daiv on a merge request Pipeline Webhook A CI result that DAIV's pipeline watch acts on DAIV starts a run to fix a failed pipeline on a merge request it published Delegated Run A coordinator's delegate_jobs call (orchestration), including a leg follow-up that continues the session One repository's part of a multi-repository change Delegation Resume The run that resumes a coordinator once its delegated batch has finished (orchestration) The coordinator checks every leg's outcome and reports

docs.title: The app sidebar
docs.text:
The sidebar lists your sessions, so any of them is one click away from every page:

  • Sessions: your own sessions, most recently active first, 8 at a time. Show more adds 8, up to 80; past that it opens the sessions list. Each has a status dot and, while it is running, waiting for your input or failed, that state; otherwise how long ago it was active. The session you are viewing is always in the list. Sessions a schedule started are listed under their schedule instead. Beside the heading, the search icon (shortcut /) opens the sessions list with its search box focused, and + starts a chat.
  • Scheduled: up to 10 schedules you own or subscribe to that are enabled or ran in the last 14 days, each with its next run. Expand one for its 3 latest runs: one row per run of the schedule, with the worst status across its repositories and, past one, how many repositories it ran on. A run on one repository opens its session; a wider one opens the sessions it started. All runs lists every session of the schedule, and the list icon beside the heading opens the schedules page. A schedule whose latest run failed or is waiting for input starts expanded; otherwise this browser remembers whether you expanded it.
  • Settings, the cog beside your account, slides in the pages you set up once (Sandbox environments, MCP servers and Memory, under Agent setup, and for admins Users, Configuration, Schedule templates, Skills and Global MCP servers, under Admin) along with the documentation links. Nothing changes on the page until you pick one. Back (or Escape) slides your sessions back in.

The lists update as runs start and finish, without a reload. Where the sidebar narrows to icons, + starts a chat, the magnifier opens the session search, and Sessions and Scheduled open their pages.

To see more of long titles, drag the sidebar's right edge to widen it, or focus the edge and use the arrow keys; double-click the edge to reset it. This browser remembers the width. The sidebar never takes so much room that the page beside it gets cramped, so on smaller windows it widens less.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Home (/dashboard/) opens with Needs you: what is waiting on you, up to 8 items. Questions come first, then failures (Failed, CI still failing, Can't run), then Found issues, then Needs attention; newest first within each.

  • Needs input: your session's latest run asked you a question. The item leaves when you answer.
  • Failed: your session's latest run failed. The item leaves once a newer run starts in the session (Retry starts one), once you run the same prompt on the same repository again, or 14 days after the failure. The session stays in Sessions. A run you cancelled does not count.
  • CI still failing: DAIV's CI watch on a merge request gave up. The item shows for 7 days.
  • Can't run: one of your schedules cannot start its runs. The item leaves when the schedule starts a run again or you pause it.
  • Found issues and Needs attention: your session's latest run was classified that way. The item shows for 7 days, because a fix made outside DAIV leaves no trace DAIV can see.

A session counts once, as the first of these it matches: a question in a session whose CI watch gave up shows as Needs input. A session with no activity for 90 days leaves the list.

Below Needs you, Home shows Your week: what the runs in your own sessions came to over the last 7 days. A column per day is stacked by outcome (Changed code, Done, no changes, Needed you, Failed), and the section lists the merge requests those runs worked on and where you started work from. A day's column opens your sessions that ran that day. Your recent sessions are in the app sidebar.

Last comes Ways to use DAIV: how to start work from your Git platform (issue labels, mentions and slash commands), from your editor (this instance's MCP URL), and right here (New chat and New background run). Fold it away with Hide; this browser remembers. A user who has not started a run yet sees only Needs you and Ways to use DAIV.

Team statistics are on Insights, linked as Team insights at the top of Home.

docs.title: Insights
docs.text:
Insights (/dashboard/insights/) shows how DAIV is used across the repositories you can see. Choose a period: Today, 7 days (the default), 30 days, 90 days or All time.

  • Agent activity: runs, success rate, runs that changed code and average duration, each compared with the period of the same length immediately before, up to the same time of day (the page names both periods). Running now is live and not compared.
  • Runs over time: a column per day (per week for 30 and 90 days, per month for all time), stacked by outcome: changed code, done without changes, needs input, failed. A column opens the sessions active in its days. The chart is hidden for Today.
  • Sessions by origin: each origin's sessions this period and the period before, the change, and a small bar per day. Every count for this period opens the session list it counts. The previous period and the bars count sessions with a run in those days, so later activity does not move them.
  • Code velocity: see merge metrics.

docs.title: Sessions list
docs.text:
Sessions lists sessions, most recently active first. Each row shows:

  • A status dot for the latest run (queued, pending, running, done, needs input or failed).
  • The title, generated from the first prompt or the issue or merge request subject.
  • The repository, the branch, and the merge request when there is one.
  • An icon for the session's origin.
  • The latest run's model, its duration and the session's cost, then the owner and when the session was last active.

An API or MCP job that continues a busy session does not start at once. It joins the session's next run for its branch, shown as Queued, which starts when the current run ends (The session inbox describes how).

The list shows your own sessions (Mine) or everyone's you can see (Everyone). A link that carries a repository, merge request, schedule or batch filter opens on Everyone.

docs.title: Filter the list
docs.text:
Filter What it does Search Matches a session's title or repository Status All, Needs input, Failed, Running, Queued, Pending or Done, by the session's latest run Type One origin, or All types Time All time (the default), Today, Last 2 days, Last 7 days, Last 30 days, or a Custom range of two dates Archived Swaps the list for the archived sessions

Six more filters have no control. They appear as chips when you arrive from a link, and each chip has a button that clears it:

Chip Where the link comes from Repository A repository filter; clearing it clears the merge request too Merge request The view sessions link in a merge request description, or a repository card's menu; always paired with a repository, since merge request numbers are per project Ran on A day's column in Your week on Home or in Runs over time on Insights Schedule The run count on a scheduled job Batch A multi-repository submission: one prompt sent to several repositories shares a batch Including archived A link that must show sessions whatever their state: the view sessions link in a merge request description, Other sessions on !N in a repository card's menu, a day in Your week on Home and its link to more merge requests, and a column in Runs over time or a count in Sessions by origin on Insights. The list then includes archived sessions

Filters combine, and they are in the URL, so you can bookmark or share a filtered list.

Sessions with a run in flight (Queued, Pending or Running) update in place, status dot and timing included, without a reload.

docs.title: Archived sessions
docs.text:
An archived session is archived for everyone, not only for the person who archived it. It leaves Sessions, the app sidebar and Needs you on Home, and it takes no follow-ups until someone unarchives it.

A filtered list that hides archived sessions says how many match: select Show archived under the list to see them.

Links that open the list with the Including archived chip are listed in Filter the list. Your week and Insights count archived sessions too.

DAIV archives a session when its merge request merges. It archives every session that carries the merge request's number, ran on it or owns it: the session that opened it, its review and comment sessions, and the issue sessions that published it. DAIV holds a session back while it has live work:

  • A session that owns another open merge request stays listed, and DAIV archives it when that merge request merges.
  • A session with a run in progress or a waiting request that would start a run is archived when that work ends.
  • A session that delegated work is archived once its legs have no run in progress and no open merge request.

Closing a merge request without merging does not archive the sessions on it. DAIV handles each merge once: a session you unarchive stays unarchived if the platform sends the same merge again.

An archived session refuses new work:

  • A chat message and a job that continues it with thread_id are refused, with a message that says to unarchive the session first.
  • A leg follow-up for it is refused, and one already waiting stops with not run: its session was archived; see Following up a leg.
  • A label or mention on its issue, a mention on its merge request, or a mention on a merge request it owns starts nothing. DAIV replies with a link to the session, once per mention and at most once a day for a label.
  • Requests already waiting in its inbox, and a CI failure or finished delegated batch that arrives, wait there until someone unarchives the session.

docs.title: Archive a session
docs.text:
You need to be able to run agents on the session's repository. Archiving hides the session for everyone else, so check that nobody needs it first.

  1. Open the session.
  2. Select ⋯ → Archive.
  3. In Archive this session?, select Archive.

docs.title: Unarchive a session
docs.text:
You need the same access. The session comes back for everyone.

  1. Open the archived session.
  2. Select Unarchive beside This session is archived., or ⋯ → Unarchive.

docs.title: Session detail
docs.text:
Select a session to open its page (/dashboard/sessions/<thread_id>/), which holds:

  • Header: the session's title (rename it with the pencil, when you can run agents on the repository), its status, and a ⋯ menu with Copy session link, the linked issue and, when you can run agents on the repository, Archive or Unarchive (archived sessions).
  • Transcript: the conversation, streaming live while a run is active, whatever started it (chat, job, webhook or schedule). Reopening the page rejoins the stream: a fresh load replays the run from its start, and an automatic reconnect replays only what you missed.
  • Up next: at the end of the conversation, what the session does next, in order. It lists each run still to start, as whom, with the requests that start it, then the updates the next run is told (The session inbox describes them). A CI failure or finished delegated batch that DAIV does not act on says why, such as not fixing: out of attempts. A request DAIV could not handle shows in the conversation as a not handled line with the reason. A run DAIV started itself opens with the message it received, and Show request expands the full prompt the run got.
  • Sidebar: repositories and merge requests, CI, the environment, usage and outputs.

The page updates in place whenever the session changes: a run starting or ending, a message joining Up next, a CI result. A page open in another tab, or watched by someone else, streams a chat turn you send. Without Redis (DJANGO_REDIS_URL unset), the page cannot hear about changes, so it checks every few seconds while a run is in flight.

Every run in the transcript has a link target, <session URL>#run-<run id>, that opens the session scrolled to that run. This includes the runs of a session whose transcript has expired. Each row of the Artifacts list and the artifact viewer's header use it.

docs.title: The sidebar
docs.text:
From 1100px wide the sidebar is always open. Below that it is a sheet, which a summary button in the header opens. The button shows the main repository, +N for the others, the merge request (!iid, or a count) and a CI dot. The sheet opens on Overview, scrolled to the repositories with that section unfolded.

The sidebar has two tabs, and your browser remembers the tab and which sections you folded:

  • Overview: foldable sections, each with a one-line summary beside its name while folded.
    • Repositories (Repository for a lone one): a card per repository.
    • Environment: the Sandbox and the Model.
    • Context and Spend: how full the model's context window is, and what the session has cost.
    • Outputs: the artifacts the session published, once there are any.
  • Info: status, who started the session, its owner, the number of runs, when it was created and its Session ID (with a copy button). On a session that delegated work, it also lists the Delegated jobs of each batch (Seeing the batch describes them).

A repository card shows:

  • The repository, tagged Main when the session spans several.
  • The branch.
  • The merge request, with its title and a Draft badge.
  • The merge request's CI status, with What DAIV found when a run explained a failure.
  • The lines added and removed, and the number of files changed.

A repository where the agent ran but changed nothing shows as a quiet card marked no changes. A repository DAIV could not publish shows the reason on its card.

Once a repository has a merge request, the card's ⋯ menu offers:

  • Open on GitLab (or GitHub) and Copy link.
  • Other sessions on !iid, on the main repository's card: the sessions list filtered to that merge request.
  • Fix CI failures, for the people who can run agents on the repository: turns the CI watch on or off for that merge request.

When the agent commits changes, DAIV creates or updates a merge request on the session's ref, and the repository card links to it and flags drafts. A repository card shows an open merge request that already exists for the ref even before the agent runs.

docs.title: Images and files in tool results
docs.text:
When a tool hands the agent an image or a file (a screenshot from an MCP browser tool, or an image, PDF, audio or video file the agent opened with read_file), the tool's row in the transcript shows it under Attached, both while the run streams and after a reload.

  • Images show as thumbnails that open full size in a new tab.
  • PDFs, audio and video show as a chip with their size, which downloads the file.
  • An image an MCP server only gives as a link to another site shows as a link, so viewing the transcript loads nothing from that site.

Anyone who can see the session can open these files, as they can read the rest of its transcript: its owner, people who can read its repository, and admins. That includes screenshots from MCP servers a person connected with their own account, so a screenshot of a page they were signed in to is visible to everyone who can see the session.

DAIV keeps these files with the run in its file storage under MEDIA_ROOT for as long as it keeps the run. DAIV does not delete runs on its own, and deleting a run deletes its files, but the session's saved agent state still holds each file as the tool returned it. DAIV keeps PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP images, PDFs, audio and video, within the size and per-run limits that Artifacts lists. A file it did not keep shows the reason instead, such as Too large to keep, and runs from before DAIV kept these files show Not saved. The agent always gets the full tool result, whether or not the file was kept.

docs.title: Artifacts
docs.text:
A run's final message is a paragraph of text, and the agent's workspace is discarded when the run ends. A task whose deliverable is a document (a dependency audit, a code-quality report, a changelog draft, a chart) needs somewhere else to put it. That place is an artifact.

The agent has a publish_artifact tool: it writes the file to its scratchpad (/workspace/tmp/...), publishes it, and gets back a URL that it includes in its final response. DAIV copies the file out of the sandbox into its own storage and attaches it to the run, so it stays available after the sandbox is gone and nothing is committed to the repository.

Published files appear in the transcript, in the turn that published them. Adjacent publish_artifact calls in one turn group into a single Artifacts card with one row per file. Each row shows the title (linking to the viewer, /dashboard/sessions/<thread_id>/artifacts/<id>/, in a new tab), a kind pill, the file size, and a download icon. A publish still in progress shows Publishing, and a publish that failed shows its path and the error message in red, in the same card as the files that did publish. Reloading renders the same rows, though publishes from consecutive model steps can land in separate cards. A session with no saved transcript still lists its artifacts on its page, one card per run, below the expired notice.

The limits on a file's size and on the files per run, and the storage that the app and worker containers must share, are on Artifacts and in the deployment guide. Deleting a run deletes its artifacts and their files.

Select Artifacts in the sidebar (/dashboard/artifacts/) for every artifact you can see across all sessions: those of your own sessions and of sessions on repositories you can read (admins see them all). The list is newest first, grouped by date (Today, Yesterday, Previous 7 days, Previous 30 days, then by month), 25 per page. Search by title or filename, and filter by kind (All, Markdown, HTML, Image, Text or File) and repository. Each row links to the viewer, back to the session and run that produced it, and to a download.

The jobs API and MCP job-status responses list artifacts too, with absolute viewer and download URLs, so a CI pipeline or an editor assistant can hand the report to a person.

docs.title: Artifact viewers
docs.text:
The viewer depends on the file type:

File type Viewer Markdown (.md) Rendered on the server and sanitized, inside DAIV; Copy source copies the raw Markdown HTML (.html) Rendered in a sandboxed frame; Full screen expands the frame Images (.png, .svg, .jpg, .gif, .webp) Shown inline on a checkerboard, so transparency shows; select the image to open it at full size Text, CSV, JSON, XML, YAML, logs Shown as preformatted text; Copy source copies it Anything else (.pdf, archives) Download only

An HTML artifact's inline CSS and scripts run, in an opaque origin with no access to DAIV cookies, storage or pages. Fetch and XHR requests and form posts are blocked, and scripts, styles, images and fonts can still load over HTTPS.

Markdown and text files over 1 MiB are not previewed, and the viewer offers the download instead.

The viewer's header shows the artifact's kind, its repository, when it was published and last updated, and a link back to the run that produced it. Open raw serves the file as is, under the same sandbox policy, so opening an HTML report in its own tab is as safe as the embedded frame. Whoever can open the session can open its artifacts, and the viewer's breadcrumb links back to the Artifacts list.

docs.title: Revise an artifact
docs.text:
Ask the agent to change a report it already published, and it replaces the file instead of publishing a new artifact: the artifact keeps its URL. You need a session that holds the artifact: the agent reads and revises only the artifacts of the session it runs in, never those of another session.

  1. In the session that published the report, send a message that says what to change, such as "add a section on licenses" or "make the table sortable". To point the agent at a specific artifact, paste its URL into the message.
  2. Wait for the run to end. The agent edits the file and publishes it again with the artifact's id. If the file is no longer in its workspace because an earlier run published it, the agent copies it back first with fetch_artifact.
  3. Open the artifact from the transcript. The URL is unchanged, the viewer's header shows when the artifact was last updated, and the transcript rows for it show the current title, type and size, marked Updated.

A revised artifact stays on the run that first published it, on the dashboard and in the per-run cards of a session with no transcript. The jobs API and MCP job-status responses list it under that run and under every run that revised it. DAIV keeps only the newest version, and a revision does not count towards the per-run file limit.

docs.title: Start a chat session
docs.text:
A chat is the interactive workspace where you work with the agent turn by turn. You need access to at least one repository that DAIV serves.

  1. In the sidebar, select New chat, the + beside Sessions (/dashboard/sessions/new/chat/).
  2. In the Workspace card, select Add repository, and pick the repository the session works on. The ref defaults to the repository's default branch.
  3. To work from another branch, select the branch button on the repository's row, and pick the branch.
  4. Optional: in Environment, pick the sandbox environment the agent's commands run in. It stays on Auto, resolved for the main repository, until you pick one.
  5. Optional: pick the agent model and thinking effort with the model picker in the message row, next to Send.
  6. Type your first message and send it. The send button stays disabled until a repository is selected.

The session now has its own URL (/dashboard/sessions/<thread_id>/), which you can bookmark or share with teammates who have access. The repositories, their refs, the model, the thinking level and the sandbox environment are fixed from your first message for the life of the session. For what the workspace shows as the agent works, see Chat workspace. To use a different repository, branch, model or environment, start a new session.

The ref is the branch the work is based on. When the agent opens a merge request, that ref is its target branch, and if the remote has deleted the branch by the time the agent publishes, the request targets the default branch instead. DAIV assigns the new merge request to you when your DAIV account is linked to the Git platform through OAuth login. If the ref already has an open merge request, the workspace shows it.

docs.title: Start a chat over several repositories
docs.text:
Use this for work that spans repositories, such as a backend change and the client that consumes it. The Workspace card takes up to 5 repositories, each listed once, on any branch.

  1. In the Workspace card, add the first repository as in Start a chat session. This is the main repository.
  2. Select Add repository again, and pick another repository.
  3. Select the branch button on a row to pick its ref.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 for each other repository.
  5. Optional: to change the main repository, select Make main on another row. Removing the main row promotes the next one.
  6. Send your first message.

Once there is more than one repository, the main one is tagged Main. Its .daiv.yml, sandbox environment, skills and memory drive the session. In Environment, Auto · <environment> shows the environment resolved for the main repository while the field is on Auto.

The list is fixed after your first message: later turns reuse it, as in the jobs API. Every repository the agent changes gets its own merge request, as Merge requests describes.

docs.title: Chat workspace
docs.text:
As the agent works, the workspace shows:

  • Assistant text: replies render as Markdown.
  • Steps: consecutive steps (thinking and tool calls) collapse into one line that summarizes what they did, such as read 3 files · ran 2 commands, with any failures. Open it to list the steps, and open a step for its details.
  • Finished runs: when a run ends, its steps fold behind one Worked for 3m 12s · 14 steps line. The answer, its artifacts and any question the agent asked stay visible below it, and an answered question collapses to one quiet line.
  • Progress: when the agent plans with a todo list, a strip behind the message box names the step the run is on, and opens into the list.
  • Files changed: the same strip lists the files the agent created or changed, with the lines added and removed. Select a file to jump to the tool call that touched it.

Only one run can be in flight per session at a time. While a run streams, select Stop to cancel it on the server. If DAIV has not started answering yet, Stop takes your message back: it leaves the conversation, the agent never sees it, and its text returns to the message box. Refreshing the page or losing the connection does not stop the run, because reopening the session rejoins the live stream. Stop is offered to the session's owner, on chat runs and on the runs a job or the session's inbox started. A run that a webhook started on an issue or merge request that no session owns streams without it.

A message you send while the session is busy is not refused. It shows as Pending and waits for the session's next run, which starts as soon as the current one ends and answers it together with anything else that arrived meanwhile. The page follows that run when it starts. The session inbox describes the rule.

docs.title: Model, thinking level and sandbox environment
docs.text:
Each session pins three choices, set before your first message and fixed afterwards:

Choice What it controls Default Agent model Which configured model the agent runs on The default an admin configured for the site Thinking level Reasoning effort, from minimal to extra high, set with the Effort control in the model picker The default an admin configured, if any Sandbox environment The sandbox environment the agent's commands run in Auto, resolved for the main repository

docs.title: Expired sessions
docs.text:
The agent's working state expires after the time set by DJANGO_REDIS_CHECKPOINT_TTL_MINUTES (Redis lists its default). DAIV saves a copy of each session's conversation when a run ends, so an expired session keeps its transcript and your next message picks up where it left off: DAIV restores the conversation from that copy before the run. If DAIV cannot restore the saved conversation, the run fails instead of starting without it. DAIV keeps saved conversations for as long as their session exists, and nothing prunes them automatically.

A session with no saved transcript, such as one whose state expired before DAIV saved it, shows This session's state has expired. Start a new session to continue. Select New session to start a fresh one.

docs.title: Answer a question
docs.text:
When a request is ambiguous, or a decision is yours to make, the agent stops and asks instead of guessing. The run ends in the Needs input status, and the last turn shows a card with 1 to 4 questions. Each question offers option buttons and a free-text field. This also happens in webhook and job sessions: the same card shows wherever a run ended on a question.

  1. Open the session. A session that needs you also appears under Needs you on Home.
  2. For each question, select an option. A question marked Pick any that apply. takes several, and selecting an option again clears it.
  3. If no option fits, or the question has none, type your own answer in the free-text field.
  4. Select Answer.

DAIV sends all your answers as one message, one line per question, and a question you left blank is sent as No preference. The agent starts a new run on the same session that picks up where it left off. You can also type a reply in the message box instead of using the card.

To decline the whole card, select Skip in step 4. The agent carries on with reasonable defaults, states the assumptions it made, and does not ask the same questions again.

The card is interactive only on the session's last turn, and only while no run is in flight. Once answered, it stays visible but inert: the options are disabled, the free-text field and the buttons are hidden, the options your answer picked stay highlighted, even after a reload, and your answer shows as the next message.

For job runs (a dashboard submission, the jobs API or MCP) and scheduled runs, DAIV also sends a notification that lists the questions. Chat runs do not notify, and webhook runs rely on the question comment on the issue or merge request, which mentions you.

docs.title: Start a background run
docs.text:
A background run hands a task to the agent without a chat: you describe the task, DAIV runs it, and you are notified when it ends. You need access to at least one repository that DAIV serves.

  1. Go to the start screen of a background run, by any of these routes:
    • On Sessions, select New, then the Background run card.
    • On Home, select New background run.
  2. In the message box of Start a run, describe what the agent should do.
  3. Select Choose repository and pick one or more repositories. The ref defaults to the repository's default branch, and you can pick another with the branch button on its row.
  4. Optional: set the fields below the message box.
  5. Select Start run.

You land on the Sessions list filtered to the run's batch, where each repository's new session has its own row. Runs started this way have the UI Run origin.

docs.title: Background run fields
docs.text:
Field What it does Prompt What you want the agent to do Repositories 1 to 20 repositories. One prompt across several repositories creates a batch: each repository runs as an independent session Ref The branch each run reads from, and the target of any merge request it opens. Defaults to the repository's default branch Sandbox environment The sandbox environment the run executes in. Auto lets DAIV choose Agent model and Effort The model and thinking level for this run, from the agent picker under the message box. Leave them on default to use the repository's defaults MCP servers The MCP servers the run can use

DAIV notifies you on outcomes that need you: found issues, needs attention, needs input and failed. To silence a run, pass muted through the jobs API or the MCP endpoint. For a scheduled run, use the schedule's Mute notifications setting.

docs.title: Retry a run
docs.text:
When a session's latest run fails, its failure marker in the transcript has a Retry button.

You can retry when all of these hold:

  • You own the session, can run agents on its repository, and the session is not archived.
  • The failed run is the newest one, and no run is working or queued.
  • The run was a chat turn, or an API, MCP, UI or scheduled run. A webhook run, or a run delegated by another session, reports back through its own flow and does not offer Retry.

To retry:

  1. Open the session whose latest run failed.
  2. In the transcript, select Retry on the failure marker.

Retry sends your next message in the same session: The previous run failed. Please try again. when the run got far enough to be in the conversation, or the run's own prompt again when it failed before that.

A run that was stopped (by you, by the session that delegated it, or by an interruption) shows a grey marker without Retry. Send a message to carry on.

docs.title: The session inbox
docs.text:
Everything that asks an existing session to act arrives in its inbox:

  • A CI result on a merge request the session published.
  • A mention or a comment on that merge request.
  • A chat message sent while the session was busy.
  • A follow-up job.
  • A delegated batch finishing.
  • A coordinator's Leg follow-up, which asks a delegated session to continue its work.

Each one either wakes the agent or is only remembered:

  • Waking: a person's request (a chat message, a mention, a follow-up job) and a leg follow-up always wake the agent. A CI failure wakes it only on a commit DAIV pushed, once per commit, while attempts are left (Pipeline watch describes them). A finished delegated batch wakes it to carry on.
  • Remembered: a CI pass, a pipeline that needs a person, a push someone else made to the branch, a merge or close, and a comment that does not mention DAIV. These start no run. They appear in the session's timeline as compact rows between runs, and the next run on the session gets them as context, so the agent knows the branch moved before it pushes.

How the inbox groups requests into runs:

  • One run per person and branch: one run handles everything one person is waiting for on the session's branch. A message you sent to your session and a CI failure that arrived during the same run are answered together, in one run, when the current one ends.
  • Slash commands run alone: a built-in slash command such as /help runs on its own, after what you sent before it and before what you sent after it, because DAIV answers a command only when it is the whole request.
  • Leg follow-ups run alone: a leg follow-up runs on its own, as a Delegated Run that answers only its coordinator, with what the session remembered as context. DAIV never retries it, and it does not run when the session's merge request was merged or closed meanwhile, or the session was archived (Following up a leg describes it).
  • Different people, different runs: requests from different people wait for runs of their own, one after another, so one person's request never runs with another's access or tools.
  • Which branch: a message you sent while the session was busy, a follow-up job sent without a branch and a finished delegated batch follow the branch the current run publishes to. A mention or a CI result stays with its merge request's branch, and a run on another of the session's merge requests updates that merge request.
  • Warm sandbox: a run that a warm sandbox started, on a branch someone pushed to, brings its checkout up to the remote first, unless it holds commits it has not published, and tells the agent it did.

A run acts as the person whose request woke it:

  • A mention by a teammate runs as the DAIV account they signed in to with that GitLab or GitHub account, with its personal MCP servers, not the session owner's. A commenter who never signed in to DAIV with that platform account, or whose DAIV account is deactivated, gets no personal tools, even when a DAIV user shares their username or email.
  • Before it starts, a run checks that the person it acts as may still run on the repository, except for a mention, which is checked where it is made. If that person may not, only their own requests fail.
  • A session that an issue or merge request comment starts is owned by the DAIV account linked to the comment author's GitLab or GitHub account. Until that account is linked, it has no owner, and once it is linked, its sessions and runs, the merge requests those sessions own and its requests still waiting pass to that user.
  • A run that DAIV woke for a CI failure acts as the session's owner. A run that resumes a finished delegated batch acts as the user who delegated it, muted when their run was.

DAIV stops waking a session on its own after 3 runs in a row that nobody asked for, and tells the owner. It still remembers CI failures and finished delegated batches. Sending a message or mentioning DAIV picks the session up again.

docs.title: Linking back to sessions
docs.text:
This applies to every session origin, wherever the agent commits.

When DAIV opens a merge request, its description carries a view sessions link. The link opens the Sessions list filtered to that request, so it covers every session that worked on it, the one that opened it and each later one that addressed a review comment, and it keeps working as sessions are added. A session that produced several requests cannot tell which one the reader came from, so the link then opens the producing session's transcript instead, and so it does before any request is known.

Every commit DAIV makes also carries the producing session as a git trailer:

Text Only
DAIV-Session: https://daiv.example.com/dashboard/sessions/<thread_id>/

Unlike the description, the trailer is per commit and append-only. It survives a rewritten description, reaches requests that DAIV only adopts (whose description it leaves untouched), and travels with the commit when it is squashed or cherry-picked. It joins any trailer block the commit message already ends with, so Co-authored-by and Closes keep working.

An admin turns both off for the whole instance under Configuration → Agent → Link sessions from merge requests, or for one repository with session_link: false in .daiv.yml (Repository configuration lists it).
