docs.title: Slash commands and skills
docs.text:
DAIV responds to slash commands in issue and merge or pull request comments, and some also work in the dashboard chat. Built-in commands have fixed behavior. Skills are packaged instructions that give DAIV expertise for a specific task. You invoke both the same way:

Text Only
@daiv /<command> [arguments]

Use /help to list everything available where you are.

docs.title: Built-in commands
docs.text:
These commands have fixed behavior:

Command Scopes Description /help Issues, MRs/PRs, dashboard chat Lists all available commands and skills /agents Issues, MRs/PRs, dashboard chat Lists available subagents with descriptions /clear Issues, MRs/PRs Resets the conversation context to start fresh

docs.title: /help
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /help

Lists the slash commands and skills available in the current scope: the built-in commands, and the built-in and custom skills of the repository.

docs.title: /agents
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /agents

Lists the available subagents with their names and descriptions. See Subagents for details.

docs.title: /clear
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /clear

Starts a fresh conversation context for the current issue or merge/pull request. Use it when DAIV's context is stale or DAIV starts drifting. The earlier conversation stays in the session's history; DAIV stops seeing it.

docs.title: In the dashboard chat
docs.text: /help and /agents are also registered for the global scope, so they work in the dashboard chat too. Typing / in the chat composer opens a list of suggestions with those commands and the global skills. Per-repository skills do not appear there: they live in the repository's sandbox, which DAIV cannot read while the page renders.

docs.title: Built-in skills
docs.text:
DAIV ships with these built-in skills:

Skill Description /plan Explores the codebase in read-only mode and produces an implementation plan /code-review Reviews a merge/pull request for correctness, security, performance, structure, changed tests, and your repository's custom review rules /security-audit Audits code for security vulnerabilities, injection flaws, hardcoded secrets, and risks /init Analyzes the repository and generates or updates an AGENTS.md guidance file /skill-creator Guides you through creating a new custom skill

docs.title: /plan
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /plan implement rate limiting for the API

DAIV explores the codebase without making any changes and posts a detailed implementation plan. DAIV runs it automatically when it addresses an issue without the daiv-auto label (see Issue addressing).

docs.title: /code-review
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /code-review

Reviews the current merge/pull request diff for correctness, security, performance, structure, changed tests (when the diff touches test files), and your repository's custom review rules. Posts numbered findings grouped by severity, as a single report comment.

How it scores on the ReviewBench benchmark, and at what cost, is on the Benchmarks page.

docs.title: /security-audit
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /security-audit

Performs a dedicated security scan of the code changes, looking for injection flaws, hardcoded secrets, authentication issues, and data handling risks.

docs.title: /init
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /init

Analyzes the repository structure and generates an AGENTS.md file: short, repository-specific guidance for AI coding agents, covering verified commands, a repository map, invariants and pitfalls, and where changes usually go. If the file already exists, /init updates it to cut duplication and low-signal text.

docs.title: /skill-creator
docs.text:
Text Only
@daiv /skill-creator

Walks you through creating a custom skill for your repository. See Agent skills for more on custom skills.

docs.title: Turn off slash commands
docs.text:
Slash commands are on by default. To turn them off for a repository, add this to its .daiv.yml:

YAML
slash_commands:
  enabled: false

Repository configuration lists every feature toggle.

docs.title: Create a custom command
docs.text:
A custom slash command is a skill: creating the skill registers the command, with no separate step. To create a command named /my-command:

  1. Create .agents/skills/my-command/SKILL.md, starting with YAML frontmatter.
  2. In a comment, invoke it with @daiv /my-command.

The command then appears in /help next to the built-in ones. Agent skills explains how to write a skill.

docs.title: Subagents
docs.text:
DAIV's main agent can delegate work to subagents. Each subagent is specialized for one kind of task: one explores the codebase quickly, another handles complex multi-step work. The main agent decides when to delegate, based on the task.

To see the subagents available in a repository, run /agents. It works in the dashboard chat and on any issue or merge or pull request. The list holds every available subagent: the two built-in subagents below, the code-review detectors, and any custom subagents the repository defines.

docs.title: General-purpose
docs.text:
The general-purpose subagent researches complex questions, searches for code, and carries out multi-step tasks. It has the main agent's tools:

  • Filesystem operations (read, search, edit)
  • Git platform tools (GitLab or GitHub)
  • Web search and fetch, when enabled
  • Sandbox command execution, when the run has a sandbox
  • Task tracking
  • The MCP tools the main agent has

The main agent delegates to it when a task needs several rounds of searching and reasoning, for example investigating a bug across several files or researching how an external library works before making changes.

docs.title: Explore
docs.text:
The explore subagent is a fast, read-only agent for navigating a codebase. Its tools list directories, read files, find files by glob pattern (for example src/components/**/*.tsx), and search code for keywords and regular expressions. It cannot modify files, run commands, or reach external resources, which keeps it fast and safe for quick lookups.

The main agent delegates to it to locate files, understand code structure, or gather context before deciding. The main agent gives it a thoroughness level: quick, medium or very thorough. Explore runs on openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 unless a configured model replaces it.

docs.title: Code-review detectors
docs.text: The /code-review skill delegates to read-only detector subagents: cr-correctness, cr-security, cr-performance, cr-structure, cr-tests and cr-custom-rules. See Subagent model precedence for the model they run on.

docs.title: How delegation works
docs.text:
The main agent chooses a subagent from the task:

  • To find a file or understand code structure, it uses the explore subagent.
  • To research, run commands, or do multi-step work, it uses the general-purpose subagent.
  • To make code changes directly, it does the work itself.

Each subagent runs in its own isolated context. It does not see the main conversation and cannot exchange messages with the main agent. It works on its own and returns a single final report, which the main agent uses to continue the task.

docs.title: Add a custom subagent
docs.text:
A custom subagent is a Markdown file in the repository. You need write access to the repository.

  1. In the repository root, create the directory .agents/subagents/ if it does not exist.
  2. In it, create one .md file for the subagent. The file name is free: the subagent's name comes from the file's name field.
  3. Start the file with YAML frontmatter that sets name and description.
  4. Optional: set model in the frontmatter to run the subagent on a model of your choice.
  5. After the frontmatter, write the subagent's system prompt in Markdown.
  6. Commit the file to the repository.
  7. On the next run, send /agents to check that the subagent is listed.
Text Only
my-repository/
├── .agents/
│   └── subagents/
│       ├── database-migration.md
│       └── data-analyst.md
└── src/

A subagent file looks like this:

Markdown
---
name: database-migration
description: Specialized agent for planning and reviewing database migrations. Use when the task involves schema changes, data migrations, or ORM model modifications.
model: openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5
---

You are a database migration specialist. When given a task:

1. Review the current schema by reading model files
2. Identify all affected tables and relationships
3. Plan the migration steps in order
4. Check for data loss risks
5. Suggest rollback strategies

A custom subagent has the same tools as the built-in general-purpose subagent.

docs.title: Custom subagent file format
docs.text:
DAIV reads the .md files directly inside .agents/subagents/, not those in subdirectories. It skips a file that breaks the rules below and logs a warning, and the subagent does not appear in /agents.

Part Required Description name Yes The subagent's unique name, which the main agent uses to delegate. It cannot be general-purpose, explore, or a code-review detector's name such as cr-security: DAIV skips a file that uses one. description Yes What the subagent does. The main agent reads it to decide when to delegate, so make it specific and include trigger phrases. model No The model to run on, as provider:model-name, for example openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5. Without it, the subagent runs on the main agent's model. A configured model takes precedence. If DAIV cannot build the model and none is configured, it skips the subagent. Body Yes The Markdown after the frontmatter becomes the subagent's system prompt. An empty body makes DAIV skip the file.

DAIV ignores any other frontmatter key.

docs.title: Write a subagent description
docs.text:
The description is how the main agent decides whether to delegate to your subagent. Include specific trigger phrases:

YAML
# Good: specific triggers the agent can match
description: >
  Specialized agent for API endpoint design and implementation.
  Use when the task involves creating new REST endpoints, modifying
  API responses, or designing request/response schemas.

# Bad: too vague
description: Helps with API stuff.

docs.title: Subagent model precedence
docs.text:
Operators can run any subagent on a chosen model by name, without editing its file: the general-purpose and explore subagents, each code-review detector, and custom subagents. A custom subagent's file lives in the repository, so the dashboard does not list it. Set its model in .daiv.yml, or for every repository in DAIV_AGENT_SUBAGENT_MODELS.

A subagent's model is the first of these that is set:

  1. Its entry under models.subagents in the repository's .daiv.yml (see Model overrides).
  2. Its entry in the dashboard or in DAIV_AGENT_SUBAGENT_MODELS. For the general-purpose and explore subagents, it is under Configuration → Agent → Subagent models. For the detectors, it is on the Models tab of the code-review skill's page.
  3. The model that its file or detector charter declares (openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 for explore).
  4. The main agent's model.

A configured model runs with the run's thinking level and falls back to the main agent's fallback models. A model that the user picks for the run does not override an entry, and a skill's model never carries over to a subagent it delegates to.

When an entry names a provider that is unknown, disabled or missing its API key, the subagent runs on its file's model, else on the main agent's model, so it is never left out of the run. DAIV logs the failure at ERROR. When a call on the configured model fails, for example because the provider does not know the model name, the main agent's fallback models serve it, as for any other model.

docs.title: Accounts and roles
docs.text:
DAIV's web dashboard requires you to sign in. Every signed-in user has one of two roles, admin or member, which decide what they can see and change. Members manage their own work: agent runs, chats, schedules and API keys. Admins also manage the deployment: users, site configuration, schedule templates, skills, and global MCP servers and sandbox environments.

DAIV does not offer email-and-password signup. Signup through your Git platform is off by default: an admin turns it on with Open social signup, described in Turn on OAuth login. Otherwise an admin creates each user, who then signs in with a one-time email code, a passkey, or the Git platform account when OAuth login is on.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
DAIV has two roles. New users are members.

Capability Member Admin Start and view agent runs and chats On the repositories they can access (see Repository access) On every repository Create and view scheduled jobs Their own, on repositories they can write to Everyone's, on every repository Create API keys Their own Their own Revoke API keys Their own Any user's key Manage notification channels Their own Their own Users: create, edit and delete users No Yes Configuration: edit the site configuration No Yes Schedule templates: create, edit and delete them No Yes Skills: open the skills dashboard No Yes Global MCP servers: manage the servers every user gets No Yes Create and change global sandbox environments No Yes Consolidate a repository's memory on demand No Yes

The admin-only pages are under Admin in the sidebar's Settings menu, the cog beside your account.

docs.title: Repository access
docs.text:
A member sees and acts on a repository only when they have access to it on the connected Git platform, GitLab or GitHub. DAIV mirrors each user's repository membership from the platform and checks it before it shows or runs anything on a repository. There is no separate DAIV-side permission to manage. Admins skip these checks.

DAIV checks two tiers, matched to the platform's own roles:

Tier Required platform role Gates Read GitLab Reporter or above, GitHub read (or higher) collaborator Repository and branch pickers, the memory dashboard, and the MCP list_repositories tool. Write GitLab Developer or above, GitHub write (or higher) collaborator Starting an agent run or chat, and creating or running a scheduled job, from the dashboard, the Jobs API or MCP.

A repository a user cannot read never appears in a listing. A repository they can read but not write to appears, and DAIV rejects their run, chat and schedule attempts with a "not accessible" message.

DAIV learns what a user can access on the platform only after that user signs in with their Git platform account once, and matches the platform account to the DAIV user by email. A user an admin created, who has only ever signed in with an email code, has no repository access until they sign in with GitLab or GitHub once.

A periodic sync copies repository membership from the platform, so a permission change on the platform takes effect at the next sync, not immediately. Git platform gives the sync schedule and how long DAIV keeps trusting access data after a sync fails.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
The login page is at /accounts/login/. A user signs in with any of these methods:

  • Email code. Works without further setup, as long as DAIV can send email.
  • Git platform account. Works once an admin has turned on OAuth login.
  • Passkey. Works once the user has added one.

docs.title: Sign in with an email code
docs.text:
DAIV emails a one-time code that signs a user in without a password. Admin-created users and the first admin use this method.

  1. On the login page, enter your email address and select Continue with email.
  2. Read the code in the email DAIV sends. The code expires after 5 minutes and accepts 3 attempts.
  3. Enter the code and select Verify & sign in.

Without an SMTP server, set EMAIL_BACKEND to django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend and read the code from the app's log with docker compose logs app. Environment variables lists the email settings.

docs.title: Sign in with GitHub or GitLab
docs.text:
DAIV offers the platform it is connected to, GitHub or GitLab including a self-managed GitLab, and never both at once. On the login page, select Continue with GitHub or Continue with GitLab.

With Open social signup off, create each permitted user under Admin → Users with the email address their Git platform account confirms. For GitLab, DAIV checks the profile's confirmed_at to verify that this primary email address is confirmed before it looks up an existing account. Matching ignores case and keeps the existing user's role. If GitLab sends no confirmation or an invalid one, DAIV does not link the account by email. An account already linked to a platform user ID stays linked when the platform email changes.

DAIV checks again, before it saves a new account, that signup is open. A pending signup form cannot create a second user by replacing an email address that already exists.

To turn on Git platform sign-in, create the OAuth app, then follow Turn on OAuth login.

docs.title: Sign in with a passkey
docs.text: A passkey is Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello or a security key. After a user signs in, they add one under Passkeys in the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar. On the login page they then select Sign in with a passkey. Email sign-in stays available, so a lost passkey does not lock the user out.

docs.title: Create the OAuth app
docs.text:
Create an OAuth app on your Git platform to get the client ID and client secret that DAIV needs for OAuth login. You need an account that can create the app on that platform, and the URL DAIV is served from (DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL), for example https://daiv.example.com.

To create the app on GitHub:

  1. Open github.com/settings/developers.
  2. Select OAuth Apps → New OAuth App.
  3. In Application name, enter a name, for example DAIV.
  4. In Homepage URL, enter your DAIV URL, for example https://daiv.example.com.
  5. In Authorization callback URL, enter your DAIV URL followed by /accounts/github/login/callback/, for example https://daiv.example.com/accounts/github/login/callback/.
  6. Select Register application.
  7. Copy the Client ID.
  8. Select Generate a new client secret, and copy the secret.

To create the app on GitLab:

  1. Open Admin Area → Applications or User Settings → Applications.
  2. Add a new application.
  3. In Name, enter a name, for example DAIV.
  4. In Redirect URI, enter your DAIV URL followed by /accounts/gitlab/login/callback/, for example https://daiv.example.com/accounts/gitlab/login/callback/.
  5. Under Scopes, select read_user.
  6. Select Save application.
  7. Copy the Application ID and the Secret.

Enter the client ID and secret under Configuration → Authentication, where DAIV calls the secret Auth Client Secret: Turn on OAuth login gives the steps, and Authentication lists the variables that override the same fields and lock them.

docs.title: The first admin
docs.text: A new DAIV install has no users, so it has no admin. Two paths create the first one: the first Git platform sign-in, and a command in a shell.

docs.title: Make the first OAuth sign-in the admin
docs.text: With OAuth login on and no user in DAIV, the first person who signs in with the Git platform account gets an account even when Open social signup is off, and DAIV makes them an admin. DAIV makes a new account an admin whenever the install has no admin, not whenever it has no user. If two people sign in at the same moment, both become admins rather than neither.

docs.title: Create the first admin from a shell
docs.text:
Use this path when OAuth login is off. The bootstrap_admin command refuses to run if an admin already exists, or if a user with that email already exists: promote that user from Users instead.

  1. Run the command, replacing admin@example.com with the admin's email address:

    Bash
    docker compose exec app django-admin bootstrap_admin admin@example.com

  2. Sign in with an email code as that address.

Deployment covers the first-run setup, including email.

docs.title: Manage users
docs.text: Admins manage users under Admin → Users, at /accounts/users/. The list searches by name or email address and filters by role.

docs.title: Create a user
docs.text:
1. Under Admin → Users, select Create user.
  2. In Name, Email and Role, enter the user's details.
  3. Select Create user.

DAIV emails the user a welcome message with a sign-in link. The new account has no password: the user signs in with an email code, a passkey, or the Git platform account.

docs.title: Edit a user
docs.text:
1. Under Admin → Users, select the user.
  2. Change Name, Email, Role or Active. Change Role to promote a member to admin or demote an admin to member.
  3. Select Save changes.

DAIV keeps at least one active admin. You cannot deactivate your own account, and you cannot demote or delete the last active admin: promote another user first.

docs.title: Deactivate a user
docs.text:
Deactivate a user when you may want to restore their access later.

  1. Under Admin → Users, select the user.
  2. Clear Active.
  3. Select Save changes.

An inactive user cannot sign in, and their API keys and MCP tokens stop working at once, not at the next sync. DAIV keeps their history and the runs they own.

docs.title: Delete a user
docs.text:
Delete a user only when you will never restore their access. Deactivating keeps their history and ownership of runs: see Deactivate a user.

Deleting a user cannot be undone

Deleting removes the user's account, their API keys and all data associated with them. You cannot delete your own account.

  1. Under Admin → Users, select the user.
  2. Select Delete user.
  3. On the confirmation page, select Delete user.

docs.title: Account pages
docs.text:
Every signed-in user, member or admin, has these pages. All but Home open from the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar.

Page Route What it does Home /dashboard/ Your landing page after sign-in, with a link to Team insights. API keys /accounts/api-keys/ Create and revoke personal API keys for programmatic access. Notification channels /accounts/channels/ Choose how DAIV notifies you about your agent runs. Notifications lists the channels. Passkeys /accounts/mfa/ Add and remove the passkeys you sign in with.

API keys authenticate calls to the Jobs API and the MCP endpoint. A member sees only their own keys, and an admin sees every user's keys in the list.
