docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
This page deploys a self-hosted DAIV with Docker Swarm or Docker Compose, puts it behind an Nginx reverse proxy, and creates the first admin. Afterwards you have a DAIV instance ready to connect to your codebase.

To try DAIV on one machine first, follow the Quickstart.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Version Docker Engine The samples pin no minimum. Docker Swarm needs Swarm mode enabled on the host. Docker Compose 2.17.0 or later, which provides the docker compose command and depends_on.restart. Only the Compose deployment needs it. PostgreSQL 15 or later, the minimum of the Django release DAIV pins; the samples run postgres:17.6. Redis 8 or later. The samples run redis:8.6-alpine. The agent's checkpoints use Redis search commands that Redis 7 lacks, and they must stay on database 0; see Redis. daiv-sandbox The samples pull ghcr.io/srtab/daiv-sandbox:latest. Update the sandbox together with DAIV: multi-repository sessions need a release with repos_archive support and path-scoped egress rules, and DAIV reports an error when the sandbox lacks it.

You also need a domain name that points to your server, with an SSL certificate for it, and a way for your Git platform to reach DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL. Your Git platform sends webhooks to that URL.

docs.title: Services DAIV runs
docs.text:
DAIV needs these services. The samples below run all of them:

  • PostgreSQL stores application data.
  • Redis holds the cache, sessions and the agent's checkpoints.
  • DAIV app (app) serves the web dashboard and the API.
  • DAIV worker (worker and worker-interactive) runs background tasks.
  • DAIV scheduler (scheduler) runs periodic tasks, among them adding webhooks to your GitLab projects and syncing repository access.
  • DAIV sandbox (sandbox) runs the agent's commands and git in isolated containers, through an egress proxy that holds the git credentials. See Sandbox.

Task queues

Background work is split in two: default carries agent runs, which hold a worker for as long as the run lasts, while interactive carries short user-visible work: session titles, run classification and notification delivery. The worker and worker-interactive services each serve one of them, so a title never queues behind a run. A worker started with no queue argument serves every queue, which suits a small deployment that accepts that wait.

docs.title: Deploy with Docker Swarm
docs.text:
Docker Swarm gives you service discovery, load balancing and rolling updates, so it suits production. These steps deploy to a single server; to extend the stack to more servers, see the Docker Swarm documentation.

Before you start, install Docker and enable Swarm, and check the requirements.

  1. Create the first seven Docker secrets listed in Swarm secrets, with this command (see Docker secret create), replacing <name> and <value>:

    Bash
    printf '%s' '<value>' | docker secret create <name> -

  2. Create the egress CA. The sandbox reaches your Git platform only through a per-session proxy that adds the credentials, so the token never enters the sandbox, and the proxy signs with this CA:

    Bash
    openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -days 3650 -subj "/CN=daiv-sandbox-egress" \
  -addext "keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign" \
  -keyout egress-ca.key -out egress-ca.crt

  3. Store the CA as the two secrets the stack reads:

    Bash
    docker secret create daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_cert egress-ca.crt
docker secret create daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_key egress-ca.key

  4. On each node, add this to /etc/docker/daemon.json. Each agent run holds many concurrent sockets (sandbox, LLM API, tracing, database, Redis, git over HTTPS), and Docker's default soft limit of 1024 open files fails under load with [Errno 24] Too many open files. Swarm ignores service-level ulimits, so the daemon must raise nofile:

    JSON
    {
  "default-ulimits": {
    "nofile": { "Name": "nofile", "Soft": 65536, "Hard": 524288 }
  }
}

  5. On each node, restart Docker:

    Bash
    systemctl restart docker

  6. Save the Swarm stack file as stack.yml, and replace each annotated value with your own. Environment variables lists the options.

  7. From the directory that holds stack.yml, deploy the stack:

    Bash
    docker stack deploy -c stack.yml daiv

  8. Wait until every service is healthy, which takes several minutes while Docker pulls the images and DAIV migrates the database:

    Bash
    docker stack ps daiv --no-trunc

  9. Put DAIV behind Nginx, so you can reach it over HTTPS.

  10. Create the first admin by running bootstrap_admin in the app's container, replacing admin@example.com with the admin's email address:

    Bash
    docker exec -it $(docker ps -q -f name=daiv_app | head -n 1) django-admin bootstrap_admin admin@example.com

  11. Open /accounts/login/ and sign in with the one-time code DAIV emails to that address.

If you turn on OAuth login before anyone signs in, the first Git platform sign-in becomes the admin instead. The first admin explains both paths, and Accounts and roles covers adding users.

docs.title: Swarm secrets
docs.text:
The stack reads these Docker secrets. Create the first seven rows in step 1, and the next two in steps 2 and 3. The last two are optional.

Secret Holds django_secret_key A random secret key for Django, such as the output of openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it backed up: see Django. db_password A random password for the PostgreSQL database. codebase_gitlab_auth_token A GitLab personal access token with the api scope. See Platform setup. codebase_gitlab_webhook_secret A random secret that GitLab sends with each webhook, for DAIV to validate. daiv_sandbox_api_key A random API key for the sandbox service. email_host_password The SMTP password. DAIV authenticates only when EMAIL_HOST_USER is also set. The stack requires the secret to exist, so create it with any value if your relay needs no authentication. openrouter_api_key An OpenRouter API key. daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_cert The egress CA certificate. daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_key The egress CA private key. allauth_client_id Optional. The OAuth client ID of your Git platform. See Authentication. allauth_client_secret Optional. The OAuth client secret of your Git platform.

A secret locks the matching field in the dashboard: DAIV reads the value from the secret and you cannot edit it under Configuration → Authentication. When you will turn on OAuth login in the dashboard instead, leave allauth_client_id and allauth_client_secret out of the app service's secrets: list and out of the top-level secrets:, as the stack file below does. To use them, create both secrets, then uncomment those lines.

For another provider's key, create a secret named after its variable in lowercase (openai_api_key, anthropic_api_key or google_api_key) add it to the secrets: list of the app service, which runs the migration that reads it, and declare it under the top-level secrets: with external: true. DAIV reads each provider key once, at its first start; see Provider API keys. For further variables you want as secrets, see Environment variables.

docs.title: Swarm stack file
docs.text:
YAML
x-app-environment-defaults: &app_environment_defaults
  # DJANGO
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: daiv.settings.production
  DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS: daiv.example.com,app,127.0.0.1 # (1)!
  DJANGO_REDIS_URL: redis://daiv_redis:6379/0
  DJANGO_REDIS_SESSION_URL: redis://daiv_redis:6379/1
  DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL: https://daiv.example.com # (2)!
  # DATABASE
  DB_NAME: daiv
  DB_USER: daiv_admin
  DB_HOST: daiv_db
  DB_SSLMODE: prefer
  # CODEBASE
  CODEBASE_CLIENT: gitlab
  CODEBASE_GITLAB_URL: https://gitlab.com # (3)!
  # EMAIL
  EMAIL_HOST: smtp.example.com
  EMAIL_PORT: 587
  EMAIL_USE_TLS: true
  EMAIL_HOST_USER: smtp-user # (13)!
  # SANDBOX
  DAIV_SANDBOX_URL: http://sandbox:8000 # (4)!

x-deploy-defaults: &deploy_defaults
  replicas: 1
  update_config:
    order: start-first
    delay: 60s
    failure_action: rollback
  rollback_config:
    parallelism: 0
  restart_policy:
    condition: any
    window: 120s

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.6
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DB=daiv
      - POSTGRES_USER=daiv_admin
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password
    networks:
      - internal
    secrets:
      - db_password
    volumes:
      - db-volume:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    healthcheck:
      test: pg_isready -q -d $$POSTGRES_DB -U $$POSTGRES_USER
      interval: 10s
      start_period: 120s
    deploy:
      replicas: 1
      update_config:
        failure_action: rollback
        delay: 10s
      rollback_config:
        parallelism: 0
      restart_policy:
        condition: any
        window: 120s

  redis:
    image: redis:8.6-alpine # (11)!
    networks:
      - internal
    volumes:
      - redis-volume:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: redis-cli ping || exit 1
      interval: 10s
      start_period: 30s
    deploy:
      <<: *deploy_defaults

  app:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv:${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main} # (5)!
    environment:
      <<: *app_environment_defaults
    secrets:
      - django_secret_key
      - db_password
      - codebase_gitlab_auth_token
      - codebase_gitlab_webhook_secret
      - daiv_sandbox_api_key
      - openrouter_api_key
      - email_host_password
      # - allauth_client_id  (14)
      # - allauth_client_secret  (14)
    networks:
      - internal
      - external
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media # (10)!
      # - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills  (9)
    deploy:
      <<: *deploy_defaults

  worker:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv:${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main} # (5)!
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-worker default
    environment:
      <<: *app_environment_defaults
    secrets:
      - django_secret_key
      - db_password
      - codebase_gitlab_auth_token
      - codebase_gitlab_webhook_secret
      - daiv_sandbox_api_key
      - openrouter_api_key
      - email_host_password
    networks:
      - internal
    volumes:
      - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media # (10)!
      # - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills:ro  (9)
    healthcheck:
      test: grep -q 'db_worker' /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    deploy:
      <<: *deploy_defaults
      replicas: 1 # (8)!

  worker-interactive:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv:${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main} # (5)!
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-worker interactive
    environment:
      <<: *app_environment_defaults
    secrets:
      - django_secret_key
      - db_password
      - codebase_gitlab_auth_token
      - codebase_gitlab_webhook_secret
      - daiv_sandbox_api_key
      - openrouter_api_key
      - email_host_password
    networks:
      - internal
    volumes:
      - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media # (10)!
      # - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills:ro  (9)
    healthcheck:
      test: grep -q 'db_worker' /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    deploy:
      <<: *deploy_defaults
      replicas: 1

  scheduler:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv:${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main} # (5)!
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-crontask
    environment:
      <<: *app_environment_defaults
    secrets:
      - django_secret_key
      - db_password
      - codebase_gitlab_auth_token
      - codebase_gitlab_webhook_secret
      - daiv_sandbox_api_key
      - openrouter_api_key
    networks:
      - internal
    healthcheck:
      test: grep -q 'crontask' /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    deploy:
      <<: *deploy_defaults

  sandbox:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv-sandbox:latest # (5)!
    environment:
      DAIV_SANDBOX_EGRESS_CA_CERT_FILE: /run/secrets/daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_cert # (12)!
      DAIV_SANDBOX_EGRESS_CA_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_key
      DAIV_SANDBOX_REDIS_URL: redis://daiv_redis:6379/3
    networks:
      - internal
    secrets:
      - daiv_sandbox_api_key
      - daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_cert
      - daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_key
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock # (6)!
      - $HOME/.docker/config.json:/home/app/.docker/config.json # (7)!
    deploy:
      <<: *deploy_defaults

networks:
  internal:
    driver: overlay
  external:
    driver: overlay

volumes:
  db-volume:
    driver: local
  redis-volume:
    driver: local
  media-volume:
    driver: local

secrets:
  django_secret_key:
    external: true
  db_password:
    external: true
  codebase_gitlab_auth_token:
    external: true
  codebase_gitlab_webhook_secret:
    external: true
  daiv_sandbox_api_key:
    external: true
  openrouter_api_key:
    external: true
  email_host_password:
    external: true
  daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_cert:
    external: true
  daiv_sandbox_egress_ca_key:
    external: true
  # allauth_client_id:  (14)
  #   external: true
  # allauth_client_secret:  (14)
  #   external: true
  1. Replace daiv.example.com with your domain name, without the scheme (daiv.example.com, not https://daiv.example.com). Keep app and 127.0.0.1 for communication between services.
  2. Replace with your full URL, including the scheme (for example https://daiv.example.com). Your GitLab sends webhooks to this URL, so it must be able to reach it.
  3. Set to your GitLab instance URL (for example https://gitlab.com for GitLab.com).
  4. Points to the sandbox service. Use http://sandbox:8000 when the sandbox runs in the same stack.
  5. Continuous deploys track the main tag. Keep the ${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main} form on every service, so the Deploy workflow can roll back to a pinned per-commit tag (for example DAIV_IMAGE_TAG=sha-XXXXXXX).
  6. Required: the sandbox needs Docker socket access to create isolated containers.
  7. Optional: remove this volume if you don't need private registry access.
  8. Scaling: increase replicas to handle more concurrent agent runs (for example replicas: 3). A worker runs one task to completion before it claims the next, so concurrency is the number of worker containers. Each claims independently from the queues named in its command.
  9. Optional: uncomment all three lines to mount custom global skills that are available across all repositories. app receives uploads from the dashboard, so it mounts the directory read-write; worker and worker-interactive run the agent, so they can mount it read-only.
  10. Required: the web and worker containers must share this directory. It holds the artifacts (reports and other files) the agent publishes: app writes them for chat turns and serves them, and worker writes them for jobs and webhook runs. Any shared filesystem works; on a multi-node swarm, use a network-backed volume driver.
  11. Redis 8 or later; see Requirements.
  12. Required: the egress CA you stored as secrets in step 3 of Deploy with Docker Swarm. The sandbox's egress proxy signs with it; without it, every agent run fails when the sandbox rejects the session.
  13. The SMTP user. DAIV sends the email_host_password secret only when this is set; delete the line if your relay needs no authentication. Without an SMTP server, replace the EMAIL_* lines with EMAIL_BACKEND: django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend and read the sign-in code from docker service logs daiv_app.
  14. Optional: uncomment the two allauth_* lines under app's secrets: and the two under the top-level secrets: only after you create both secrets. DAIV then takes the OAuth client ID and secret from them and locks the fields under Configuration → Authentication. Leave them commented to set up OAuth login in the dashboard.

docs.title: Deploy with Docker Compose
docs.text:
Docker Compose runs every service from one file, which suits development and smaller production setups. Before you start, install Docker with Compose, and check the requirements.

  1. In the directory that will hold your docker-compose.yml, create the egress CA for the sandbox. The sandbox reaches your Git platform only through a per-session proxy that adds the credentials, so the token never enters the sandbox, and the proxy signs with this CA:

    Bash
    mkdir certs
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -days 3650 -subj "/CN=daiv-sandbox-egress" \
  -addext "keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign" \
  -keyout certs/egress-ca.key -out certs/egress-ca.crt

  2. Make the key readable, because the sandbox service runs as UID 1001:

    Bash
    chmod 644 certs/egress-ca.key

  3. Save the Compose file as docker-compose.yml, and replace each annotated value with your own. Environment variables lists the options.

  4. Start the services:

    Bash
    docker compose up -d --wait

    The command returns once every service is healthy. If one isn't, docker compose logs <service> shows why.

  5. Put DAIV behind Nginx, so you can reach it over HTTPS.

  6. Create the first admin by running bootstrap_admin, replacing admin@example.com with the admin's email address:

    Bash
    docker compose exec app django-admin bootstrap_admin admin@example.com

  7. Open /accounts/login/ and sign in with the one-time code DAIV emails to that address.

If you turn on OAuth login before anyone signs in, the first Git platform sign-in becomes the admin instead. The first admin explains both paths, and Accounts and roles covers adding users.

docs.title: Compose file
docs.text:
YAML
x-app-defaults: &x_app_default
  image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv:${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main}
  restart: unless-stopped
  volumes:
    - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media # (1)!
  ulimits: # (2)!
    nofile:
      soft: 65536
      hard: 524288
  environment:
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: daiv.settings.production
    DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: secret-key # (3)!
    DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS: daiv.example.com,app,127.0.0.1 # (4)!
    DJANGO_REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    DJANGO_REDIS_SESSION_URL: redis://redis:6379/1
    DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL: https://daiv.example.com # (5)!
    # Database settings
    DB_HOST: db
    DB_NAME: daiv
    DB_USER: daiv
    DB_PASSWORD: daivpass # (6)!
    DB_SSLMODE: prefer
    # Codebase settings
    CODEBASE_CLIENT: gitlab
    CODEBASE_GITLAB_URL: https://gitlab.com # (7)!
    CODEBASE_GITLAB_AUTH_TOKEN: gitlab-auth-token # (8)!
    CODEBASE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET: gitlab-webhook-secret # (9)!
    # LLM Providers settings
    OPENROUTER_API_KEY: openrouter-api-key # (10)!
    # Email settings
    EMAIL_HOST: smtp.example.com # (11)!
    EMAIL_PORT: 587
    EMAIL_USE_TLS: true
    # Sandbox settings
    DAIV_SANDBOX_API_KEY: daiv-sandbox-api-key # (12)!
    # Optional: Git platform sign-in (OAuth). Setting these locks the fields at /dashboard/configuration/
    # ALLAUTH_CLIENT_ID: oauth-client-id
    # ALLAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: oauth-client-secret

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.6
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: daiv
      POSTGRES_USER: daiv
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: daivpass # (13)!
    volumes:
      - db-volume:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U daiv -d daiv"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      start_period: 30s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:8.6-alpine # (14)!
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - redis-volume:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  app:
    <<: *x_app_default
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    # volumes:  (15)
    #   - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media
    #   - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true
      sandbox:
        condition: service_healthy

  worker:
    <<: *x_app_default
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-worker default
    # volumes:  (15)
    #   - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media
    #   - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "grep -q 'db_worker' /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    ports: []
    deploy:
      replicas: 1 # (16)!
    depends_on:
      app:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true

  worker-interactive:
    <<: *x_app_default
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-worker interactive
    # volumes:  (15)
    #   - media-volume:/home/daiv/data/media
    #   - ./custom-skills:/home/daiv/data/skills:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "grep -q 'db_worker' /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    ports: []
    deploy:
      replicas: 1
    depends_on:
      app:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true

  scheduler:
    <<: *x_app_default
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-crontask
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "grep -q 'crontask' /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    ports: []
    depends_on:
      app:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true

  sandbox:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv-sandbox:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    group_add:
      - 987 # (17)!
    environment:
      DAIV_SANDBOX_API_KEY: daiv-sandbox-api-key # (18)!
      DAIV_SANDBOX_EGRESS_CA_CERT_FILE: /home/app/certs/egress-ca.crt
      DAIV_SANDBOX_EGRESS_CA_KEY_FILE: /home/app/certs/egress-ca.key
      DAIV_SANDBOX_REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/3
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - ./certs:/home/app/certs:ro # (19)!

volumes:
  db-volume:
    driver: local
  redis-volume:
    driver: local
  media-volume:
    driver: local
  1. Required: every service built from this anchor shares this directory. It holds the artifacts the agent publishes: app writes them for chat turns and serves them, and worker writes them for jobs and webhook runs.
  2. Raises the open-file limit for every service built from this anchor. Each agent run holds many concurrent sockets (sandbox, LLM API, tracing, database, Redis, git over HTTPS), and Docker's default soft limit of 1024 open files fails under load with [Errno 24] Too many open files.
  3. Generate a Django secret key, a long random string such as the output of openssl rand -hex 32.
  4. Replace with your domain name, without the scheme (for example daiv.example.com). Keep app and 127.0.0.1 for communication between services.
  5. Include the full URL with the scheme (for example https://daiv.example.com). Your GitLab sends webhooks to this URL, so it must be able to reach it.
  6. Generate a random password for the database, such as the output of openssl rand -hex 16.
  7. Set to your GitLab instance URL (for example https://gitlab.com).
  8. The personal access token of DAIV's own GitLab user, with the api scope and the Maintainer role on your projects. Use a dedicated account: DAIV ignores comments written by the account its token belongs to. See Platform setup.
  9. Generate a random webhook secret for GitLab webhook validation, such as the output of openssl rand -hex 32.
  10. An OpenRouter API key for LLM access. DAIV copies it into its database on the first start. To change it later, edit the provider under Configuration → Providers in the dashboard; see LLM providers.
  11. The SMTP server DAIV sends sign-in codes through. Without one, replace the three EMAIL_* lines with EMAIL_BACKEND: django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend and read the codes from docker compose logs app.
  12. Generate a random API key for the sandbox service, such as the output of openssl rand -hex 32.
  13. Use the same password as in annotation 6.
  14. Redis 8 or later; see Requirements.
  15. Optional: uncomment the volumes: block of app, worker and worker-interactive to mount custom global skills that are available across all repositories. app receives uploads from the dashboard, so it mounts the directory read-write; the workers run the agent, so they can mount it read-only. A service-level volumes: replaces the anchor's list instead of merging with it, so keep the media-volume line.
  16. Scaling: increase replicas to handle more concurrent agent runs (for example replicas: 3). A worker runs one task to completion before it claims the next, so concurrency is the number of worker containers. Each claims independently from the queues named in its command.
  17. Replace 987 with the group of the Docker socket, the output of stat -c '%g' /var/run/docker.sock. The sandbox starts a container for each agent run through it.
  18. Use the same API key as in annotation 12.
  19. The egress CA from step 1 of Deploy with Docker Compose.

docs.title: Put DAIV behind Nginx
docs.text:
An Nginx reverse proxy gives your DAIV instance HTTPS access and domain routing. This page gives an Nginx configuration only; it has none for Apache, Traefik or other proxies.

DAIV needs HTTPS. Its session cookie, which also carries the CSRF token, is a secure cookie, so a browser keeps it only on https:// URLs and on localhost. Over plain http:// to any other address, sign-in fails with CSRF verification failed.

Before you start, install Nginx, and have an SSL certificate for your domain and a domain name that points to your server.

  1. Save the Nginx configuration as /etc/nginx/conf.d/daiv.conf. The path may vary by operating system. Replace each annotated value with your own.

  2. Restart Nginx:

    Bash
    systemctl restart nginx

  3. In a browser, open https://daiv.example.com/accounts/login/, replacing the domain with yours. You see the DAIV login page.

docs.title: Nginx configuration
Next steps
docs.text:
• Platform setup connects DAIV to your GitLab or GitHub repositories.
  • LLM providers configures your LLM providers and API keys.
  • Repository configuration customizes DAIV's behavior per repository.
  • Site configuration manages settings from the dashboard instead of environment variables.
  • MCP tools connects the agent to external MCP servers.

docs.title: LLM providers
docs.text:
DAIV runs on these LLM providers:

  • OpenRouter (default)
  • OpenAI
  • Anthropic
  • Google Gemini

You can mix providers, for example OpenRouter for the main agent and a direct provider for one model override. An admin can add any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint as a custom provider.

docs.title: Provider API keys
docs.text:
DAIV reads a provider's API key once, at its first start, from the provider's environment variable or from a Docker secret named after the variable in lowercase, such as openrouter_api_key. From then on you change the keys, and the providers' other settings, under Configuration → Providers in the dashboard. A change to the variable or the secret after the first start has no effect.

LLM providers in the environment variables reference lists the variables. Providers in the site configuration reference describes the fields of a provider.

docs.title: Set up a provider
docs.text:
Set up a provider before DAIV's first start. You need an API key from the provider, and the default models need only OpenRouter's key.

Provider Get an API key Variable OpenRouter OpenRouter Settings OPENROUTER_API_KEY OpenAI OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY Anthropic Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Google Gemini AI Studio GOOGLE_API_KEY
  1. Get an API key from the provider's page in the table.
  2. In DAIV's .env file, set the provider's variable to the key. Alternatively, mount a Docker secret named after the variable in lowercase.
  3. Start DAIV.

A provider whose key was not set at the first start begins disabled. To set up a provider on a running install, open Configuration → Providers, set the provider's API key, turn on Enabled, and select Save configuration. Saving a key does not enable a disabled provider. Providers describes the fields.

docs.title: Model specs
docs.text:
A model spec names a model and its provider. OpenRouter models take the openrouter: prefix. Direct providers' models take no prefix, and DAIV picks the provider from the start of the name:

Provider Model spec Example OpenRouter openrouter: followed by the model name from OpenRouter openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 Anthropic (direct) A name starting with claude, from the model names Anthropic lists claude-sonnet-5-5 OpenAI (direct) A name starting with gpt-4, gpt-5, gpt-6 or o4, from the model names OpenAI lists gpt-6.1-sol Google Gemini (direct) A name starting with gemini, from the model names Gemini lists gemini-3.8-flash

A provider's slug also works as a prefix, so anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5 is the same model as claude-sonnet-5-5. The slug of Google Gemini is google_genai, and DAIV also accepts google:.

To use a model spec for one repository, set it in .daiv.yml; Model overrides lists every option. For example:

YAML
models:
  agent:
    model: "claude-sonnet-5-5"

In the dashboard, the agent picker offers a model dropdown built from each enabled provider's API and cached for 15 minutes, so you can choose a model without typing its spec. Free-text entry stays available as a fallback.

docs.title: Default models
docs.text:
Role Model Fallback Main agent openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 openrouter:openai/gpt-6.1-sol Max mode openrouter:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 The main agent's models Explore subagent openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 The main agent's models

Smaller tasks such as titling, merge request metadata and memory have their own defaults, listed in Environment variables. All defaults route through OpenRouter, so only OPENROUTER_API_KEY is required for a basic setup. Choose the explore subagent's model with an explore entry in the subagent models: see Subagents.

docs.title: Retries on provider errors
docs.text:
DAIV retries a failed call to a provider's API when the failure is transient. For Anthropic's API, that means a connection error, or a 408, 409, 429 or 5xx response. DAIV retries up to DAIV_MODEL_MAX_RETRIES times (default 2; see Model requests). A 400 or 401 response is not retried. If the call still fails, DAIV tries the fallback model, when one is set. If that fails too, the run ends with the error.

If runs end on rate-limit errors, raise DAIV_MODEL_MAX_RETRIES or ask Anthropic for a higher rate limit.

docs.title: Custom providers
docs.text:
An admin can register providers beyond the four above, mainly self-hosted, OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as vLLM, llama.cpp, LiteLLM or an internal gateway. A custom provider works with any of the supported wire protocols.

You need the admin role to add a custom provider. Under Configuration → Providers, the steps in Add a custom provider create the provider with a slug, a provider type, a base URL, an API key and a few options. Provider fields describes them.

Once the provider exists, reference its models with the slug as a prefix:

Text Only
<slug>:<model-name>

Replace <slug> with the provider's slug and <model-name> with a model the endpoint serves. You can use this prefix anywhere a model is specified, including the .daiv.yml model overrides.

docs.title: Keep prompt caching on a self-hosted model
docs.text:
The agent loads most of its tools on demand. On models listed in DEFERRED_TOOLS_FROZEN_TOOLS_MODELS, loading a tool keeps the provider's prompt cache. On any other model, the first use of each tool re-sends the conversation uncached.

Before you add a self-hosted model to that list, check that it can call a tool it only saw in a tool_search result: run tests/integration_tests/test_deferred_tools_frozen.py against it, using the command in that file's docstring. List the model name without your provider slug, for example qwen3-coder for vllm:qwen3-coder. Environment variables describes the setting.

docs.title: Platform setup
docs.text: DAIV connects to one Git platform at a time, set by CODEBASE_CLIENT: GitLab (GitLab.com or self-managed) or GitHub (GitHub.com or GitHub Enterprise Server). Once connected, DAIV addresses labeled issues and reviews merge and pull requests in the repositories it can reach. Follow Connect GitLab or Connect GitHub.

docs.title: Connect GitLab
docs.text:
DAIV works as a GitLab user: it comments, pushes and opens merge requests as the user its token belongs to, and it ignores comments written by that user. Give DAIV its own account. With a token from your own account, DAIV ignores your comments, including the one that approves its plan.

You need:

  • DAIV running, from Deployment.
  • Permission to add a member to each project DAIV works on.

  • On GitLab.com, a second account for DAIV. On a self-managed instance, an admin to create the user.

  • Create a GitLab user for DAIV, for example daiv. On GitLab.com, sign up a second account; on a self-managed instance, an admin creates it under Admin → Users → New user. The username is how you mention DAIV, for example @daiv.

  • Add the user to each project DAIV works on, with the Maintainer role.
  • Sign in to GitLab as the DAIV user.
  • Select your avatar → Edit profile → Access tokens.
  • Enter DAIV Integration as the token Name.
  • Set the expiration according to your security policy.
  • Select the api scope.

  • Select Create personal access token.

    Warning

    GitLab shows the token once. Anyone who holds it acts as DAIV's user in every project that user belongs to. Store it in a secret manager, and never commit it to version control.

  • Copy the token.

  • If Deployment has not set a webhook secret, generate one. It is a random value that GitLab sends with each webhook for DAIV to validate. DAIV registers each webhook with the secret it already holds, so keep an existing one:

    Bash
    openssl rand -hex 32

    Warning

    A Compose file holds the token and the webhook secret in plain text. Keep it out of version control, and readable only by the users who deploy DAIV.

  • On Docker Compose, in the environment of x-app-defaults in your docker-compose.yml, set CODEBASE_GITLAB_URL to your GitLab URL (for example https://gitlab.com), CODEBASE_GITLAB_AUTH_TOKEN to the token and CODEBASE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET to the webhook secret.

  • On Docker Swarm, set CODEBASE_GITLAB_URL in x-app-environment-defaults of stack.yml.
  • On Docker Swarm, check whether the codebase_gitlab_auth_token secret, which step 1 of Deploy with Docker Swarm created, already holds the token from step 9. If it does, skip to the redeploy step. Otherwise Docker cannot change it, so replace it with the next steps.
  • On Docker Swarm, remove the stack: docker stack rm daiv.

  • On Docker Swarm, remove the secret: docker secret rm codebase_gitlab_auth_token.

    Warning

    A value you type in a command is saved in your shell history and visible in the process list. Run the next command from a shell that does not record history.

  • On Docker Swarm, create the secret again, replacing <token>:

    Bash
    printf '%s' '<token>' | docker secret create codebase_gitlab_auth_token -

  • Redeploy DAIV so it reads the values: docker compose up -d on Compose, or docker stack deploy -c stack.yml daiv on Swarm.

  • Wait up to 5 minutes. DAIV's scheduler adds a webhook to each project where its user is a Maintainer or Owner. To add them at once, run setup_webhooks.
  • In a project, open Settings → Webhooks and check for a webhook that points to https://daiv.example.com/api/codebase/callbacks/gitlab/, with the events in GitLab token, role and webhooks.
  • Select Test → Push events, and check that GitLab reports a successful delivery.
  • Create an issue titled "Add hello world function" in the project.
  • Add the daiv label to the issue. If the project has no daiv label, create it from the label picker.
  • Wait a few seconds. DAIV reacts with 👀, then comments with a plan.
  • From your own account, comment on the issue mentioning DAIV's user, for example @daiv proceed. DAIV implements the plan and opens a merge request.

To change DAIV's behavior in a repository, add a .daiv.yml file to its root; Repository configuration lists the options. Issue addressing explains what DAIV does with an issue.

docs.title: GitLab token, role and webhooks
docs.text: Item Value Token A personal access token of DAIV's user, with the api scope. Role DAIV lists only the projects where its user is a Maintainer or Owner, and sets up webhooks on those. Webhook URL <DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL>/api/codebase/callbacks/gitlab/. GitLab must be able to reach DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL. Webhook events Push events, Issues events, Comments (Note events), Merge request events and Pipeline events. Webhook creation DAIV's scheduler runs setup_webhooks on the CODEBASE_WEBHOOK_SETUP_CRON schedule, every 5 minutes by default. See Management commands and Environment variables.

docs.title: Webhook delivery fails
docs.text:
The webhook URL is not reachable from GitLab, or the certificate is invalid. Check that DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL is reachable from GitLab, that its SSL certificate is valid, and that no firewall blocks GitLab.

A self-managed GitLab refuses webhooks to private network addresses by default, with the error Url is blocked: Requests to the local network are not allowed. An admin allows them under Admin → Settings → Network → Outbound requests.

docs.title: DAIV ignores an issue
docs.text:
• The issue has no daiv label. Add it.
  • DAIV's user is not a Maintainer or Owner of the project, so the project has no webhook. Change its role.
  • issue_addressing.enabled is false in .daiv.yml. It is true by default.
  • Check DAIV's logs for errors.

docs.title: DAIV ignores your comments
docs.text:
• DAIV ignores comments written by its own user. Comment from another account.
  • Mention DAIV's username, for example @daiv.

docs.title: DAIV does not respond to merge request comments
docs.text:
• The webhook does not send Comments (Note events). Run setup_webhooks --update.
  • The webhook secret in GitLab does not match CODEBASE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET. DAIV rejects the request.
  • DAIV's user lacks access to the project.

docs.title: DAIV reports an error in a comment
docs.text: DAIV comments "An unexpected error occurred" when a run fails. The worker and sandbox logs show why, for example docker compose logs worker sandbox.

docs.title: Connect GitHub
docs.text:
DAIV authenticates to GitHub as a GitHub App, which you create and install on the repositories DAIV works on. You need:

  • DAIV running, from Deployment.

  • Permission to create and install a GitHub App on your account or organization.

  • Open Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps in your account, or in Organization Settings for an organization.

  • Select New GitHub App.
  • Enter a unique name as the GitHub App name, for example DAIV - <org-name>, replacing <org-name> with your organization or account name. GitHub rejects a name another App uses.
  • Enter your DAIV URL, for example https://daiv.example.com, as the Homepage URL.
  • Enter https://daiv.example.com/api/codebase/callbacks/github/ as the Webhook URL.

  • Generate the webhook secret, and keep it for a later step:

    Bash
    openssl rand -hex 32

  • Enter the webhook secret as the Webhook secret.

    Warning

    The Workflows permission is optional, and it lets code that runs in the sandbox change files under .github/workflows/. Those workflows run with the repository's Actions secrets, which exposes the secrets to that code. Set it only if DAIV must push to those files.

  • Set the repository permissions listed in GitHub App permissions and events.

  • Subscribe the App to the events listed there.

  • Select Create GitHub App.

    Warning

    The private key lets whoever holds it act as the App on every installed repository. GitHub offers the .pem file once, so store it where only DAIV's operators can read it.

  • Under Private keys, select Generate a private key. Your browser downloads a .pem file.

  • Copy the App ID from the top of the App's settings page.
  • Select Install App in the left sidebar.
  • Select your account or organization.
  • Select All repositories or Only select repositories, and choose the repositories DAIV works on.
  • Select Install.
  • Copy the installation ID from the page's URL, https://github.com/settings/installations/<installation-id>.

  • On Docker Compose, in the environment of x-app-defaults in your docker-compose.yml, set CODEBASE_CLIENT: github, CODEBASE_GITHUB_APP_ID to the App ID and CODEBASE_GITHUB_INSTALLATION_ID to the installation ID. For GitHub Enterprise Server, also set CODEBASE_GITHUB_URL, for example https://github.example.com.

    Warning

    A Compose file holds the webhook secret in plain text. Keep it out of version control, and readable only by the users who deploy DAIV.

  • On Docker Compose, set CODEBASE_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET in the same environment to the webhook secret.

  • On Docker Compose, add the private key as a file-based secret. Under x-app-defaults, add secrets: [codebase_github_private_key]. At the top level, add:

    YAML
    secrets:
  codebase_github_private_key:
    file: <private-key-path>

    Replace <private-key-path> with the path of the .pem file. DAIV reads it from /run/secrets/codebase_github_private_key. The secrets: key in x-app-defaults reaches only the services that merge that anchor with <<: *x_app_default, which the Compose file does for app, worker, worker-interactive and scheduler. 21. On Docker Compose, give the .pem file to the user DAIV runs as, daiv with UID 1001, because Compose keeps the file's owner and permissions. Replace <private-key-path> with the path of the .pem file:

    Bash
    sudo chown 1001:1001 <private-key-path>

  • On Docker Compose, make the file readable by that user only:

    Bash
    chmod 600 <private-key-path>

  • On Docker Swarm, in x-app-environment-defaults of stack.yml, set CODEBASE_CLIENT: github, CODEBASE_GITHUB_APP_ID and CODEBASE_GITHUB_INSTALLATION_ID. For GitHub Enterprise Server, also set CODEBASE_GITHUB_URL.

    Warning

    A value you type in a command is saved in your shell history and visible in the process list. Run the next command from a shell that does not record history, or from a script that reads the value from a protected file.

  • On Docker Swarm, create the webhook secret, replacing <webhook-secret>:

    Bash
    printf '%s' '<webhook-secret>' | docker secret create codebase_github_webhook_secret -

  • On Docker Swarm, create the private key secret from the .pem file, replacing <private-key-path>:

    Bash
    docker secret create codebase_github_private_key <private-key-path>

  • On Docker Swarm, add codebase_github_private_key and codebase_github_webhook_secret to the secrets: list of app, worker, worker-interactive and scheduler, and declare both under the top-level secrets: with external: true, as the stack file does for the other secrets.

  • Redeploy DAIV so it reads the values: docker compose up -d on Compose, or docker stack deploy -c stack.yml daiv on Swarm.
  • Create an issue titled "Add hello world function" in a repository where you installed the App.
  • Add the daiv label to the issue. If the repository has no daiv label, create it.
  • Wait a few seconds. DAIV comments with a plan.
  • In your GitHub App's settings, open Advanced → Recent Deliveries, and check that the issues delivery for the test issue shows a 204 response. The ping and installation deliveries from before DAIV was configured show an error, and you can ignore them.

To change DAIV's behavior in a repository, add a .daiv.yml file to its root; Repository configuration lists the options. Issue addressing explains what DAIV does with an issue.

docs.title: GitHub App permissions and events
docs.text:
GitHub sends the events of every repository that has the App installed to the one webhook set on the App. DAIV does not create webhooks on GitHub, and setup_webhooks does nothing there.

Repository permission Access DAIV uses it to Contents Read & Write Create branches and commits. Issues Read & Write Read and comment on issues. Pull requests Read & Write Create and update pull requests. Actions Read-only Read workflow runs and job logs for pipeline watch. Workflows Read & Write (optional) Push changes to files under .github/workflows/, such as a conflict resolved there. Metadata Read-only GitHub selects it for you.

Subscribe the App to these events:

  • Push
  • Issues
  • Issue comment
  • Pull request review comment, for mentions and comments on diff lines of a pull request a DAIV session owns
  • Pull request
  • Workflow run, which GitHub lists only once Actions is Read-only

If you grant a new permission to an App that is already installed, each installation owner must accept it. Until they do, the features that need it do not run on that installation.

docs.title: Webhook delivery fails
docs.text:
• Check that DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL is reachable from GitHub and has a valid SSL certificate.
  • Check that the Webhook secret in the GitHub App matches CODEBASE_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET. Without a match, DAIV answers 401.
  • Check that CODEBASE_CLIENT is github. Otherwise DAIV answers 403.
  • A ping or installation delivery fails even when DAIV is configured, because it has no repository. DAIV answers 422. Check the issues delivery instead.
  • Check DAIV's logs for the incoming requests.

docs.title: DAIV ignores an issue
docs.text:
• The issue has no daiv label. Add it.
  • The App lacks the Issues permission with Read & Write access.
  • issue_addressing.enabled is false in .daiv.yml. It is true by default.
  • Check DAIV's logs for errors.

docs.title: DAIV does not respond to comments
docs.text:
• The App is not subscribed to Issue comment, Pull request review comment or both. See GitHub App permissions and events.
  • The App is not installed on the repository.

docs.title: DAIV fails to start with permission denied on the private key
docs.text: The log shows permission denied on /run/secrets/codebase_github_private_key. The .pem file is not readable by UID 1001. Run sudo chown 1001:1001 <private-key-path> and chmod 600 <private-key-path>, then restart DAIV.

docs.title: Authentication fails
docs.text:
• The private key is not in PEM format, or lacks its header and footer lines.
  • CODEBASE_GITHUB_APP_ID or CODEBASE_GITHUB_INSTALLATION_ID is wrong.
  • The App is not installed on the repositories DAIV works on.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• LLM providers configures your LLM provider and API keys.
  • Repository configuration customizes DAIV's behavior per repository.
  • Issue addressing explains how DAIV handles issues.
  • Pull request assistant explains how DAIV reviews code.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This page gets you from a clean machine to a first merge request in about 15 minutes: you run DAIV on one Linux host with Docker Compose, connect a GitLab project, and let DAIV turn an issue into a merge request.

It is a trial setup: one worker, no email, no single sign-on. For a production install, or to connect GitHub, follow Deployment and Platform setup.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • A Linux host with Docker Engine and Docker Compose v2. About 3 GB of free disk: the DAIV images are about 1.1 GB, and the image the sandbox runs the agent in is another 1.1 GB, pulled on the first run.
  • An OpenRouter API key. To use another provider, see LLM providers.
  • A GitLab project on GitLab.com or a self-managed GitLab, where you are a Maintainer or Owner.
  • A URL GitLab can reach DAIV at. GitLab tells DAIV about new issues and comments with webhooks, so it must be able to open DAIV's port 8000:
    • Self-managed GitLab on your network: the host's address, such as http://192.168.1.10:8000, is enough once an admin allows requests to the local network under Admin → Settings → Network → Outbound requests. Without that, GitLab refuses the webhook with Url is blocked: Requests to the local network are not allowed.
    • GitLab.com: a public URL, such as a server with a domain behind a reverse proxy, or an HTTPS tunnel to port 8000 on your machine.

docs.title: Create a GitLab account for DAIV
docs.text:
DAIV works as a GitLab user: it comments, pushes and opens merge requests as that user, and it ignores comments written by that user. Give DAIV its own account; if it uses your token, it ignores your comments, including the one that approves its plan.

Can't create a second account?

Use a token from your own account, and label issues daiv-auto instead of daiv in Get your first merge request: DAIV then plans and implements without waiting for an approval comment. You won't be able to talk to DAIV in comments.

  1. Create a user for DAIV, for example daiv. On GitLab.com, sign up a second account; on a self-managed GitLab, an admin creates it under Admin → Users → New user.
  2. In your project, add that user with the Maintainer role under Manage → Members → Invite members. DAIV only sets up webhooks on projects where its user is a Maintainer or Owner.
  3. Sign in to GitLab as that user.
  4. Select your avatar → Edit profile → Access tokens, and create a personal access token with the api scope.
  5. Copy the token. GitLab shows it once.

docs.title: Create the configuration
docs.text:
Create a directory for DAIV, and in it a certificate authority for the sandbox's egress proxy. DAIV runs git inside the sandbox; the proxy is what lets those commands reach GitLab, adding the credentials so the token never enters the sandbox.

Bash
mkdir daiv && cd daiv
mkdir certs
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -days 3650 -subj "/CN=daiv-sandbox-egress" \
  -addext "keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign" \
  -keyout certs/egress-ca.key -out certs/egress-ca.crt

The sandbox service runs as UID 1001, so it needs read access to the key. Make the key readable:

Bash
chmod 644 certs/egress-ca.key

Create the .env file. The command fills in the random secrets and the Docker socket's group for you:

Bash
cat > .env <<EOF
DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL=http://192.168.1.10:8000
CODEBASE_GITLAB_URL=https://gitlab.com
CODEBASE_GITLAB_AUTH_TOKEN=<gitlab-token>
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<openrouter-api-key>
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
DB_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
CODEBASE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
DAIV_SANDBOX_API_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
DOCKER_GID=$(stat -c '%g' /var/run/docker.sock)
EOF
chmod 600 .env

Then replace the first four values. <gitlab-token> and <openrouter-api-key> are placeholders for the values of CODEBASE_GITLAB_AUTH_TOKEN and OPENROUTER_API_KEY:

Variable Set it to DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL The URL GitLab can reach DAIV at, without a trailing slash (see Before you start) CODEBASE_GITLAB_URL Your GitLab's URL, as DAIV's containers reach it CODEBASE_GITLAB_AUTH_TOKEN The token of DAIV's GitLab user, from Create a GitLab account for DAIV OPENROUTER_API_KEY Your OpenRouter API key. DAIV reads it once, on the first start; see Provider API keys

Create docker-compose.yml next to it:

YAML
x-daiv: &daiv
  image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv:${DAIV_IMAGE_TAG:-main}
  restart: unless-stopped
  env_file: .env
  environment:
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: daiv.settings.production
    DJANGO_REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    DB_HOST: db
    DB_NAME: daiv
    DB_USER: daiv
    DB_SSLMODE: prefer
    CODEBASE_CLIENT: gitlab
    EMAIL_BACKEND: django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend # (1)!
  volumes:
    - media:/home/daiv/data/media
  ulimits:
    nofile:
      soft: 65536
      hard: 524288

x-background: &background
  <<: *daiv
  healthcheck:
    test: ["CMD-SHELL", "grep -q -e db_worker -e crontask /proc/*/cmdline 2>/dev/null"]
    interval: 30s
  depends_on:
    app:
      condition: service_healthy

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.6
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: daiv
      POSTGRES_USER: daiv
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - db:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U daiv -d daiv"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:8.6-alpine # (2)!
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - redis:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5

  app:
    <<: *daiv
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

  worker:
    <<: *background
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-worker # (3)!

  scheduler:
    <<: *background
    command: sh /home/daiv/start-crontask # (4)!

  sandbox:
    image: ghcr.io/srtab/daiv-sandbox:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    group_add:
      - ${DOCKER_GID}
    environment:
      DAIV_SANDBOX_API_KEY: ${DAIV_SANDBOX_API_KEY}
      DAIV_SANDBOX_EGRESS_CA_CERT_FILE: /home/app/certs/egress-ca.crt
      DAIV_SANDBOX_EGRESS_CA_KEY_FILE: /home/app/certs/egress-ca.key
      DAIV_SANDBOX_REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/3
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock # (5)!
      - ./certs:/home/app/certs:ro

volumes:
  db:
  redis:
  media:
  1. Prints sign-in emails to the app's log instead of sending them, so you need no mail server. Deployment shows how to configure SMTP.
  2. DAIV needs Redis 8 or later: the agent's checkpoints use its search commands, which Redis 7 does not have.
  3. One worker that serves every queue. Deployment splits agent runs and short interactive tasks across two.
  4. Runs DAIV's periodic tasks, among them adding the webhook to your GitLab projects.
  5. The sandbox starts a container for each agent run through the Docker socket.

docs.title: Start DAIV
docs.text:
Start the stack from the directory that holds docker-compose.yml:

Bash
docker compose up -d --wait

The first start pulls about 1.2 GB of images and runs the database migrations; the command returns once every service is healthy, usually within three minutes. If it reports an unhealthy service, docker compose logs app shows why.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Signing in is optional for the first merge request, but the dashboard is where you watch DAIV work.

Sign in over HTTPS or on localhost

DAIV's session cookie, which also carries the CSRF token, is a secure cookie, so a browser keeps it only on https:// URLs and on localhost. Over plain http:// to any other address, sign-in fails with CSRF verification failed. If DAIV runs on another machine, forward the port with ssh -L 8000:localhost:8000 <host> and open http://localhost:8000, or put DAIV behind HTTPS.

  1. Create the first admin with bootstrap_admin, replacing you@example.com with your email address:

    Bash
    docker compose exec app django-admin bootstrap_admin you@example.com

  2. On the DAIV host, open http://localhost:8000/accounts/login/.

  3. Enter that email address.
  4. Select Continue with email.

  5. Read the one-time code from the log:

    Bash
    docker compose logs app | grep -A2 "sign-in code"

  6. Enter the code.

  7. Select Verify & sign in.

docs.title: Connect your GitLab project
docs.text:
DAIV adds a webhook to every project its user maintains within five minutes. To add it now:

  1. Run setup_webhooks:

    Bash
    docker compose exec app django-admin setup_webhooks

  2. In your project, open Settings → Webhooks. It lists <DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL>/api/codebase/callbacks/gitlab/, with <DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL> replaced by your DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL value.

  3. Select Test → Push events. GitLab shows HTTP 204.

docs.title: Get your first merge request
docs.text:
1. In the project, create an issue, for example Add a hello_world() function that returns "Hello, world!".
  2. Add the daiv label to the issue. If the project has no daiv label yet, create it from the label picker.
  3. Wait for the plan. DAIV reacts to the issue with the eyes emoji (👀) within seconds, and posts an implementation plan as a comment, usually within a minute.
  4. Approve the plan with a comment that mentions DAIV's user, for example @daiv proceed.
  5. Wait for the merge request. DAIV implements the plan and opens a merge request, usually within a few minutes. The first run takes longer while the sandbox pulls its image.

See Issue addressing for what else you can do on an issue.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Nothing happens after you add the label The webhook is missing, or GitLab can't reach DAIV_EXTERNAL_URL Run setup_webhooks as in Connect your GitLab project and check that DAIV's user is a Maintainer. Under Settings → Webhooks → Edit → Recent events, GitLab shows each delivery and its error DAIV ignores your comment You commented as DAIV's own user, or didn't mention its username Comment from your own account and mention DAIV's user DAIV comments An unexpected error occurred The run failed docker compose logs worker sandbox shows the error Sign-in fails with Server Error (500) DAIV couldn't send the sign-in email Keep EMAIL_BACKEND as above, or configure SMTP as in Deployment Sign-in fails with CSRF verification failed You opened DAIV over plain HTTP on an address other than localhost See Sign in

docs.title: Remove DAIV
docs.text:
Remove DAIV and everything it stored when you are done with the trial.

This deletes the database

docker compose down -v removes the volumes, including the database volume db: every user, session and setting is lost, and you cannot restore them.

  1. From the directory that holds docker-compose.yml, remove the containers and volumes:

    Bash
    docker compose down -v

  2. Remove the containers the sandbox started:

    Bash
    docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq --filter label=daiv.sandbox.type)

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Deployment — a production install: Docker Swarm, a reverse proxy with HTTPS, email and single sign-on
  • Repository configuration — tune DAIV per repository with .daiv.yml
  • Pull request assistant — mention DAIV on a merge request to get a review or a fix

docs.title: Request Tracker triage
docs.text:
DAIV triages each new Request Tracker (RT) ticket as soon as it is created. The DAIV agent reads the ticket and classifies it as a bug, a configuration issue, a how-to question or unclear. When the ticket is code-related, the agent also runs a root-cause analysis against the queue's repository. DAIV posts the report on the ticket as an internal comment: staff-only, and not emailed to the requester.

The whole integration is a single RT scrip. It needs no bridge service, no webhook receiver and no polling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a ticket is created, RT runs the scrip. The scrip looks up the queue's repository and submits a job to DAIV's jobs API. DAIV's agent then loads the ticket through the RT MCP server, triages it, and posts the report on the ticket through the same server.

Text Only
RT ticket Create
      │
      ▼
RT scrip (Perl, "On Create", applies to allow-listed queues)
   1. Resolve queue → repo_id
   2. Build prompt (ticket id, url, queue, subject)
   3. POST $DAIV_URL/api/jobs
      │
      ▼
DAIV agent runs asynchronously
   - Reads the full ticket via its RT MCP tool
   - Does triage; if code-related, performs RCA against the repo
   - Posts the report as an internal comment on the ticket via RT MCP

The scrip is fire-and-forget. It submits the job with a 5-second socket timeout and a 10-second hard wall-clock ceiling (through alarm), and it traps any die from the HTTP client or the JSON parser in eval. A DAIV outage, including a DNS failure or a malformed response, never blocks or aborts the ticket-create transaction.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A DAIV deployment that the RT host can reach, with the jobs API.
  • The RT MCP server added to DAIV as an MCP server (see Add a server). The RT MCP server must authenticate as an RT user with rights to comment on the target queues. A dedicated daiv-bot RT user keeps the comments clearly attributed.
  • A system default model in DAIV, or an agent_model in the scrip's request. The scrip sends no agent_model, and DAIV refuses a job with 400 when no model is available (see Error responses).
  • A DAIV API key for a dedicated service user, with write access to every repository you map. See Create an API key.

DAIV shows an API key once

The key has the form prefix.secret. Store it when you create it: you cannot retrieve it later.

To create the key from the command line for a service user named rt-triage:

Bash
docker compose exec app django-admin create_api_key rt-triage --name rt-scrip

docs.title: Add the DAIV endpoint and key to RT_SiteConfig.pm
docs.text:
1. Open RT_SiteConfig.pm on the RT host.

  2. Add these lines:

    Perl
    Set($DAIV_URL,     'https://daiv.example.com');
Set($DAIV_API_KEY, 'prefix.secret');

  3. Reload RT, for example with apache2ctl graceful, or whichever reload command your RT host uses.

Replace https://daiv.example.com with your DAIV base URL and prefix.secret with the API key.

docs.title: Install the scrip
docs.text:
1. In the RT web UI, open Admin → Scrips → Create.

  2. Enter these values:

    Field Value Description DAIV triage on create Condition On Create Action User Defined Template Blank Stage TransactionCreate Applies To (leave empty; you set it in Attach the scrip to queues)

  3. In Custom action preparation code, enter return 1;.

  4. In Custom action cleanup code, paste the body of rt-daiv-triage.scrip.pl. Cleanup runs after RT commits the ticket transaction, so the agent can load the new ticket through the RT MCP server.
  5. In the pasted code, edit the %QUEUE_REPO_MAP hash at the top, so that each queue you want triaged maps to its DAIV repo_id, for example group/project.
  6. Leave Custom condition empty.
  7. Save the scrip.

A queue can map to several repositories. To have one agent session work across them, send them as one repos list with "shared_session": true. Without shared_session, each repository runs as a separate job. See Multi-repository sessions.

docs.title: Attach the scrip to queues
docs.text:
The Applies To list and the keys of %QUEUE_REPO_MAP must stay in lockstep. For a queue where the scrip runs but no repository is mapped, the scrip logs a warning and skips the ticket: it changes nothing and submits no job.

Start with a single pilot queue, and add more only after the pilot looks healthy.

  1. In the RT admin UI, open the scrip's Applies To tab.
  2. Select the pilot queue.
  3. Save the change.

docs.title: Verify the pilot
docs.text:
1. File a test ticket in the pilot queue.
  2. Follow the RT log, for example with tail -f /var/log/request-tracker4/rt.log, or your RT log path.

  3. Look for this line:

    Text Only
    daiv-triage: submitted job <uuid> (batch <uuid>) for ticket <id> (queue=... repo=...)

  4. In DAIV, open Sessions and confirm that a new API Run session exists for the target repository.

  5. Wait a minute or two for an internal comment with the triage report to appear on the ticket.

If no comment appears, check the session's detail page: the agent may have failed mid-run, or failed to post through the RT MCP server.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix No log line at all after ticket create The scrip is not attached to the queue, or its condition or stage is wrong Re-check the scrip's Applies To list, and confirm Condition=On Create and Stage=TransactionCreate DAIV_URL or DAIV_API_KEY not set in rt.log RT did not reload RT_SiteConfig.pm Reload RT, for example with apache2ctl graceful queue '<name>' in Applies-To but missing from QUEUE_REPO_MAP Applies To and the inline map drifted apart Add the queue to %QUEUE_REPO_MAP with its repository, or remove it from Applies To failed to submit job … 401 Wrong or expired DAIV API key Create a new key with create_api_key and update RT_SiteConfig.pm failed to submit job … 400 The request names no agent_model, and DAIV has no system default model Set a system default model, or add agent_model to the scrip's request. A model set only in .daiv.yml does not count rate-limited for ticket … 429 (warning) The jobs API rate limit was exceeded Raise the rate (see Rate limiting), or give each queue its own API-key user (see Cost considerations). The scrip logs it at warning, so you can alert on error only failed to submit job … <other non-2xx> DAIV returned a 4xx or 5xx other than a rate limit Check the DAIV sessions list and access log. The log line holds the status line and body exception in triage scrip: daiv-triage timeout The 10-second hard ceiling tripped, usually on DNS resolution or a stalled TLS handshake Check DNS and the network from the RT host to $DAIV_URL, and the certificate chain if you use HTTPS exception in triage scrip: <other> An unexpected die from LWP, the RT ticket object or elsewhere Inspect rt.log around the timestamp: the captured $@ points at the source The job completes in DAIV but the ticket has no comment The RT MCP server's RT user lacks comment rights on the queue, or the MCP call failed Grant that user the CommentOnTicket right on the queue, and inspect the run's tool calls in the session detail

docs.title: Cost considerations
docs.text:
The scrip sends agent_thinking_level: high, which asks for high reasoning effort. This gives better triage and costs more. The scrip sends no agent_model, so the run uses the model DAIV resolves for the repository (see Model overrides). To force the most capable model, also send an explicit agent_model in the scrip. See the request fields of the jobs API.

For high-volume queues:

  • Lower or omit agent_thinking_level in the scrip body for a cheaper first pass.
  • Give each queue its own DAIV API-key user, so one busy queue cannot use up another's allowance. The jobs API applies one site-wide rate to each user separately, and you cannot set it lower for one user (see Rate limiting).

docs.title: Files
docs.text: • rt-daiv-triage.scrip.pl: the scrip body to paste.

docs.title: Agent tools
docs.text: DAIV's agent works through tools: it reads and edits files, runs commands, searches the web and reports back on your git platform. This page lists each tool, when the agent has it, and which settings turn it on or off. The agent is built on Deep Agents and runs on LangGraph.

docs.title: Tools bound up front
docs.text:
DAIV binds these tools to the model at the start of every run.

Tool What it does When the agent has it ls, read_file, glob, grep List directories, read files, find files by pattern and search file contents by regular expression Always write_file, edit_file Create a file, or change an existing one Always bash Run a command in the persistent, isolated sandbox, after the command policy checks it When the run has a sandbox. How an environment is resolved says when it has one. write_todos Track the steps of a task Always skill Run a skill Always task Hand work to a subagent Always ask_user_question Ask you 1 to 4 questions and end the turn, and your answer arrives as the next message On the main agent only, and not on a run nobody can answer: a scheduled run, a pipeline watch run or a delegated job. Answer a question shows it from your side. delegate_jobs Start independent jobs on other repositories or on the same one, and resume when they finish When orchestration is on, which is the default, and the run is not a delegated leg

docs.title: Tools loaded on demand
docs.text:
The agent loads these tools through tool_search, a tool that finds a tool by what it does and loads its definition. This keeps the list of tools the model sees short. A tool the agent loads stays available for the rest of the session. Setting DEFERRED_TOOLS_ENABLED to false binds every tool up front instead; Deferred tools describes it and its related settings.

Tool What it does When the agent has it gitlab Inspect and update issues, merge requests, pipelines, job logs and releases On a GitLab repository gh The same, through the gh command line On a GitHub repository web_search Search the web through DuckDuckGo, Tavily or SearXNG When web search is on, which is the default. Web search describes the settings. web_fetch Fetch a URL, convert it to Markdown and answer a prompt about its content When web fetch is on, which is the default. Web fetch describes the settings. publish_artifact Copy a workspace file, such as an HTML report, a CSV or a chart, into DAIV as an artifact and return its viewer URL. With artifact_id, it replaces the file of an artifact the session already published. Always fetch_artifact Copy an artifact the session already published back into /workspace/tmp, so the agent can revise it Always check_delegated_jobs, cancel_delegated_jobs Check, or cancel, the jobs the agent delegated When delegate_jobs is available MCP tools The tools of the MCP servers the run has, such as Sentry or Context7 When an MCP server is enabled for the run

docs.title: Model priority
docs.text: The agent runs on the first model that a source sets, from a model you pick for the run, through the daiv-max issue label and the repository's .daiv.yml, to the site's settings. Model overrides lists the order. A subagent follows its own order, described in Subagent model precedence, and Environment variables lists the settings.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: DAIV's /code-review is measured on ReviewBench, an open benchmark of real pull requests. Each pull request comes with a human-reviewed golden set of known issues. This page reports a baseline measured on 2026-10-27 at commit d3f513a56, how it was measured, and what it does not tell you.

docs.title: Code review on ReviewBench
docs.text: Benchmark The ReviewBench test set: 25 pull requests from 25 repositories, 352 known issues Reviewer The /code-review skill as merged in #1711, run at d3f513a56, on Claude Haiku 5.5 (anthropic:claude-haiku-5-5) with thinking level xhigh Judge Claude Sonnet 5.5, as ReviewBench's matcher and classifier Runs One pass over all 25 pull requests, on 2026-10-27

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Precision and recall are macro averages: every pull request weighs the same.

Metric Result Grounded precision 92.1% Grounded recall 44.6% Augmented precision 88.9% Augmented recall 58.6% Known issues found 150 of 352

The review reported 301 findings. 125 matched a known issue, 136 matched none but the judge classified them as valid (novel true positives), and 40 were false positives. One finding can match more than one known issue, so known issues found (150) is higher than matched findings (125).

docs.title: Recall by category and severity
docs.text:
Known issues found out of all known issues in that category or severity, pooled over the 25 pull requests rather than averaged per pull request.

Category Known issues Found Recall Correctness 133 63 47.4% Reliability 58 32 55.2% Maintainability 44 7 15.9% Testing 35 13 37.1% Security 27 15 55.6% Documentation 21 5 23.8% API architecture 12 4 33.3% Performance 12 9 75.0% Accessibility 10 2 20.0% Severity Known issues Found Recall High 36 21 58.3% Medium 134 79 59.0% Low 182 50 27.5%

The weak spots are low-severity issues, maintainability and documentation.

docs.title: Cost and time
docs.text:
Cost, all 25 reviews $7.75, about $0.31 per review Cost per review From $0.05 to $1.47 Time per review 8.3 minutes on average, 20.3 at most

Cost is the model usage of the review agent and its detectors, priced by DAIV's usage tracking at Anthropic's list prices. It does not include the judge or the sandbox.

docs.title: How it was measured
docs.text:
Review. evals/reviewbench.py fetches each pull request's base and head from its ReviewBench mirror and runs /code-review on the head in a DAIV sandbox. The network is off and the reviewer has no MCP servers and no web tools, because the upstream pull request's review comments are a source of the golden set. The driver writes the findings in ReviewBench's judging format.

Judging. ReviewBench's judge compares the findings with the golden set. A matcher model pairs each finding with the known issues it describes. A classifier model labels each finding the matcher left unmatched as valid or a false positive. Both ran on Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Grounded and augmented. Grounded metrics count only the golden set. Grounded precision looks only at findings matched to a golden-set entry: the share whose entry is a known issue rather than one the golden set labels a false positive. Grounded recall is the share of known issues found. Augmented metrics also count the classifier's verdicts on unmatched findings. Augmented precision is the share of all findings that are valid, and augmented recall adds the novel true positives to both the found and the total. ReviewBench's methodology defines all four.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• 25 pull requests. The test set is a sample of the 219-pull-request full set, which DAIV has not been measured on.
  • One pass. Results move between identical runs. Two identical runs on the 14 smaller pull requests found 70 and 67 known issues, with single pull requests moving by up to 3.
  • An LLM judge. The judge model changes the scores. On the same findings, Sonnet 5.5 counted 32 false positives where Sonnet 5 counted 17.
  • Augmented recall grows with the reviewer's own findings. Its denominator includes the reviewer's novel true positives, so ReviewBench recommends grounded recall for comparing reviewers.
  • One reviewer configuration. Only Claude Haiku 5.5 at xhigh was measured on this version of the skill. Other models will score differently.
  • One retried pull request. jadx took three attempts: the driver rejected the first report because it lacked the ## Code Review heading, and the second review skipped the skill. The third is the one scored. The first two cost $0.13, which is not in the cost above.

Not a leaderboard result

This is an offline run. The ReviewBench leaderboard scores all 219 pull requests three times through its own portal, judged by Claude Sonnet 5. These numbers are not a leaderboard submission and are not comparable with leaderboard entries.

docs.title: Experiment log and reproducing
docs.text:
The experiment log lists each measured change to the code-review skill with its result and verdict, the changes that were dropped included. The baseline files hold the findings, the judge's scores per finding and the usage per agent.

To reproduce the run, follow How to run: start a local DAIV stack, run evals/reviewbench.py on the 25 pull requests, then score the findings with ReviewBench's npm run judge on Claude Sonnet 5.5.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
This page lists the environment variables DAIV reads, with the default and an example for each. Use it to find the variable for a setting, or to check a default you rely on.

In the tables, marks a sensitive variable (an API key, password or token) that you should provide as a Docker secret or from a secure credential manager, and marks a variable you must set.

Site configuration can change many of these settings at runtime. A variable that has a Site Configuration field overrides the stored value and locks the field; How environment variables and the UI interact gives the order. Variables marked env-only have no field there. The provider API key variables are a different case: DAIV reads them once, as LLM providers explains.

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
Variable Description Default Example DJANGO_DEBUG Toggle Django debug mode False True DJANGO_SECRET_KEY Secret key for Django (none) super-secret-key DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS Comma-separated list of allowed hosts * example.com,localhost DJANGO_SESSION_COOKIE_NAME Name of the session cookie; give each instance on one host its own __Secure-sessionid __Secure-sessionid-1

DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS limits the hosts that can reach DAIV. The default * allows any host, so list the host DAIV runs on to restrict it.

Warning

Do not turn on DJANGO_DEBUG in production. It exposes sensitive information and breaks the security of the application.

Warning

Keep DJANGO_SECRET_KEY stable and backed up. Unless you set DAIV_ENCRYPTION_KEY, DAIV derives the key that encrypts stored secrets from it, so a lost or changed DJANGO_SECRET_KEY makes every stored secret unreadable. See External URL and encryption key.

docs.title: Time zone
docs.text: DAIV runs in the Europe/Lisbon time zone. It is fixed in the settings and is not a variable. A time you give without an offset, such as a schedule's run time or the value of create_api_key --expires-at, is read in that zone. Add an offset, for example +00:00, to give a time in another zone.
